GRANDMOTHER'S KNITTING.

Grandmother sits in her easy chair, With wrinkled forehead and silver hair, Knitting and counting stitch after stitch, Musing or dreaming you know not which; Perhaps she's thinking of bright days fled, Joys that have vanished, hopes that are dead. When a simple child by the home fireside, Her mother's darling, her hope and pride; Or tripping lightly over the lawn, To sorrow and care alike unknown; A pretty blue-eyed winsome thing, Bright as the flowers that deck the spring. Then a maiden fair on the village green, Chosen to be the first May Queen; An ardent lover clues by her side, Waiting to make her his fur young bride; Sweet, happy moments too bright to stay, Yet fresh to the mind as if yesterday. Then a loving wife, 'mid the busy throng, Hoping and trusting, brave and strong, Fighting life's battles day after day, As years move onward and pass away; Till weak and feeble and worn at last, She sits and waits and dreams of the past; Knitting, knitting, silently sitting. Round after round, knitting, knitting.
BEN. SAWDON.
J. 11. ECCLES.

"TELL THE WIFE."—.I woman's advice is generally worth having; so if you are in any trouble tell year mother, or roar wife, or sister, all about ie. Be assured that light will flesh upon your derknees. Women are toe commonly adjudged verdant in all hat purely womanish affairs. No philosophical students of the sex thus jadge them. Their intnitions, or insights, are the most subtle. I advise a man to keep none of his affairs- a secret from his wife. Many a home has been happily K!tved, and many a fortune retrieved, by a man's fall confidence in hie wife. Woman is far more eetrand prophet than a men, if she be given a fair chanceel As a- general rule, the wives confide the minuteet of their plane and thoughts to their husbands. Tter, Hatt OF Xenanee.—The_most remarkable buildings an the Pereepoliten platform (which vanes in height from twenty to fo,tv-live feet) are two great pitlared halls—one called the Hall of a Hundred. Columns, the other the H all of Xerxes The roof of the or ler is believed to have been suppoqed by a hue-'fed pl. ar, e with sixteen additional in 1 the porch ; and the effect ot the whole, when the structure i was perfect, nau:,t have been extremly noble, though some. what wanting in height. Sculptures depicting the monarch surrounded by his oten•at-artne, or by figures supposed to 1 represent natives of the sveral Persian provinces, appear in various parts of this stately building; and the vast chamber was lighted by fifteen wirdows, perhaps also by apertures in the roof. The hall of Xemes, though contain- ino only forty columns (a number indicated by the native appellation of the building, the aehl Minors-), is far more magnificent than the hundred-pillared edifice. It has been , remarked by a great modern authority on such subjects that ' ne English cathedral at all approaches the Hall of Xerxes ia dimensions, and that neither in France nor Germany is there one that covers so much ground.—From "Cassell's _lllustrated ET,iversal History" for February. PitEic cPAL lIIINTEa's WITTY Wire.—St. Andrews has still floating in its social atmosphere many a queint story of her characteristic humour. I gather from his notes here that she was often troubled with moods of depression and gloom, but the tales told of her only suggest a bright, odd, witty spirit, saying the drollest things in the simplest way, and even when cutting meet deep, giving somehow no no ground of offence, no ground for anything but large mirth and laughter. What could be neater than her reply to a pert coxcomb who had bored her at the dinner-teble,and at last informed her that he was just starting for China? "Oh na, my man," she answered, "ye maunna gang there; they tell me they eat puppies there* When her eldest son, John, was an infant, she-saw some ladies coming evidently to pay her a visit, and turning to the housemaid, she said, "There's the Misses So-and-so; they'll want to see the bairn, and he's a perfect fricht Rin down, lassie, and get a loan o' the baker's wean; he's aye clean, and they'll be sure to say he's the vera image o' his tether." Her husband, Professor of Hebrew in St Andrews, was a pleasant com- panion at the social gatherings in the old university town, bat seems to have been somewhat quiet and undemonstra- tive at his own fireside. When some one therefore was praising his qualities as a boon companion to her. "0 ay," she said, "he's like some other folk, and hangs his fiddle up at his sin door cheek, for we-never hear scrape of it"— " JOHN HUNTER OF CRAIGCROOK," in "Good Words." INTELLIGENCE ter BIEDS.—The correspondent of a North- country contemporary writes :—A gentleman, who was at .me time schoolmaster at Fenwick, by Beal, had a pied rook, which he took from a nest in Kyloe Plantation. This bird could talk very distinctly, followed the good lady of the house wherever she went; and seemed to understand every word she said to it, just about as well as if it had belonged tothe genus horno. Bat the most'remarkable bird that ever came under the writer's notice was a bullfinch kept by a friend of his who resided at Haagerstone. This bird when young was taken from a nest in Fenwiek Wood, and, strange to say, its trainer was a totally blind man. He, however, not only fedit, but anon taught it to whistle 20/Id9 toneg with great accuracy. The "Keel Row" was its masterpiece which it could whistle with the utmost exactness. It haii eta. hai . • .. _ aterty oa ...e ..ouse ante door, anu never attempted to escape. Indeed it would not allow it cage door to re- main shut: but would turn the Fire catch with its bill? and, I open the door as soon as ever left to itself. It svaa passion- 1 ately attached to its master, and seemed =hippy when he was out of the house. When from home for a few days to -1 gether, as he had occasionally to be, the bird seldom left his cage, and never chimed a note daring his absence; but the moment he entered the door it struck up the "Keel Row," flew at him, perched upon his shoulder or head, and ex- hibited many evident signs of joy. When at home the bird was constantly hopping about him, or flying gaily fromtone piece of furniture to another, and whistling his favourite tune. "Where is Bally ?" my friend would say, and im- mediately the bird .would perch upon his arm, shoulder, or head, and sing out "Here." "Bully, go to the door and call that dog in," his Master would say, and Bully at once flew to the door and whistled so exactly in imitation of his master that the dog did not know the difference' but came running in, wagging his tail, and crouching down behind his master, believing that his master and not the bird had called him in. But Bully also knew the tread of his master's foot, . ad his knock at the door. No matter what time of night my friend went home, and he was sometimes late, and would sometimes tap on the door or window to see if the bird would recognise him, the bird at once commenced to sing lustily, and flew to him the moment he entered the house. My friend kept this bird for five or sia years, and had several times been offered a large sum of money for it, but he would not sell it.

TII6' INTERESTS OF THE "SITTING" TENANT.—At a re- cent meeting of the farmers' Alliance, Mr. J. Howard said he attached fourfold importance te securing what the Scotch called the sitting tenant azairist his rent being raised upon his own improvemente than he did to compensating the out going tenant for his improvements, because the former would affect nineteen timea as many tenants as the provi• sion for compensating the outgoing tenant. He said he would not walk across the floor of the House of Commons to pass a bill of tenant-right which did ant secure the tenantry of the kingdom against the injustice of their liability to rents being raised after years of outlay to increase the fer- tility of the soil. MGR FARMING IN T.',TORFOLIC—The great consumption of cake and other artificial foods in Norfolk is the key to our successful agriculture. On the best managed farms in the county as much money is spent under this head as amounts to the 'rents; whilst, taken in the aggregate, the number of tons consumed is enormous. Under such a system it is no wonder that in a kind season oar wheats cast from five to seven quarters per acre on the best lands. Wesan cite in- stances where, in the neighbourhood from which we write, 12 and 14 sacks of wheat per acre have this year been grown. Never would it have proved so had not the tenants previously spent a great sum in the purchase of cake or some equivalent. It may be questioned by some of our readers whether high farming pays in these times of low prices. We reply, if it does not, low farming never will. Nothing helps a man so much in bridging t ver the bad times as em- ploying a large outlay of capital, keeping it well used in carrying a heavy head of stock, and by this means endea- vouring to retain the soil in its highest state of productive- ness.—Agricultural Gazette. IMPORTANT SUGGESTIONS FOR FARMERS.—The first of a series of papers by Professor Custance has been published by the Agricultural College of South Australia. He recom- mends that farmers should individually try a few simple experiments embracing the following inquiries :—How far the soil of his farm may- be improved by a certain process, or by the application ot a certain substance as manure. How his crops may be increased in quantity, improved in quality, protected from this or that insect, or from this or that form of blight. What manure ought to be given to a particular crop on that particular farm, the beet way of destroying in- sects, iSzc. Fox HUNTERS.—Mr. Joseph Smith, of Chesterton, Ciren- ceater, writes as follows to the Wilts and Gloucester Stan- dard :—" A short time since the V. W. H. Hounds brought a fox across my farm, which ran through a field adjoining my sheep (ewes in lamb). One gentleman threw the gate open, and left it open, rode right through the sheep in the pen, and drove them in all directions. Some of the sheep jumped the hurdles, others were not able to do so. One very fine ewe died two days after, with three fine lambs. Here was a loss of one ewe and three lambs, through sheer thoughtlessness, and I may say more than that. I think gentlemen who delight in hunting should be more careful, and not ride through sheep pens or near to sheep, at this time of the year particularly." GEEALT REDUCTION Or Th.flNT.—Whlt will the landlords sty to this? At the la,t meeting of the -Colchester Town Council it was aenounced tnat the Corporation had agreed to lease a farm of between 300 and 400 acres, at the rental of one shilling per acre for two years, and for a third year at £1 an acre. The farm includes some excellent land, there is a good dwell ing.house attached, and a capital market to be had in Colchester, only two ar three miles distant. S:tveral members of the Council rubbed their eyes in astonish- ment when the terms of the lease were read out; and it was I suggested that the newspapers should be asked not to pub- lish the facts, lest the tenants on other portions of the Cor- poration estate should use up in arms and the landlords in the district be ruined, But it was explained that there could be no secrecy in such a matter, as the facts were sure to leak out. Besides it was made evident that the Council had obtained the very best terms possible, and that a prac- tical farmer having been secured as a tenant, the lease, in the present depressed st tte of agriculture, might be consi- dered rather favourable than otherwise. Thera are many farinS in the district which cannot be let at any price, and one member of the Council said there were several land- lords near Colchester who would be glad to get tenants on the above terms. No opposition was offered to the lease, but some of the councillors clearly thought its publication would greatly disgust neighboutitig landlords.

EMILY Laanamo.—The lambing or yeaning season takes place at very different seasons of the year, accordiog to dis- trict and race. In South Hants, Dorset, and the hie of Wight, lambs are looked for in September, an d are fit for the butchers by Christmas. This extreme earliness is an idiosyncrasy of the Dorset horned sheep, and is not shared by our other races. Probably the next in order of earliness is the Hampshire Down. Ewes of this breed will occasion- ally drop lambs in November, and there is no difficulty in "arranging" a fall of lambs about Christmas Day. Ram breeders prefer their ewes to lamb down early in January, and breeders of wether lambs prepare for yeaning three or four weeks later. The greater proportion of the Hampshire Down flocks of Hants and Wilts are now in the midst of this critical period. On the Cotswolds, February is more pro- perly the yeaning month, but there Cotswold breeders do not bring out their young rams as lambs, but as shearlings, and have a year longer to bring them to perfection. March is the month in which according to popular notions young lambs are first to be seen skipping in the meadows and usher- ing in the spring. In the North of England about the 20th of that month is considered to be a good time to commence, while further north, among the mountains and the black- faced sheep of the Scotch moors, April and May are soon enough for the lambs to encounter the troubles of early life. Thus, like wheat -growing, lambing, taken as a whole, ex- tends over a large proportion of the year, accord ing to cir- cumstances of soil and race. Perhaps nothing would more Etrike and please a North Country farmer than to visit a flock of some 1,000 or 1,200 ewes on Salisbury Plain, near the sacred precincts of Stonehenge, or the time-worn rennin; of Old Sarum. Such a visit paid now would afford a more fascio.ting object of contemplation to him than he r.l.stry and skill. He of Drniciical supeig,;:l,9ll 9r 11119.naslic would flncl most ot i'wes through their trouble, and ac tOmpanied by their offspring, in well sheltered and littered folds, picturesquely placed in the midst of vivid green turnip fields, RESlkEtiig ON MILS.—An address on this subject was de- livered by Dr. Augustus Voelcker, F.R.S., February 1, at the conclusion of the business of the Council. Dr. Voelcker said, with regard to the results of the milking trials at the last Dairy Show, the statistics showed that quantity and quality were very frequently separated. In several in- stances a large quantity of Milk gave also a large quantity of butter fat. One shorthorn cow gave 451 b. Noz. of milk in the morning and evening milkings, with a percentage of 507 of pure butter fat. The general results from the short- horn cows were highly satisfutory, and as he regarded the animal in the light et a manufacturer into milk of the food that was given to her, it appeared very clear to him that the better the food given to cows and the larger and better would be the produce in milk. The variations in richness he ascribed to the quality of the food, and he had proved this by experiments. He had found that a cow would pro- duce milk in six hours from the food given her, and by com- paring the results with the variety of the food, he had found that the most nutritious and digestible foods produced the most butter fat, and that a rapid improvement irr the quality immediate followed improved feeding. In the selection of food, he placed bean or pea meal in the first rank of all the nitrogenous foods, and lentil meal next. Of cakes, he con- sidered the decorticated cotton cake superior to all other kinds, and a most valuable food. He strongly recommended its use for grass-fed cows, and pointed out that the grass

Of roots, he considered mangels the best, but where ro )ts were difficult to obtain, and were dear, malt combings, infused with warm water and mixed with hay or chaff, proved a good and inexpensive substitute. The points he wished to urge were that good feeding was economical feed- ing, and that much more depended upon the food that was given to the cow than on the animal itself, but at all times alloNiug that good animals could only come from careful selection. Upon the question of skimming no ilimbt could possibly exist that mechanical skimming was immeasurably superior to hand skimming, and he trusted that before long a satisfactory separator would be manufactured which could be worked by horse or hand power. A saving of 25 per cent. of cream can be effected by the separator, and from the experiments made at the Dairy Show of 1831 with the im- proved Laval separator, he was fully satisfied that the above result would be obtainable.-

"Never in the history of the State," says a Topeka corre- spondent of the Chicago Tribune, "has the wheat looked so healthy and promising at this time of the year as now. The reports from every county are unanimous as to its rank, growth, and prime condition in all respects. In Cumberland the wheat plant never looked more pro- mising at this time of year; in some cases, perhaps, it may be a little too forward, but that will he remedied by turning sheep on later to crop the too luxuriant blades. The pas- tures generally present a better appearance than they usually do in April. The lambing season has commenced in the low- lands, and under auspicious circumstances. Grass being plentiful, should the weather continue for any length of time, flock masters will not be pat to such a heavy expense with their ewes as has been the case for a few previous years.

If this consolidation of authorities and rates can be ac- complished, it will save the vast sum which is nOw being wasted annually in the salaries of unnecessary officials. An instance of the benefit of such a reform occurred in Man, cbester not many years ago, and Sir Joseph Heron, the Town Clerk, writing in 1874, said that £3,000 per annum had been thereby saved, A wide dissemination of the information Contained in Pi:, last publication of the Cobden Club, viz., "Local Govern- ment and Taxation in the United Kingdom," which comes to hand as these lines are penned, will do much to educate the nation as to the need for Reform and Retrenchment.

As to Railway Rates, a few cases mentioned by Professor Hunter, that wet e brought in evidence before the Railway Committee (which was appointed by the House of Commons, and sat during several months of the last session of Parlia- ment) will give some idea of the importance of the subject. The railway companies make a difference of a most de- cided character in the charge for goods or cattle when they are of foreign produce as compared with home cultivation. For instance, if a truck of cattle is sent from Newcastle to Manchester the railway company do not;inquire the weight of the cattle, but whether they are foreign or home cattle. If they are foreign they charge them for the truck £2 9s. 9d., but if they are home cattle the charge is £3 13s. 6d. American meat can be brought from Chicago to Manchester as cheaply as it can be from Limerick to Manchester, al- • though from Limerick to-Manchester the distance is only 300 miles, while in the case of Chicago the meat has to travel about 1,000 or 1,200 miles on the American railway, besides having to come over the Atlantic. The charge to bring a ton of batter from New York to Manchester is 53. less than the charge from Limerick. It is therefore clear that foreign produce is carried ata cheaper rate than home produce. Many other instances could be given, but the above are quite sufficient to show that it is a question of great importance, and farmers would do well to make them- selves acquainted with such subjects, and bring pressure to bear on their Parliamentary representatives.

div.head: "ALTERNATIVE SYSTEM" IN FARMING.
div.p: THE "ALTERNATIVE SYSTEM" IN FARMING.

Must farmers continue to cultivate land at a loss instead of at a fair remuneration for capital, skill, and labour? To this question we said "No" in 1879, and we say "No" still. The British public is prepared to spend annually some thirty millions sterling with farmers, at present paid to foreign producers for meat, poultry, butter, eggs, milk, and some other articles, exclusive of corn, that might profitably be reared, grown, or made at home, on the very farms, by use of the very same buildings, and cultivated by the very same tenants now in possession. Encouraged by the great favour with which our recommendations were received in 1879, and again last year, we would once more bring promi- nently before our friends the method which, now that it is rapidly coming into use, we venture to call our " Alterna- tive System." "Grass is king," say even the American farmers, although their cornfields produce sixty million quarters of wheat, two hundred million quarters of maize, besides barley and oats. And in these islands, which seldom now give us twelve million quarters of wheat, it may be ex- pected tbat the "King shall have his own again," and grass recover the acreage which was yielded up to grain crops in the early part of the century. At one time it was thought anyone could manage grass land—that, in fact, it managed itself, and this mischievous creed did serious harm through past generations of farmers, most of whom believed they were doing justice to their land and to themselves when they devoted pains and skill solely to their arable acres. But it should be remembered that pasture crops suffer quite as much from weedets do arable ones. In either case weeds are eVer robbers, and should be treated as such. Had pas- toral band ry received one half of the Care, botanic 4 re, liC4 search, and fostering devolopment that have been devoted to tillage operations and arable fertilisation, the pastures of this country 'would be producing thirty per cent, more keep. If half the mechanical ingenuity and inventive power had been given to the saving and harvesting of forage and hay crops that have been lavished on threshing machines, &c.; we should no lotwer be doubtful as to the best means of sav- ing the hay and clover crops, instead of seeing then Lunged to the extent of forty or fifty per cent. Nor would it have been reserved for the year 1882 to be marked by a prize being offered for the best means of drying and saving grass. But the country is awake at last, and important advances have been made in the setection of seeds suitable te soil and climate, and in the processes of laying down land to pasture, as well as in the cultivation of artificial grimes alternately with roots and corm _

. _ What turnips did kr 'Yorkshire, our "Alternative System" may 'de expected to accomplish for all England. Crop rota- tion has done very much in the past for English husbandry, making it the cleanest and most productive agriculture in the world, and although the -cry for freedom of cultivation is natural at such a painful crisis, it is not license and free- dom from system which is needed, but such a change as the :iltered circumstances dearand. However valuable the rota- tion Poinptta iFsih; [iAii have been, it ievhiont diffazent and fresh results are required to meet ale present conditions ct the agricultural world. As simple cereal cultivation has ceased to pay, our "Alternative System" of grass, rocts, and corn affords good promise to the farmer. In trn.th success is fairly assured in several directions—a crop 2,t least three years out of four, a near market fo3 the prciduce, and the early prospect of a simple process that tvill make hay "always good alike," and that notwithstag the weather. This system means growing a marketal*a commodity at a 1 remunerative price, where wheat, (to., under foreign com- petition, has lost its profitable market. It rears stock for meat, butter, and milk close to centres of demand, instead of growing grain that finds its sale challenged on its own local exchanges by samples drawn from many parts of the world. •

Quite apart from the need there is on every farm for a certain proportion of tfie, best permanent pasture (which, if not in existence, can only be formed at scme considerable expense), our present object is to urge the importance of having a large portion of. every farm sown with artificial grasse?, which shall remain down from two to four years, and produce very heavy cops of hayeand feed dearinee the term chosen. If grass thus comes to be looked upon as the principal crop, instead of a mere incident in a four or six course rotation, then little more corn and roots will in future be grown than the large head of stock will require for win- ter consumption. This " Alternative System" we conceive to be the real alliance of pastcral and arable husbandry, and the need of the present day. We contend that this reystem ensures the formation of a great reserve of fertility in the land, o that in case of any national emergency, by putting the land again into wheat, a sudden demand for grain could be met in a single year. Hence the production of wheat may safely be left to the foreigner while he is able and will- ing to deliver it to us at prices at which it will not pay us to produce it on the spot. It means such a resting and con- ditioning of the hard cropped and impoverished soil as it has long been needing. „It means also a large increase in our flocks and herds, and much greater attention being given to breeding, rearing, and fattening stock after more natural methcds than at present. It means, further, the reduction of the labour bill by a third or even one-half. And, as a crowning advantage, this "Alternative System" permits the lucrative manufacture, by consumption en the farm of the late-priced produce there grown into high-priced articles such as grass-fed meat, milk, and cream, which are now comparative luxuries, but which are long will become neces- saries that all classes in England will increasingly demand. —Franz Sutton's Farmer's Year-Book and Grazier's Manual for 1882.

THE 00ZE FROSI THE ATLANTIC FLOOR.—Previous to the laying down of the first cable which united the Old World to the New, it was deemed advisable to make a pre- liminary survey of the ocean floor upon which the cable was to repose, extending between Ireland and Newfound- land. In the course of the survey samples of the mud lying upon the sea floor were dredged from the bottom, and sub. mitted to Drs. Ehrenberg and Huxley for examination. This mad was found to be actually a whitish or grayish matter, not unlike thick cream in general appearanco. It is known to the sailors as ooze a word derived from the Anglo-Saxon term souse, mud, and familiar to most of us as the this of some of the more sluggish mud-bearing rivers of England. When dried, it hardens into a soft mass, not un- like chalk in outward appearance; while, like chalk again, it is composed almost entirely of carbonate of lime. Not only did the dried ooze resemble chalk in chemical composi- tion and outward appearance, but there was another and most important respect in which the great investigators we have named found the ancient chalk and this modern de- posit to be identical. When a small quantity of the ooze was placed under a microscope, it was 11 oticed at a glance that it was filled with the peculiar bodies so abundant in a slice of chalk. Here, then, it was immediately acknow- ledged, a substance wasilleing laid down upon the sea-bot- tom at the present day which might eventually be consoli- dated into a rock identical with chalk, and laid down, too, over an area as enormous as that covered by the chalk it- self- and at the same time, like the chalk, preserving the same general characteristics everywhere within that area. The chalk formation ought henceforth to be regarded as a consolidated deep-sea ooze, which must have been laid down upon the floor of an ancient Atlantic that once overspread the western half of the Old World, from Britain to the flindoo Koosh.—Science for All.

div.head: LAND QUESTION.
div.p: THE LAND QUESTION.
XXI.

To some people the above subjects may appear dryi:and uninteresting, but they are nevertheless highly important, are inseparably connected with the Land Question, and are now in the very fore-front of our igattical politics. This is evidenced from 1.0 iact that the Queen's Speech stated that ea CAtifii3trunerit propose during the present Session to ZStablish in English and Welsh. counties local self-govern- ment, similar to that which has been so long enjoyed by the towns, together with enlarged powers of administration, and with financial changes which will give an opportunity of considering, both as to town and country, what may be the proper extent and the most equitable and provident form of contribution from imperial taxes in relief of local charges It would be impossible in the short space of a single article to do more than glance at the above subjects, but we will endeavour to do so in as simple and clear a manner as possible. The principal objects of local government are the preser- vation of peace and order, the education of the people, the relief of the poor, the erection and maintenance of public buildings, lunatic asylums, halls, and libraries; the making, paving, and lighting of roads and streets; the repairing of bridges; the regulation of markets, hackney coaches, and public carriages; the laying down of rules for preserving the public health, and convenience, &c. The money required for these purposes is raised by levying rates. Every person who is not exempted by extreme poverty, or some privileges, which need net be particularised, is rated. according to the value of the premises which he occupies. The sum required for the rate is estimated, and each Labia person is called upon to pay his portion. When it is said, therefore, of a poor, or any other rate, that it is one shilling in the pound, it means that for every pound at which a per- son is rated, according to the value of his house or property, he has to pay that sum. What is the position of local government to-day in this country? There is no higher or more reliable authority on the subject than Mr. Go3chen, and but a few years ago he. said, " We have a chaos as regards authorities, a chaos as regards rates, and a worse chaos than all as regards areas." In confirmation, and as a farther illustration, afew extracts from a Memorandum by Messrs. Rathbone and Whitbread, two highly-respected M.P.'s, will give more in detail some idea of the confusion which exists. They say " The in- habitant of a borough lives in a fourfold area for purposes of local government ; viz., in a borough, in a parish, in a union, and in a county. None of these are conterminous (unless by accident) with any of the others, and different parts of the borough are or may be in different parishes, and in different unions, and in different counties; He is, or may be, governed by a sixfold authority—the council, the vestry, the burial board, the school board, the guardians, and the county quarter sessions; all these ars different bodies, ana inhabitants of different parts of the same t orou?,h are or may be under' different vestries, burial boards, guardians, and county quarter sessions. He is, or may be, subject to a borough rata, a general district rate, a poor rate, a burial rate, and a county rate. The inhabitant of a local board district also lives in four kinds of districts--the local board district, the parish, the union, and the county. He also is, or may be, under six governments, the local board, the vestry, the union, the burial board, the quarter sessions, and the school hoard. And any of these distritts or authorities except the local board and its district, may be different for inhabitants of different parts of the same local board dis- trict. The inhabitant of a rural parish lives in a parish, in a union, probably in a highway district, and in a county. He is, or may be, governed by a vestry, a school board, a burial hoards a highway board, the gaatdiauis, and the ins-, tices."
Such is our present system of local govarnment, and its very recital reads more like the chapter about Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, than a simple statement of well. known fact%

While. lttaiever, the local government of our borQtrghs, as well as of our country districts, is equally open tO the charge of being not only confusing but very unnecessarily expen- sive, the former is free from many of the obiections to be found in the rural districts. The local self-government which exists in towns has educated the people in self- government, and to take a real and lively interest in how public money is spent, and the feeling that they have a voice and a vote in the election of the local authorities, causes them to feel that they have a stake in the town they live in. On the other hand, what do the inhabitants of a country village know of local affairs? A short review of "the powers that he" in country districts will supply t,'," answer. The hiehest functionary in each county is tthe Lord- Lieutenant, who in the English counties is alweh4,,s a peer, a great landowner, and the possessor of a lar:se park. With 1 this dignitary virtually rests the eltit-a.ctott tea° shall be the! magistrates for his oPre'Llt-7! `as he recoameilds the names of those he thinks at f. 7.) the Lord Chancellor, who really ap- points then. on behalf of the Crown. Mr. Arthur Arnold , writn--" If a man cheose to invest --C20,000 in a landed es-1 estate, and is a person el fair character, he has no difficulty, especially if he he a Churchman, and is not vehemently op- posed to the political policy of the Lord-Lieutenant, in ob- taining for his name a place upon the Commission of the Peace." These megistrates are members of the Quarter Sessiont, ex•officio members of Boards of Guardians and other bodiate, and have very considerable local power and influence. As constituting the Quarter Sessions they have the super- vision of the county-ga.ole, the county police, and county • lunatic asylums, subject to the Home Office. They also regulate county finance and taxation, subject to the Local Government Board. In these capacities they have the spending of large sums which are collected from the rate- payers as poor rates. According to a return which has just been issued, it would appear at the present time that out of £13,000,000 collected in England for poor rates the follow- ire, sums were disbursed :—.-C3,000.000 to police authorities, £lOOO,OOO for highways, 1.1.20,000 for sanitary purposes, £560,000 for education, £91,000 for registration, £87,000 for vaccination, £Ol,OOO for Parliamentary and municipal regis- trations. Of course a large amount of this applies to boroughs, &c., but a considerable portion represents an ex- penditure entirely in the hands of the county magistrates. Now these gentlemen, who thus have the control oi county finance and taxation are not responsiele to or elected by the ratepayers who find the money, hut as before mentioned only to the Home Office or Local Government Board in London. But what is the influence or the effect of the social position of those rural magnates "the Squires," even in those districts where there is some attempt at local go- vernment. The Squire is often a little king in his own dis- trict, .he only rich or great man. The clergyman, who is like Joseph, the second after Pharoah, is usaally his nomi- nee, and often his relative. The farmers are yearly tenants, and perhaps a bit behind with their rents, and the few local shopkeepers are also the tenants of the great man, and their policy naturally is not to cross him. The labourers live in his cottages, and are glad to keep in with the bailiff or steward for wcrk or favours. As a landowner and a magis- trate the Squire is well nigh omnipotent. It stands to reason, then, that on the Board of Guardians or other local authorities there is often this great man's Steward or bailiff, or some of his tenants, who will be naturally anxious to " make things pleasant" for their lords and masters. This is sufficiently shown by the fact that although "the stately homes of England" have become a household word, out of 4,976,674 inhabited dwelling-houses in Great Britain in 1871, there were only 72,951 rated at above £lOO per annum. The Financial Reform Almanac mentions ala in- stance where some years ago and for many years a noble mansion and extensive grounds were assessed at .£lOO. A retired tradesman who had settled in the neighbourhood was appointed assessor, and he, thinking that this was not alto- gether right, raised the assessment to £6OO. How many more cases are there like this one, used to be if they were only looked up Lord Salietrary'smaenificent mansion and park at Hatfield are only assessed to ate poor rate at IWO', and it would be very interesting if the aesee.sments of the residences of a great number of our landed aristocracy could be published. There has been a great deal said lately on the subject of local taxation, which it is alleged presses unduly on real property, on land and houses in fact, and thereby depresses agriculture, as the farmera bear an unequal proportion of these burdens: It has been advocated that these burdens should be lightened by grants from the Imperial Exchequer, or by banding over certain taxes in a distaict to the local audio' hies for local purposes. There is not space here to deal with such a subject at any length, nor is there occasion, as the whole matter will be shortly threshed out in Parlia- ment. To our mind, however, it appears that the result of any such a change would be to benefit the landowners at the expense of the general public. If local taxatien was lightened by such means, and farmers thereby have so much less to pay, would it not be followed by an advance in rent whenever a farm was to be let, and even in many cases where the tenancy had not been changed, as soon as the agricul- turil prospects brighten a little. If "the landed interest" want to show themselves the farmers' friends, they had better support the movement for the landlerds to pay at least one half the rates, and the rents not to be increaed. There is however, one class of property which hitherto 1 has escaped local taxation altogether. A landowner sellsl farming land, let at so much per acre, on chief for building 1 purposes, at so ranch per yard, but the largely increased In 1 incense hç ;hereby receives, although it is on the best se- ' carity, einiply pays income-tax to Government, and con- tributes nothing to the local taxation. A change might be made in this respect.

What is wanted is such legislation as will totally reform our existing chaos of local authorities, consolidate all into One scheme of local governMent, and consolidate the rates at the same time. GiVe the inhabitants of country districts the same control c'rer the public rates that the people of the boroughs have. Let us have a proper *stem of county government, a thorough representation of owners and °cala piers, or in other words the inlubitants and persons inter- tsted in each district, by means of direct household or rate- paying franchise, like we have for the election of the Imperial Parliament. Let us have increased local responsi- bility, not only lightening the labour:: Of the Central Government, but educating the people of the rural districts In their duties as citizens of a civilised coantry, and creating an interest in local affairs in the whole rural population, for, as Mr. Rylands so ably expressed It, "The true Conserva- tive policy is to throw open-, by means of popularly elected county boards, a new opportunity for the exercise of public rights, and for the fulfilment of public duties, by the in- habitants of our rural parishes, and by so doing we shall make the people`more fitted to take part in the working of our institutions, and make them value more highly the insti- tutions under which we live."

Abolish all this complicated system of quarter sessions, highway districts, unions, parishes, &c. If necessary, let there be stbordinate boards or committees or councils in parishes, or in a union of parishes, or districts, as may be determined, but as Mr. Goechen said at Rugby, in November last, "Let all local elections take place on the same registry, on-the same qualifications, on the same forms, and on the
Never turn a blessing around to see whether it has a dark side to it.

People glorify all sorts of bravery, except the bravery they might show on behalf of their nearest neighbour.— George E.'?i9,t, . . Wedience is a habit, and must be-learned, like other habits, rather by practice than by theory—by being orderly, not by talking about order. It may frequently be observed that the man who always states what he would have done if he had been there is the kind of person who never gets there. A TALE OF COVENT GARDEN. —Au amusing story in con- nection with Covent Garden—more especially with reference to the derivation of its name from Convent Garden—is told respecting the old Marquis of Worcester. His lordship being made prisoner, was committed to the custody of the Black Rod, who then lived in Covent Garden ; the noble Marquis, says the histriographer, demanded of Dr. Bayly and others in his company," What the thought of fortune- tellers ?" It was answered, "That corns of them spoke shrewdly." Whereupon the M-atquis said, "It was told me by some of them, before ever I was a Catholic, that I should die in a Convent, bar I never believed them before now ; yet I hope they will not bury me in a Garden."—Cassell's " Old and New London!' DE-AN STANLEI'S HANnwßlTlNG.—Professor Max Muller writes to the Atheneum from Oxford, Feb. 4th, as follows : —ln one of the last conversations I had with my friend Dean Stanley, I, complained to him about some difficulty I felt in writing, which some doctors called Schreibekrampf, others rheumatism, &c. " A'n, don't you know," he broke in, "that I have had something of the same kind all my life? I cannot control my fingers, and that is why my handwriting has always been so wretched." As many people still believe that handwriting is indicative of a man's cha- racter, it is but fair to our friend's memory to make this known. I never heard of it till he told nie himself. It should also be stated that his handwriting never varied. It was the same for the highest and for the lowest among hia many friends, and this is indicative of the man's charac- ter. The anecdotes about misunderstandings arising from his illegible letters were many. No one delighted more in telling them than the Dean himself.

No. VIIi.—JOIIN PHILPOT CURRAN. I ask not for his lineage, I ask not for his name, If manliness be in his heart, He noble birth may claim; I care not, though of world's wealth But slender be his part, If yes you answer when 1 ask Hath he a true man's heart ?—Robert Nicoll. Daring the progress of all political reforms and national revolutions men have been found pressing themselves for- ward into public notice solely by the strength of their talents and the power of their energies—springing at once from the humblest ranks to a lofty niche in the temple of fame. John Philpot Curran was one of this class—one who shot like a meteor beyond the sphere Of his contemporaries, and whose brilliant genius shed its lustre over one of the darkest periods in the history of Ireland. This Illustrious Irishman was of very humble origin. He could not trace his pedigree back to some Norman robber, nor could he discern his family features on the Bayeux tapestry. His parents wexe poor, and we may add for the benefit of those who believe with Miss Kilmanseg "that people with naught are naughty," they were also respectable. "The only in- heritance," said he, in after years, "that I could boast of from my poor father was the very scanty one of an unat- tractive face and person like his own. But if the world did ever attribute to me something more valuable than face or person, or than earthly wealth, it was that another and a dearer parent gave her child a portion from the treasures of her mind." But Curran was one who did not require a genealogy. When some laborious sycophant attempted to derive Napoleon's birth from the Princes of Italy, he flung the parchment on the ground, saying, "My pedigree dates from Montenetto" (his first battle). When a French Mar- shal was asked at college some question about his ancestry the soldier turned on his heel and exclaimed "I am my own ancestor." Curran's contempt for ancestry was equally characteristic. On visiting a London physician to consult him on some illness produced by overstadying, the phy- sician compassionating his emaciated look, asked him whether he might not be suffering under hereditary di- sease." "No, sir," s,id Carran, "my father left me neither money nor malady. He left me nothing but a great deal of good advice," adding, "which I have kept righteously, having never used an atom of it slice."

In I-769 he entered Trinity College, Dublin, as a sizer, being then 19 years of age, having resolved to prepare him, self for the legal profession. His mother had des.lgned him for the Church, and though she, lived lotlg tnough to see the eruntenea of het' Son at the bar, yet she always regretted Lis choice." "On yes, it is very fine," she said, on one occasion, "but it breaks my heart to think what a noble preacher was lost to the Church when John disappointed us all and insisted on becoming a lawyer." All his subsequent SUCCGS.3 and celebrity at the bar could never completely reconcile her to the chatage; and in her latter years, when her friends, to gratify and censole her, used to remind her that she had lived to see her favourite child one of the Judges of the land, she would still reply, "Don't speak to me of Judges. John was fit for anything, and had he but followed our advice it might hereafter be written upon my tomb that I had died the mother of a Bishop." When t:11. excellent and pious woman died it was not written upon her tomb that she died the mother of a Bishop or of a Judge; but there is to be seen upon it an attestation to her worth from the son who was her pride, in these words : Here lies the body of Srab Qarran. She was marlied by iliahy years, Many talents, Many virtues, Few failings, No crime. This frail memorial was placed here by a son _ _ _ Whom she loved. _

Having completed his college studies in the early part of the year 1773, and having qualided himself to take a Master's degree he passed over to London, where he became a student of law in the society of the Middle Temple. After Mr. Curran had concluded his terms he was detained for some time in London in expectation of a remittance from Ireland, without which he could neither discharge his arrears at his lodgings, nor rettirn to his country. At length, just tiPon isg-.; batinig as his purse had attained "the last stage of inanition," he received a fill Of chari house in Lom- bard-street, tat On presenting it he discovered that a neces- sary endorsement was omitted, and of course the bank re- fused to pay. Hiving left the bankers', and being without a shilling in his pocket, he strolled into tit. James's Park, where he remained during his usual dinner hour considering the means of relieving himself from his present necessity ; but after long reflection he could only come to one certain conclusion, that th 2 misfortune could never have happened more inopportunerk, every one of his Irish friends, to whom alone he could have applied, having quitted London, leaving him behied awaiting this remittance. As he sat upon one of the benches exhausted with devising expedients, he began to whistle a melancholy old Irish air. An old gentleman seated at the other end started at the well known sounds. " Pray, sir," said the stranger, "may I venture to ask where you learned that tune ?" "Indeed, sir," replied the whistler, in the meek and courteous tone of a spirit which affliction had softened; "indeed you may, air. I learned it in my native country, in Ireland." "But how comes it, sir, that at this hour, while other people are dining, you con- tinue here, whistling old Irish tunes ?" " Alas ! sir, I too have been in the habit of dining of late, but to-day, my money being all gone, and my credit not yet arrived, I am. even forced to come ard dine upon a whistle in the park.'' Struck by the mingled despondence and playfulness of this confession, the benevolent veteran exclaimed, "Courage, young man! I think I can see that you deserve better fare; come along with me and you shall have it." About ten yllars after this interview Ma:dclin came to Dublin ; Mr. Curran, who in the interval had risen to eminence, was invited one evening to a party where the actor was one of the re nap toy. They :wax() presented to each other, but Macklin failed to rec in the now celebrated advocate and orator the dis- tressed stadent in St. James's Park." Perceiving this Curran abstained front claiming any acquaintance; but in a little time contrived tb introduce a conversation on acts of kind- ness, and as a proof related an incident of ten years before when a generous old man had befriended him. A glow of recollection was soon observed upon the player's countenance. He started, and fixed his eyes upon the speaker. "If my memory fails me not, sir," said he, "we have met before." " Yes, Mr. Macklin," replied Curran, taking his hand, "in- deed we have met ; and though upon that occasion you were only performing upon a private theatre, let me assure you that (to adopt the words of a high judicial personage, which you have heard before) you ;lever acted better." Mr. Curran 'Was called to the Irish bar in 1775. A race of illustrious men had preceded him, and there were those still riving whose talents were of the highest order. But Curran rose at once to give new lustre and spirit to an already enlightened and spirited profession. Ho had been at the bar four or five years when an opportunity presented itself for the display of his rare powers as an advocate. It was a case at the Cork Assizes, in which a Roman Catholic priest, the Rev. Mr. Neale, brought an action against a nobleman of that county (Lord Doneraile) for an assault and battery. The. circum- stances attending this case mark the melancholy condition of the times. They afford a single but a very striking ex- ample of what a member of the "ascendancy faction" might dare to do to a Catholic, and of what a Catholic, however venerable and sacred by reason of his years and office, might be obliged to endure in the days of the penal fews. The incident is remarkable, too, as being one of the first instances in which a case between the scion of a•Protes- taut aristocratic house on the one side, and a poor and influ- ential member of the Catholic body on the other, a Court of Law in Ireland did something like justice. And more singu- lar still the complainant whose grievance was redressed in this instance belonged to the despised, and hated, arid perse- cuted class, the Catholic priesthood of Ireland. Well might the most renowned of all Irish advocates, John Philpot Curran, feel proud of winning this triumph. The circumstances of the cas3 were these: Some time previously Lord Doneraile seduced a country girl. Her brother in some manner incurred the censure of his Bishop. At the persuasion of his concubine Lord Doneraile deter- mined to interfere in the affair. Attended by a Mr. St. Leger, ' hie kinsman, and an ex-captain cf dragoons, he rode to the humble cabin which was the dwelling of the parish priest, Father Neale, a man both old and poor. The haughty nobleman with an imperious voice summoned forth the good old man. Interrupted at his devotions, the pious priest rose from his knees and tottered forth, bareheaded, with breviary in his hand. He stood submissively by Lord Doneraile's stirrup. His Lordship commanded him to remove the cen- sure from the poltroon who was probably base enough to feel proud of his Lordship's patronage, purchased by his sister's• infamy. The feeble old priest would fain avoid defiance of the great man's anger as long and s far as his conselen,...-,-, would allow him, but refusing at length tO rttiAor!he cen- sure Lord Doneraile, regardless of hie tttay hair and feeble- ness, raised his horsewhip, rained blots upon the defenceless old priest and drove him inte his cabin, staggering and covered with blood. The old man sought prorection from the law. He commenced proceedings against the titled mis- creant. At first, his chance of gaining any redress seemed hopeless. Every barrister on the circuit refused to plead for him till the brave and fiery-souled Curran volunteered to take up the case. And right nobly and manfully he struggled in the cause of justice so shamefully outraged in the person of the old priest. He boldly denounced Done- raile, holding up to withering ecorn the character of that scoundrel. He called Captain St. Leger "a renegade soldier and drummed-out dragooh, who wanted the courage to nreet the enemies of his country in battle, but had the heroism to redeem the ignominy of his flight from danger by raising his arm against an aged and unoffending minister of religion, who had just risen from putting up before the throne of God a prayer of general intercession, in which his heartless in- sulter was included." Out of their own mouths he covered with shame the servile witnesses which his Lordship had prevailed upon to appear on his behalf. His words were irresistible. Appealing to the jury as men he made them thrill with men's natural indignation at wrong and outrage. Their noble feelings and their sense of justice were roused from sleep. Forgetting all else for the time but truth and right, and the sacredness of their Oath, they gave a verdict for Father Neale. Thirty guineas were awarded as damages to the illused priest. The sum in itself was little enough, but when we consider the circumstances of the case—the period and the persons concerned—a poor, old, despised, and unprotected priest against a powerful peer—the jury full of all the prejudices of the time against the priest's creed and class and race—the triumph of Curran must be regarded as at once splendid and surprising. Under the spell of his in- spired speech the demon of bigotry was for a brief space at least exorcised from the souls of those who listened to it. And if Napoleon could date his pedigree from Mentenetto, his first battle, John Philpot Carran could date his from the defence of Father Neale, his first great forensic triumph.

st As soon as the trial was over he was summoned to ma— . public apology for those expressions which he had made reference to the "renegade soldier," or to III_ meet the " drummed-out dragoon" oft the field. The dauntless adso: • cate preferred to risk his life rather than his reputation. duel accordingly followed, in which Curran not only PreV„ his courage, bat afforded infinite entertainment to the v.Y: standers by a series of those spo.tive sallies which he alwaY? found difficult to suppress. When each had taken hie ground Mr. St. Leger called out to his adversary to fire' "No, sir," replied Curran, "I am here by your invitationl and you must open the ball." St. Leger having fired, and declining to return his fire, the affair ten:ulna:ea after a single shot. A more solemn and interesting scene soon followed. The red venerable priest was dying, and in his last moments des' f to see his benefactor. Curran hastened to the bed side 0r his expiring client. The dying man had neither gold rio silver to give, but such as he had he was anxious to bestovb Raising himself up in his bed, and placing his hands on the • head of the young advocate, he pronounced over lure the formal benediction of the Roman Catholic Church as the re'

ward of his eloquence and intrepidity. This defence of Father Neale is not only a striking tration of Curran's love of justice, but of his sympathl for , the Irish people. A good anecdote is related of ocone' who, while holding forth at one of his mass meetingg, wa'as suddenly interrupted by some factious person in he crovr asking him "if the handkerchief he held in his hand WO ° Irish manufacture." " Yes," promptly replied the Liberal;Or "and my coat, and the man in Carran might ha;lu given a similar reply. He was an Irishman to the los:: bone. His sympathy for the Irish people was int°7 From the commencement to the conclusion of his public life he was their invincible champion and advocate. He ne;vt.,,e, thought or spoke of them but with tenderness, and and indignation. At the Bar, in the Senate, on the amidst his family and friends, or in the society of the illustrious personages of the Empire, the sufferings of 1,1 Irish peasant were remembered, and their cause pleaded WIL'S an energy and reality that proved how well he knew al/. how deeply he felt for that class whose calamities he de plored. Notwithstanding much temptation and mall dangers, he never for a moment deserted their interest o.a abandoned their defence. "At any time of my life," .91,1 he, "I might to a certain degree, as well as others, have tie" up my countrymen in bundles, and sold them at the WI market of corruption, and have raised myself to wealth, an,,, station, and remorPe —to the envy of the foolish and t'to contempt of the wise; but I thought it more becoming_ mmain below among them, to mourn over and console tbe! or where my duty called upon me, to reprimand and reboes9: them when they were acting against themselves." 111,1, are brave and beautiful words, but no less brave and bean t" than the public conduct of the man who uttered She/ We have seen him statt from obscurity with the loVeoe Ireland and its people inihis heart. We shall hereafter him climbing to a high position—enjoying the fellows"'Ps of the whole of the noble and the great, but we hall see him the friend of the suffering, of the needy, of the red, tint of a cruel greed, of all that were desolate and oPPreE" of the brave champion of their rights, de hold denunciator their wrongs.

THE BRADLAUGH INCIDENT IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Describing the scene in the House of Commons, on Tues- day evening, when Mr. Bradlaugh, immediately after the result of the division on Mr. Labouchtre's motion was made known, attempted to take his seat, the Parliamentary corres- pondent of the _itranchester Guardian says :—Xs the tellers retired from the table Mr. Bradlaugh was found to be march. ing with a resolute air and quick stride up the floor towards the table. •A slight hiss, together with a cry of " Oh, oh," came from the crowded Conservative benches, but the general disposition on that side of the House was obviously to indulge in scornful and contemptuous tittering, for it was supposed that Mr. Bradlaugh had only come up to be turned back again, as had so often occurred. But Mr. -Bradlaugh had a startling surprise in store, and he sprang it upon .the assembly Se abruptly as almost to paralyse every onlooker. Directly he reached the bottom of the table, where the mace reclined in state, unconscious of threatening indignation, he leant upon the big box at which Ministers stand when addressing the House, and bringing from his breast pocket a little volume bound in black leather and having red edges, he held it in his hand while he repeated with the utmost baste a form of words. "I, Chailes Brad- laugh, do swear" he was heard to say, and the rest was lost. Enough bad fallen on the astounded ears of the assembly to awaken suspicion as to his design, and before any single member of the bewildered House could recover his presence of mind, Mr. Bradlaugh bad carried his scheme into execution. Sir T. Erskine May had started to walk in front of the Treasury Bench to meet Mr. Bradlaugh at the end of the table where new members are always sworn, but ere the clerk arrived at the box. Mr. Bradlaugh dropped his book, and producing a sheet of foolscap from another pocket with the dexterity of a conjuror laid it flat out before him, and hastily scribbled something at the foot of the page, which was already nearly covered with writing. Still acting with great haste, Mr. Bradlaueh seized up this docu- ment, and holding it out towards the Cleric said he tendered it as the oath duly subscribed according to law. There could no longer be any doubt, even irt the minds of the sturdiest member of the country party, that Mr. Bradlaugh professed to have brought with him his own Bible and his owe form of oath, and-to have sworn himself in without the slightest assistance, and before anybody could. exclaim "Jack Robinson." He certainly looked as though he fancied he had been very clever, and apparently he was prepared to boast "Alone I did it." His colourless face expressing cold defiance, and his down-drawn lip indicating something like disdain, he stood with arm out- stretched close in front of the Prime Minister, and steadily kept his glance upon the Speaker, while murmurs of aston- islimeateend indignation began to spread around him. Every sound died away as the Speaker rose and directed him to withdraw below the Bar. Mr. Bradlaugh, in harsh accents, answered that lie would "obey," but added boldly, "but I have now taken my oath." A few young Tories, sadly in in want of a fugleman, and having no clue as to how they should act, laughed, but the prevailing aspect of the excited House was one of bepuze.lement. As Mr. Bradlaugh retired, instead of passing from the Bar to the seats under the gallery, be stopped as he went up the gangway at the third bench, and, motioning to members to make room, sat down beside Mr. Burt. Stretching forward from that place he waited for what might occur. The Opposition lost no time in directing attention by their outcry to his latest proteeedings, and the Speaker reproved him for not carrying out his directions. Mr. Bradlaugh, with a quibble, replied that he had been below the Bar, but had also taken his seat. However, before the gathering storm could burst he consented, having asserted himself thus far, to go back to his former retirement below the bar, and on removing thither he put on his bat in further assertion of his claim to be a duly and fully admitted member of Parliament. Lord Randolph 'Churchill, in a sort of frenzy, came out to lead his party and the House and re- proposed the motion for a new writ which he had only just defeated. While be went to the table to put it in writing the tension was relieved by universal conversation, and during the interval which ensued the Tories had decided on the line they ought to take. Consequently they burst into a fury at the insult which had been oftereello the House, and made a strenuous effort to turn the strange incident which had occurred to account in the interests of their party. Ministers counselled moderation, and Mr. Gladstone con- trived, despite Mr. O'Donnell's profession of incredulity, to convince the House that lie had been as much taken aback , as the rest, and that the Government had not been in Mr. Bradlaugh's secret. So the Tory leaders agreed to give Ministers a respite on the distinct understanding that they must on Ash Wednesday give incontrovertible proof of their non-complicity in what was regarded as a profanation of the oath and an outrage to Parliament. The scene on Wednesday evening is thus described by the Parliamentary correspondent of the Manchester Examiner —"An: incident occurred which changed the pre- vailing feeling. Mr. Lakouchere asked on the part of Mr. Bradlaugh that he should be heard at the bar.. This was received with loud cries of "No," mingled with many cries of " Yes, yes." The Speaker, however, after standing in his place for some time, calmly noting the uproarious de- monstration of feeling, decided that the sense of the House was against the bon. member being heard. Thereupon Mr. Bradlaugh at once left his place under the clock, and, passing the bar, took his seat on the third bench below the gangway, on the Ministerial side, near the seat which he occupied last session. The Speaker's attention was, of course, directed at once to the circumstances by the shouts of the Tory members, and rising in his place he announced the fact of Mr. Bradlaugh's presence within the bar. Mr. Bradiaugh - interrupting him said in a subdued tone•that lie desired the indulgence of the House while lie insisted on his right to take his seat. The Speaker, without noticing the interruption, called the attention of the House to the repeated disobedience of the hon. member, and then abruptly sat down without calling upon him to with- draw. There were loud calls for Mr. Gladstone, and the Prime Minister was advancing to the table when the Sneaker, who had been in consultation with the principal clerk, Sir Erskine May, again rose and peremptorily required Mr. Bradlaugh to retire below the bar. Mr. Bradlaugh at once I did so, as he said, in obedience to the direction of the Chair, but protesting, as he went to his place below the gallery, I that he claimed his right to take his seat. Mr. Gladstone, on the ground that Mr. Bradlaugh had yielded to the authority of the Chair, declined to propose any resolution to the House, being of course groaned at by the now almost infuriated. Tories. Nr Stafford Northcote at , once rose and asked leave to withdraw his amend- ment in order to substitute another expelling I Mr. Bradlaugh on the ground of disobedience and con- tumacy. Mr. Gladstone, on his part, acquiesced in tie withdrawal of the amendment,. Dr. Lyons, who had moved a strong resolution declaring Mr. Bradlaugh disqualified from sitting in the present Parliament, also withdrew his proposal in favour of that of which the Tory leader had given notice. There was some dettrar on the part of Radical members to the withdrawal of Sir Stafford's amendment, but the objection was not persisted in. Then, the way being clear, Sir Stafford Northcote, in a few sentences, moved Mr. Bradlaugh's expulsion. Mr. Gladstone, while declining to take any part in the matter, admitted that this- motion was strictly consequential upon the previous proceedings of tne House. Mr. Labouchere having in vain repeated his appeal that his colleague • should be heard, a division was* called for. The sensation of the division was Mr. Bradlaugh's own proceeding. On going below the bar lie had taken advantage .of the mem- bers' privilege of wearing his hat in the House. He now walked into the division lobby and recorded a vote in his own favour, being the fourth or fifth man to reenter the House. He bowed low as he passed the Speaker's chair, but Sir 11. Brand, who was engaged in conversation with other members, did not observe the act or take notice of P. After the numbers 2PI to 83 by which Sir Stafford Northcote's motion had been carried were announced, the fact of Mr. Bradlaugh leaving voted was communicated to, the Speaker, who in turn announced it to the House, and asked for in- structions. Mr. Gladstone, who had returned to his place, made no proposal, and Sir Stafford Northcote, assuming the duty of leader, suggested that it was not -worth while lead- ing to a new debate and opening up difficult questions by moving any resolution. A secood formal division took place, with the result of confirming the decision by a slightly increased majority.

The death is announced of Mr. Richard Fryer, one of the Reform Bill agitators in 1832, and subsequently a prominent leader in the Free-trade movement. All the Irish members who have in the past two years been temporarily expelled from the House of Commons, and who chanced to be present when the divisions were called, voted for Mr. Bradlaugh's expulsion. The Ltovernor of Her Majesty's prison at Armley has re- ceived from the Home Secretary a communication notifying that the sentence upon John Ross, who was to have been executed on Tuesday for the murder of John Manley,at Leeds last Christmas Day, is respited with a view to its ultimate commutation.

...... On Tuesday a chair was placed on the down line near Damen on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway before the passing of the express for the North. Fortunately the chair was smashed to pieces, some atoms being thrown a distance of thirty yards. Another attempt occurred last week to a Mamchester express near Congleton. Both are being inves- tigated.

The Spanish Government is at present engaged upon the question of concluding treaties of c4inmerce with Switzer- land, Holland, Italy, and Portugal. The Bulgarian Chamber of Deputies has pa2sed a bill making a provision in the Penal Code for the punishing of public functionaries who divulge State secrets. Mrs. Scoville, Guitean's sister, has addressed a pathetic appeal to 'Airs. CrArfield, asking her to jorgive her brother, whom she describes as a brain-sick, deluded, and crazy man.

The profits on the Pest-office telegraphs for the year ended March 31, 1881, were equivelent to a dividend of ef.:4 13s. on the capital expended. Mr. Jesse Collings has secured the 17th of March for his motion affirming the desirability of peasant proprietorships. The motion will be seconded by Lord Lymington. Tito Claimant has again been writing to "Dear Onelow." It appears that now all his hopes A centred in the return of a Conservative Government to power; and he remarks that he will not give up his inheritence so long as blood runs through his veins. The Preston Tramways Bill was down on the list of cases as to compliance with the standing orders to be heard by Mr. Robinson, one of the examiners of the House of Com- mons, at Westminster, on Tuesday, but upon its being called none of the parties interested appeared. It was accordingly ordered to be struck out. The coroner's inquiry into the murder of the young girl Georgina Moore at Yalding was brought to a conclusion en Monday. A verdict of wilful murder was returned against the woman Esther Pay, who, it is alleged, decoyed the child from her home in Pimlico, and, after killing her, threw the corpse into the Medway. On Monday, the lifeless body of James Bates, platelayer, of Baraford-street, Heaton Norris, was found on the Cheshire Lines Rail way, near Teviotdale Station, Stock-port, where he had been at work. Deceased had been knocked down by a passing train, and his head was almost severed from his body. He was 54 years of age and married. Another miscarriage of justice is reported, the victim this time being a Wiltshireman, named Pearse, who two months ago was sent to gaol for six months, on a charge of poaching and wounding a keeper. Another man, who, it appears, was the first to be suspected, now says that he, and not Pearse, was the poacher. 'Tile Home Secretary is being memorialised on the subject. The villa which the Queen is about to inhabit at Men- tone is a modern structure sumptuously furnished, and filled with all the most modern appliances for health and com- fort. It was built by Mr. Henfrev, the same gentleman n'hose villa was occupied by Her Majesty during her visit to Baveno. Mr. Henfrey is to be congratulated ; it is not often that an English subject, however wealthy, has a chance of twice being honoured by his sovereign as his guest. A special inspection of the new Channel Tunnel was made at Dover, on Tuesday, by a large company, including some 60 newspaper representatives. The total length of the head- , ing is now 1,050 yards, and the rate of progress one-third of an inch per revolution of the boring machine, which re- volves 4- times per minute. The course of the tunnel is perfectly straight up to the present, and stretches about 50 yards under the sea. After the inspection luncheon was given at the Lord Warden Hotel. Judgment was given, on Monday, in the Board of Trade inquiry held in Liverpool respecting the Wreck of the Cul- zean, of Greenock, in the Sound of Jura, on the 21st of November. The master of the tug Conqueror was acquitted of blame, and it was found that the Culzean had been navi- gated in a seamanlike manner, but the court thought it would have been better to have had two hawsers attached to the ship. The cause of the sad disaster was the breaking of a hawser, whereby the ship was driven ashore. Mr. Gladstone having declined..owing to pressure of busi- ness, to receive a deputation appointed by the meeting in the Mansion House to present its resolutions against the opium trade, Lord Shaftesbury sent to him a memorial on the subject, bearing 361 signatures, including those of the Archbishops of Canterbury, York, and Dublin, Cardinal Manning, the Duke of Westminster, the Earl of Shaftesbury, several bishops. and other eminent persons. Mr. Gladstone transmitted the memorial to Lord Hartington, from.whom the following reply has been received :—"lnelia Office, Feb. 14, 1882.—Dear Lord Shaftesbury,—l have received from Mr. Gladstone the important memorandum from the Society for the Suppression of the Opium Trade, which you have forwarded to him on the subject. I will, of course, give it my most careful consideration, though I need hardly say that I entirely dissent from many of the statements and conclusions which it contains.- --'Yours sincerely, HAR- TINGTON." Mr. Commissioner Kerr has had before him in the Lord Mayor's Court a curious action arising out of the arrange- ments for a battwe in Bedfordshire. A country gentleman "put down" as a pure matter of business a large number of pheasants, and then arranged with other "sportsmen" to come and shoot them. These sportsmen were to pay a fixed sum per day and to receive a small percentage of the "fur, and feather" that might fall to their guns. The Com- missioner expressed the opinion that such " sport " as this was unworthy of English gentlemen, and hinted that the attention of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals might be called with advantage to the system of "putting down these wretched pheasants and then sending dogs to rouse them up to be blazed at." It was stated by the defendant in the action that Lord Stamford had " put down" 6,000 pheasants in his preserves prior to the visit of the Prince of Wales to Bradeate Park. BRUTAL MURDER OF A WOMAN IN LEEDS. Shortly before midnight on Saturday, a brutal murder was com- mitted in Charlie-street, \Vest-street, Leeds, by a man named Arthur Lannagan, aged 28 years, employed as a fore- man hammer driver in a machine works. The victim was Margaret Lofthouse. Lannagan, by whom the deceased had a child before her marriage, had lodged with the Loft- houses for several years. At a few minutes past 11 on Saturday night he went home and commenced to quarrel with the deceased regarding his food. He kicked her on the face, knocking her off a stool upon which she was sit- ting, and inflicted a severe wound on her abdomen. A woman named M'Garry, hearing the deceased's screams, went into the house and said to Lannagan, "You havedone it now." Lannagan turned round and threatened to knock M'Garry's head off. He thea left the house. Mrs. Loft- house was carried to bed, and medical aid was obtained, but she never spoke, and died at 20 minutes past twelve o'clock. Lannagan was arrested soon afterwards wed taken to the police-station. He threatened to commit suicide, and had to be guarded. A MESSAGE FROM THE CONDEMNED CELL. On Tues- day, the Rev. William Reid, of Levenshulme, Manchester, delivered a lecture in the Mechanics' Institution, Burnley, having special reference to the late Robert Templeton, who was executed in Manchester on Monday last for the murder of Betty Scott, at Lowerhouse. It having been announced that Mr. Reid had a special message from Templeton, to the working men of Burnley, the Mechanics' Hall was crowded, and an overflow meeting had to be held. Mr. Reid read the following letter, which Templeton had written as a warning:—" Sunday, February, 12, 1882.--I hope that this will be a great lesson to all others at Lowerhouse and Burnley, and elsewhere, who" follow the steps of intemper- ance, to which I attribute this crime. As God knows, that morning, I was not in my proper mind, and far from being so. I would be the last in the world to annoy or injure any person to my knowledge. I now close, hoping again You will all forgive me. God bless you, and the Lord Jesus Christ have mercy on my soul.—e-Your's truly, ROBERT TEMPLETON." NEWSPAPER STATISTICS.—From The Ncir.spope;- Press Directory for 1882 we extract the following on the present position of the newspaper press:—" There are now published in the United Kingdom 1,817 newspapers, distributed as fol- lows :—England—London, 375; provinces, 1,012-1,387; Wales, 71; Scotland, 183; Ireland, 156; isles, 20. Of these there are 124 daily papers published in England, 5 daily papers published in Wales, 22 daily papers published in Scotland, 16 daily papers published in Ireland, and 2 daily papers published in British isles. On reference to the first edition of this useful directory for the year 1846 we find the following interesting facts—viz , that in that year there were published in the United Kingdom 551 journals; of these 14 were. issued daily—viz, 12 in England and 2 in Ireland; but in 1882 there are now established and circulated 1,817 papers, of which no less than 169 are issued daily, showing that the press of the country has more than trebled during the last 36 years. The increase in daily papers has been still more remarkable; the daily issues standing 169 , against 14 in 1846. The magazines now in course of publioa- tion, including the quarterly reviews, number 1,180, of which 326 are of a decidedly religious character, representing the Church of England, Weslevans, Methodists, Baptists, Independents, Roman Catholics; and other Christian com- munities." TIIE SARDINIAN.—Some passengers by the disabled steamer Sardinian, which left Canada for Liverpool on the 28th January, and subsequently ldst hefrudder, have reached Manchester by way of Antwerp, whither they werq conveyed by the steamer Nederland. They give a full account of the voyage of the Sardinian up to the date of their transference to the Nederland, when the Allan steamer was still about eight or nine hundred miles from Queenstown. The voyage had been an eventful one. The rudder was lost on the fifth day after leaving Halifax, and the rudder-post went with it. At the same time the vessel began to leak, but the pumps were quite able to keep the water down, and as the vessel is built with watertight compartments, no fearlvas entertained on that score. The weather continued very rough, and efforts to fix a temporary rudder were attended with very little success. Ultimately, however, the vessel, under a jury- rudder, succeeded in making about eight knots an hour. This was on the day that the Nederland came in sight and took on board thirteen saloon and six steerage passengers, these being all, in the prevailing rough weather, who cared Ito leave the Sardinian.
