There is a good expectation at Calcutta that the forth- coming Budget will show a large surplus. The newspapers are *pressing upon the Government the necessity of abolish- ing the Licence Tax. The Khedive has given orders to prepare the Palace of Kasr-el-nusa, at Cairo, for the sons of the Prince of Wales on their arrival there. His Highness's yacht will be placed at their disposal for visiting Upper Egypt. The United States Senate has passed without a dissenti- ent vote Mr. Edmund's Anti-Polygamy Bill, making poly- gamous mal riages punishable by fine and imprisonment, and depriving those who contract them of all the rights of citi- zenship. The base against the fabricators of Egyptian money in Switzerland has been dismissed on the ground that, inasmuch as Egypt possesses no recognised system of coinage, the offence imputed to the accused was one which the laws of Geneva did not recognise. . The New Brurnwick Legislature has been opened by the Lieutenant Governor, warn, in his speech, said that the affairs of the province were in a very favourable position. He announced that the Government proposed starting a cattle-breeding farm for the improvement of stock. .

A telegram' from Sydney, New South Wales, dated Wecl- nesday, says:—The English cricket team, under the cap- taincy of Alfred Shaw, after returning from New Zea- land have played a return match here against a combined Australian Eleven. The Atstralians won by five wickets.

A " movement " has been commenced in Bulgaria for the imprisonment or expulsion of all who are hostile to Prince Alexander. Petitions were got up praying the Government to put a stop to the "agitation " of which M. Zanlroff is the acknowledged leader. M. Zankoff was promptly arrested and imprisoned at Vratza. The negotiaLions fOrthe renewal of a commercial treaty with France are now regarded as having finally collapsed. The Times correspondent states that means of warding off the application of the general tariff to English productions aro being sought, either by offering England the treatment of the most favoured nation " or I y some other device." Fires and explosions at Chester, Pennsylvania, and Haver- hill, Massachussetts, have caused the loss of a considerable number of lives and the destruction of an immense amount of property. The Massachusetts town was almost entirely devoted to the,manufacture of shoes, and very few shops or factories remain. The loss is estimated at two millions of dollars. _

Commander Selby, the British officer who was attacl-;ed and seriously wounded by Albanians, has just died of his in- juries. Lord Dufferin, it will be temembered, took prompt action to bring the perpetrators of the outrage to justice, and at his instigation they were arrested. It will now be his duty to see that justice does not fail to reach the cowardly criminals.

There are rumours in Russia of a projected Turcoman incursion into Boliliara. The official organs of St. Peters- bur, declare that these alarming reports, although not wholly groundless, are intentionally and systematically circulated by the Jews of Bokhara, who are anxious, in order to ameliorate their present condition, to have that state officially incorporated with Russia. Some time ago, it will be remembered, the Viceroy of India was obliged to make strong representations to the King. of Burmali on the subject of certain monopolies which his Majesty insisted on enforcing. All apprehensions as to any trouble arising on this head have been removed by a definite promise of the King to the Viceroy that the monopolies complained of shall cease from the 16:h instant. A plot, it is said, has been discovered against Prince Milan of Servia, and the same report states that a serious , agitation is in progress ;r. Bulgaria. The rumour, however, comes from Vienna, and is unconfirmed; and as the Vien- nesse are at present singularly susceptible to any stories which point to disquietude amongst any branch of the Slav nationalities, it must be taken with reservation. A very curious statement is made by the Russian Gobs. It says that the Russian Government, to keep on good terms with England, will advise Ayoub Khan to remain in Persia, and will subsidise him there. This is a specially Musco- vite way of showing friendship; it would be much more to the point if Russia were to leave Ayoub alone. Another story is that a party of Cossacks are about to march to Merv. Possibly the object of this expedition may also be to keep on good terms with England. Both in Berlin and St. Petersburg the speech of General Scobeleff to the Servian students in Paris has been the sub- ject of a great deal of comment. The most influential organs in Berlin say that they Nylll hear the judgment pronounced by the civil and military authorities of Russia on the utter- ' ances of the general, while the Official. Illessenyep of St. Petersburg declares that there is DO ground for the alarming rumours to which the address has given rise. Private utter- ances of this nature, the Russian print maintains, can have no influence on the national policy.

SACKING OF A TOWN AND FRIGHTFUL MASSACRE.— Particulars have been received at Buenos Ayres of a massacre of the inhabitants of the seaport town of Pisco by Peruvian soldiery. It appears that Colonel Mas, with 600 troops from Ica, attacked Villavicencio. The latter being routed, the force under Colonel Mas proceeded to sack the town of Pisco, with the aid of Villavicencio's troops. One thousand pipes of wine were distributed among the men who set the houses on fire and murdered the inhabitants. Four hundred foreigners assembled to resist these mara7ders, but they were cut to pieces, and 300 of them were killed. The total number of victims exceeded 1000, and the French consul is reported to have lost his life in the fray. It is rumoured that Colonel Mae has been shot by Garcia Calderon's troops. Madame Celeste, who some forty years ago was one of the most popular actresses on the London stage, died recently in Paris, at the age of seventy-eight. She began her theatrical career as a dancer, and gradually made her way to the front rank as a melodramatic actress. She made her first appear- ance in London in 1830, as Fenella in " Massaniello," and her performance in "The Green Bushes" at the Adelphi some fourteen or fifteen years afterwards will be in the memory of all old playgoers. She paid several visits to America, where she was the object of some extraordinary popular demonstrations. In 1834 the people yoked them- selves to her carriage and proclaimed her a citizen of the Union, President Jackson himself officially confirming the compliment. Madame Celeste took her farewell of the steel!, at the Adelphi in 1870, but has since reappeared at that theatre in "The Green Bushes " and other pieces.
THE INSURRECTION IN THE HERZEGOVINA._

The Herzegovinian insurgents have captured an Austrian fort on the Upper Drina, and put the garrison to flight with considerable loss. The result of this success has been a large accession to their strength. The special despatch from Ragusa which conveys this information adds that General Jovanovich has left that city in order to direct the opera- tions against the Crivoscians, whe. areawaiting their enemies in their mountain strongholds. The Vienna correspondent of the Cologne Ga.:ette referring to the insurrection, states that the Austrian authorities have, as the result of inquiiies that have been made, found no foundation for the reports of movements of the Russian troops. Russia has, moreover, it is stid, declared in Belgra le, as well as Cettinje, that the Principalities should observe the strictest neutrality towards the insurrection. THE EGYPTIAN QUESTION. _ _ _

The Egyptian Chamber of Notables has demanded of the I Ministry the communication to the Chamber of all treaties and conventions concluded with other countries, with the object of enabling the Chamber to avoid involuntarily in- fringing any engagements entered into. - The Republique Francaise has published a communication from the British and French Comptrollers-General at Cairo, in which those gentlemen bear testimony to the present prosperous condition of Egypt, but point out that the power of the Khedive is being gradually weakened and destroyed. Sir Auckland Colvin and M. de Blignieres declare that to accept the state of things recently created would be to nullify the action of the Comptrollers, already rendered powerless by having to deal with the Ministers dependent upon the Chamber of Notables and the Army, and would, moreover, endanger the reforms carried out in Egypt up to the present. The British and French Ambassadors at Constantinople have communicated to the Turkish Minister for Foreign Affairs an identical note in reply to that of the Porte, dated the 13th ult., on the joint Anglo-French declaration to the Khedive. The two Governments maintain their right to address the Note directly to the Egyptian Government, refute the Port's assertion that no occasion existed for the declaration, and point to the danger of the situation respect- ing Egyptian affairs. The aim of the two Governments being ever to maintain the sovereignty of the Sultan in Egypt, and to promote the prosperity and progress, both moral and material, of the Egyptian people, they considered the circumstances warranted the action taken on that occa- sion. The Sultan is reported to have received the note with satisfaction.

The visit of the Marquis of Salisbury to Liverpool, which was to have taken place during the middle of next week,has been unexpectedly postponed. Saturday was observed in all the London synagogues as a day of special prayer for the Jews of Russia, under the direc- tion of the venerable Chief Rabbi. • • In the collection of prints of the late Lord Beaconsfield, about to be sold by Messrs. Sotheby, Wilkinson, and Hodge, are some of the works of William Blake, the poet-artist. The malleable ironworkers of the West of Scotland on Sato'. lay received an advance of 7-!2- per cent., and the pud- dlers one of Pd. per ton, under the award of a board of arbitration.

Mr. William Thomas Lewis, agent for the Marquts of Bute, and one of the members of the Royal Commission on accidents in mines, has been appointed President of the Min- ing Association of Great Britain for the ensuing year. . William Knowles, a master painter, and a collector of taxes, has disappeared from Wakefield wlth £286 of the Queen's money. His wife believes he has committed suicide, but another theory is that he has gone to America. A warrant has been issued for his arrest.

Lord Stanhope has introduced a bill in the House of Lords to limit the hours of labour in shops and warehouses of the drapery class to 10 hours daily. There are special provisions for extension of time by licence to be given by the Home Secretary on particular occasions.—Lancet. What promises to be the longest amendment on record in connection with the Estimates is being prepared. It will recite the names of 183 members of the House of Commons • who receive pay in connection with the army or navy ; and the lion. member in charge proposes to reduco the Estimates by the aggregate sum.

A conaitional order has been granted by the Dublin Ex- chequer Division for a new trial of the breach of promise case, in which Miss Wislulty obtained a verdict for £450 damages against Dr. Macauley, the grounds of the applica- tion being alleged misdirection on the part of the Lord Chief Baron, who tried the case, and also that the Statute of Limitations barred the action.

A terrible disaster has happened at Ccvmbpark Colliery, in the Rhondda Valley. A tremendous fall of coal, consisting of hundreds of tons, has taken place below the ground and killed four men instantly. One man was miraculously saved by falling timber, and another was injured. Great and general excitement prevails. The pit belongs to the Ocean Company, of which Mr. D. Davies, M.P., is the principal member. •

At the London Bankruptcy Court, on Wednesday, a peti- tion for liquidation was presented by Mr. George Hampden Whalley' who describes himself of St. Albin's-road, Vic- toria-roacl, Kensington, Plasmadoc and Delph (Denbigh), Trevor (Denbigh), and Clochfaen (Montgomeryshire), late of Gloucester-place, Portman-square, Lond6n, and Taplow, Bucks, M.P. The debts are stated at £66,000. _ _

The Lord Chancellor on Wednesday delivered judgment in the case of Martin v. Mackonochie. His lordship, speak- ing for the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, said it was for the learned judge in the curt below to say what punishment would be most proper for the offences provcd. Their lordships world accordingly advise her Majesty to reverse the judgment of June, 1880, and remit to the court below to decree canonical censure or punishment at dis- cretion.

At Nottingham, on Saturday, Thomas Charlton, son of a Nottingham county magistrate, was fined -£5 for an assault on a schoolmaster named Prust. Miss Charlton, the defend- ant's sister, is to be married shortly. The complainant plays the organ at the Parish Church, and declined to allow a re- lative of Miss Charlton to officiate at her marriage. The defendant called Prust out of school, gave him three minutes to apologise, and on his declining thrashed him. A public subscription has been started in North Stafford- shire by Mr. Craig, M.P., for the assistance of the released convicts Johnson and Clowes. There is a widespread feeling that while the £5OO compensation given by the Home Secre- , tary will place them in the same financial position they occupied before conviction, it does not include any solatium for the sufferings of their prison life. The-recovery of the men is very slow, neither having yet been able to undertake any employment. A sad accident occurred at Lytham on Wednesday after- , noon. Three youths, named Dean, Crossley, and Smith, -students at Pembro,ke School, were at play on the sandhills close to the school. They were making a burrow in one of the hills. Dean and Crossley had worked some distance into the hole when about a ton of sand fell and buried Dean. His companions, after doing their utmost to extricate him, ran off for assistance. When taken out about half an hour afterwards the unfortunate youth was dead. The deceased was the only son of Mr. G. Dean, manufacturer, of Helm- shore, and was 13 years old. Mrs. Langtry puts rather too high a price on her dramatic ability. Being asked on what terms she would go to Sheffield for six nights, she answered, through Mr. Geo. Keogh, that her terms were 60 per cent. of the receipts, "she finding nothing but herself and her company." But this was not all. The " properties " must be good, and "she does not accept the scenery found in stock," and that everything must be of the best possible description." It is not surprising that Mr. E. B. Cdllendar, of the Sheffield Theatre, did not accept Mrs. Langtry's terms. ' LONGEVITY.—The obituary of the Times of the 17th inst. contained some remarkable illustrations of prolonged exist- once in the case of 10 persons, viz., three ladies and seven gentlemen, whose united ages amounted to 857 years, giving an average of 85 Years and over eight months to each. . The eldest was a gentleman who had reached the great age of 95 years, the youngest of the same sex being 84; of the ladies the oldest was 84, and the youngest 80. The same obituary also recorded the deaths of 10 septuagenarians, averaginc, 76 years and ever eight months each. That a single day's , obituary of the Times .should record the deaths of a score of persons averaging 61 years and ever two months each is remarkable.

Felicia Dorothea Kate Dover, who was sentenced by Mr. Justice Cave to penal servitude for life for the manslaugh- ter of Thomas Skinner, by poison, at Sheffield, is still at Wakefield Prison. There she was seen by her Mother and sisters on Wednesday. They found her very cheerful and in excellent health. She said she had nothing to complain of in her treatment, but she spoke bitterly of it ha;ing been suggested to the jury that she put the arsenic in the food which caused Skinner's death. The prisoner says she is determined to meet bravely all that is before her, conscious in her innocence, which she hopes she will yet live to see made clear to the world. She is to be removed to Penton- ville.

THE COLLIERY EXPLOSION IN DURHAM.—Thoumands of people flocked to the scene of the colliery disaster at Trim- don on Saturday and Sunday, and the few trains which run to the village had to be supplemented by relief trains. Work in connection with the catastrophe was carried on with vigour. The bands of volunteers divided into two sections for the reeevery of the bodies, and the exploration of the mine continued unceasingly until late in the day, when five explorers were overcome by gas, which had pre- viously demonstrated its existence in different parts of the mine. A number of bodies were interred at Kelloe and Trimdon, in one large trench at the latter place and in separate graves at the former. It is estimated that 20,000 persons visited the scene of the disaster on Monday. At six o'clock the whole of the bodies were recovered, the total number of lives lost being 75. A CLERICAL PAUPER.—AI the meeting of the Colchester Board of Guardians the following note was presented by Mr. Quilter, master of the Union House :—" I regret to re- port that the late chaplain of the house, the Rev. Carter W. D. Moore, was admitted on Sunday last, the 12t1 inst., , being brought in by Mr. Dedman, the relieving officer. He ' had £3 7s. 9d. in his possession, also a gold watch and Chain, and he informed me that he had an income of £36 a year, and £2l in the Post-office Savings Bank. He likewise said that the auctioneer who sold his furniture must have a large swplus in hand, as his debts were very small. Will the Board advise me upon this case ? Mr. E. Smith, one of Guardians, said that an attempt was about to be made to get Mr. Moore lodgings in the town.—We find on reference to the Clerical Directory, that Mr. Moore, who is of the University of London, mid St. John's College, Cambridge, never advanced beyond a curacy in charge.

TIIE RATING OF MESSRS. SMITH AND SON'S BOOK- STALLS.—In the Queen's Bench Division of the High Court of Justice, Westminster, the case of the Queen v. the Justices of Lancashire, came before Mr. Justice Field, Mr, Baron Huddleston, and Mr. Justice Bowen, sitting in bane°. In this case a rule nisi had been obtained calling upon the res- pondents to show cause why a writ of certiorari should not issue compelling them to bring up an order made by them at quarter sessions, quashing a poor-rate made upon Messrs. Smith and Son, in respect of a bookstall at Ulverston Station. The rule was obtained on the ground that the appel:ants (Messrs. Smith and Son) had not given to the Assessment Committee twenty-One days' notice in writing of their intention to appeal against the rate. 'The appellants admitted that they did not give the necessary notice, but argued that the 'Assessment Committee relieved them of

that duty, and that they appeared before the committee, who, after hearing their objections to the rate, refused their relief. The Assessment Committee, on the other hand, argued that, as the appellants had not given them the notice prescribed by statute' they werellentitled to have the rule made absolute. Mr. Hulton appeared to show cause against the rifle being made absolute, and Mr. Glen supported it.— Their lordships discharged the rule with costs. AN OFFENDING PICTURE.—A case which has caused much amusement in Paris came before one of the law courts. Two years ago, M. Alexandre Dumas purchased from M. Jacque', the water-colour painter, a Pleture exhibited in the Palais de Plndustrie, at a price which the artist says was nominal, and which he only accepted for the pleasure of having his work of art in the collection of such a distinguished writer and connoisseur as M. Dumas. Recently M. Dumas sold this painting for 10,000 francs. The artist, furious at a profit having been nude out of what he considered a sort of present, revenged himself in a curious fashion. He made a striking portrait of M. Dumas for the water-colour exhibition, repre- senting him as sitting among all sorts of curiosities on sale, and described the picture in the catalogue as a "Portrait of I a Bagdad Jewish Stallkeeper." The picture naturally at- tracted vast crowds to the exhibition. M. Dumas made an attempt to have it removed, but M. Jaequel, as a member of the Society of Water-colour Painters, asserted his right to so many square inches on the wall, and the attempt failed. Just as the exhibition was about to be closed, M. Lipmann, the son-in-law a Alexandre Dumas, came into the salon, smashed the glass which covered the offending portrait, pushed his stick through the picture in several places, and would have destroyed it altogether but for the intervention of the attendants. Meanwhile, M. Alexandre Dumas had caused a summons to be served on the proprietor of the gallery and the secretary of the Water-colour Society, de- manding the removal of the portrait. The case was heard, and the court made a provisional order for the remoyalAof - the picture, pending further proceedings.

div.head: OPINF)INS OF THE PRESS.
div.p: OPINF)INS OF THE PRESS.
THE HOUSE OF LORDS COMMITTEE

The FiTeman's Journal says that "any tn:-:n must see that the future of Liberalism is with the Radical wins, and if the Radical wing succeeds to its inheritance, it will make short work of that. Assembly the sole keys to which are accident of birth or favour of the Sovereign. The wonder is that the House of Lords has lasted so long."

The Daily News remarks :—The action of the House of Lords is practically indefensible, and happily the protnpti= tude of the Ministry in counteracting it by Mr. Gladstone's proposed resolltion has so far prevented any mischievous results. A hostile inquiry into the working of the Land Act which Parliament has so lately patsed would have terrorised the commissioners and assistant commissioners, shaken the confidence of the tenants in the permanence of the Act, and produced the gravest .mischief in provoking resistance by one class and discontent in the other.

' The Stanclaed has the following in anticipation of the situation between the Lords and Commons :—ln spite of all • Mr. Gladstone may say or the House of Commons may resolve, the Select Committee of the Lords will be appointed, Avill hold its sitting., aud will take evidence. The House of ' Commons, after a prolonged and embittered discussion, mis- chievous to Ireland and to be deprecated for its probable influence on England, will accept Mr. Gladstone's motion. The Government will have received a declaration of confi- dence fairly proportionate to the numerial strength of their majority. But what will be the next step? There is really no step at all that Ministers can take. They might, indeed, go to the country. But upon what pretext can they do that when the House of Commons declares that it is satisfied with them? The only aim of such a proceeding would be to quash the Select Committee of the Lords by a dissolu- tion but it would be rather too high a price to pay for such an Object. The Government will receive from the House of Commons the vote they want, and the Lords will be left in reality the masters of the situation. The Times thus counsels moderation to the Peera :—The Conservative majority in the House of Lords have laid upon them in this matter a responsibility which cannot be lightly dismissed. The Prime Minister has declared that the resolu- tion of which he has given notice is justified in the opinion of the Cabinet ty "grave reasons having relation to the first necessities of society in Ireland." This declaration, made on the responsibility and with the official knowledge • of the Executive, may be grounded in error, but the House of Lords, which has given abundant proofs within the past fifty years of its public spirit and its moderation, will under- stand that a statement of such a character is a most im- portant factor in the question. Keeping this in view, it is now the duty of the Conservative peers to consider dis- passionately whether from their own point of view the ad- vantages of proceeding with the inquiry by Lord Donough- more's Committee are not out-weighed by the manifold mischiefs of a constitutional crisis—a conflict between the two houses, not en a question of principle, but on one of ex- pediency, and a plunge into a whirlpool of controversy. The Pall Nall Gazette slvs:—The inquiry will be, and is designed to be, a sort of Vigilance Committee for intimi- dating the Land Court. What will be the effect on the Irish peasants? What will be the state of mind of a tenant who has (possibly at the risk of his life) been induced to go ' into the court, and whose rent has been lowered? He sud- denly hears—for this is the version that will certainly reach him—that one House of Parliament is already far on the way to repudiating the authority under which relief has been afforded to him, and that the judges who decided his case have been summoned, like criminals to the dock, before a select inquisition of his hereditary oppressors. This, we repeat, is the light in which the committee will strike him., What, again, will. be the effect of this reopening of tke question in Ulster, where even Tory candidates have to pledge themselves to reopen the question, indeed, but in the sense of making the Act go further, not of cutting it down ? The Lords who voted for the committee cry more loudly than anybody.else how alarming ic the condition of Ireland, and how ,critical, how honeycombed the population is with Communism, disaffection, and the spirit of violence. It this be so, if the alarmists believe their own charges, what can be more rash and mischievous than to pour oil on the flame by playing fast and loose with the Land Act ?

div.head: BRADLAUGH DEBATE.
div.p: THE BRADLAUGH DEBATE.

The limes says :—Whatever justificttion they may have been for Mr. Gladstone's abdication of his functions as leader of the House when it resolved against his advice to forbid , Mr. Bra(llaugh to take the oath, it is evident there is no analogy between that case and the one under discussion last night. Granting that the Minister of the day may decline to give effect to a resolution of whi ch be does not approve, it in no way follows that he may properly refuse to assist the House in repelling a wanton insult. The Daily News says that Mr. Gladstone acted through- out the exciting scenes of yesterday with the consistency, courage, and dignity which has marked his conduct in deal- ing with this question from first to last. In all these respects his behaviour was in marked coatrast with th4t of the leader ' of the Opposition. The Daily Telefpraph observes :—The House has done more than merely shake off an offensive incubus, which was exposing it to popular ridicule and paralysing the work of legislation. By its vote of yesterday it has vindicated, as it was bound to vindicate,.its.own dignity and honour. Mr. Bradlaugh committed political suicide when he went through his profane pantomime. The Standard says :—The overwhelming majority which pronounced in favour of Mr. Bradlaugh's ejection faithfully reflects the national feeling, and the country will hear to- day of the decisive step that has been taken with genuine relief. •

The Daily Chronicle remarbti :—The expulsion of Mr.' Bradlaugh must be regarded as an exercise of power wholly out of accord with the instincts and spirit of the age. Throughout the whole of his ntest Mr. Bradlaugh has undoubtedly had constitutional right on his &de. • The Morning Post says :—The House rightly vindicated its outraged uignity. The Morning Adrestiser observes :—Sir Stafford North- cote's complaint of Mr. Gladstone's conduct will be shared by the constituencies. The Dublin Express says :—Should the constituency re- cover its senses, and reject Mr. Bradlaugh, the greatest scandal of modern times will be at an end. The Freeman's Journal says that Mr. Bradlaugh's chances of re-election are very dubious. The Irish Times says:—To be consistent, Mr. Gladstone should accompany the Liberal zandidate to the borough, and stump it in his behalf.

div.head: MARRIAGE OF PRINCE LEOPOLD.
div.p: THE MARRIAGE OF PRINCE LEOPOLD.
ARRIVAL OF THE PRINCESS HELEN.

Prince Leopold and the Princess Helen landed at the Queenborough pier on Tuesday, and left the station in a special train en route for Windsor. The platforms of the pier were crowded with visitors, who gave their Royal Highnesses a hearty welcome. The Marchioness cf Ely met their Royal Highnesses on the landing sage, and, as representing Her Majesty, welcomed the Princess to Eng- land. Prince Leopold accompauied the Princess to the Royal sateen. The Princess, who carried a bcuquet, was dressed in a travelling costume of dark green satin cloth, trimmed with velvet, a velvet jacket to match, a green velvet hat, trimmed with green tulle and relieved with a single bird's wing of silver grey. Airal Sir Reginald Macdonald and several officers of Duncan accom- panied the l'rincess from the Victoria and Albert. The Prince and Princess's travelling companion was Fraulein von Lobell, and their Royal Highnesses were accompanied on board the yacht from Flushing by Prince Waldeck, Baron Steckhausen, Captain van der Wence, and General du Plat. The Victoria, Royal yacht, left Flushing at 10-30 on Mon- day night, and had a fine passage across, the only impedi- ment being a heavy haz,, which necessitated steaming slowly, and this acceunted for the arrival off Sheerness at least an hour after she was. expected. At 12-30 the train conveying Prince Leopold and the Princess Helen arrived at Windsor.. Princess Beatrice met the travellers at the station, whence they drove to the Castle. A large number of persons bad assembled to witness their Royal Hignesses' arrival, and cheered them heartily. Windsor was decorated with flags, and the bells of St. Geo Age's and the parish church were rung.

div.head: EMPRESS OF AUSTRIA.
div.p: THE EMPRESS OF AUSTRIA.

Her Imperial Majesty will have no pleasing recollection of the day's hunting with Sir Watkin Wynn's hounds on Saturday, owing to the shocking character of the weather. The meet was at Whitchurch, and by 10 o'clock the hounds had arrived by special train from Ruabon, via Chester, a large number of horses and gentlemen also coming by the same train. There was likewise a special train from Oswestry and Crewe. The field was a large one. Her Majesty artived at Sandford Ilall at 11-15, but the whereabouts was only known to a few, and, to put the crowd off the scent, the hounds were taken to , Ighttield, and thence on to Sandford, by which time the ' crowd had considerably decreased. Her Majesty being in waiting the hounds were at once taken to the covers about Sandford, all of which were drawn blank, as was also Ash- ford Pool. The party then trotted to Cloverley, where a fox was found in one of the woods near the hall. He made for the Styche, passing by which he went down the hill, over the brook, across the Market Drayton and Wellington Rail- way, then over the highroad, crossing the river Tern, and then right into Buntingsdale Park (Mr. J. Tayleure's), where a check occurred,being afterwards hunted to Pell Wall, where, after an exceedingly fast run, he was given up. The whole of this run was in the midst of a blinding storm of hail, rain, and wind, and everyone was drenched to the skin. Sir Watkin Wynn's hounds met at the Higher Wych, on Mon- day, and, for the first time within living memory, this was ' done simply to hoodwink, the public and to prevent her Majesty being too numerously interviewed. The i'itse had the desired effect. Her Majesty, attended by Prince Lich- tenstein, Major Bulkelev, and her pad groom, Tom Healey, ; had ridden across the country from Combermere Abbey to ' Iscoed Park, the residence of Mr. Godsal, J. P., where the hounds were taken. A fox was found directly in a cover near the hall, but, owing to indifferent scent, he gained a good deal at start. He headed first of all for Hanmer, then bore to the right as if for Burton's Wood, short of which he turned and made back for Icoed, near where, after a nice run of forty minutes over a beautiful country, he was I ultimately lost. The Empress had a thoroughly enjoyabl,

Iday's sport with the Cheshire hounds on Tuesday. The dar was one, and a large an distinguished company attended the meet at Wrenbury Statibn. The hounds were taken to Major Starkey's Gorse, which proving blank, a move was made to CJinbermere. where_a fox was found. He, however, soon got to ground. The field then trotted to Baddiley Gorse, where a grand fox was disturbed. At a rattling pace he went away, heading for Hurleston, but, leaving it to the right, he turned towards Ridley. Wood, short of which, however, he again turned round to the right over the brew of the hill, and ran a good ring round the valley; close to Baddiley Gorse, where after a very fine and fast ran of forty-five minutes, he was killed. The hounds then got on to a travel- ling fox, and ran him round Wrenhury, where he escaped. After this an attempt was made to dig outra fox that had gone to ground about noon, failing which her Majesty and suit, the afternoon being well advanced, left for Combermere.

div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.
At a crowded nucting of the Leeds railway servants, resolutions were passed in favour of a reduction in the hours of labour.
At a meeting of chainmakers, on Monday, at Cradley Heath, it was announcQd that the masters had conceded advances ranging from 10 to 15 per cent.

A month's notice has been tendered by all the operative spinners employed by Messrs. Simpson and Co., at their Hartford Mills, Preston. The men, who are members of the association, state that they are underpaid. IRONWORRERS.—FoIIowing the recent advance of iron- workers' wages in the North of England, South Stafford- shire, 311 d Shropshire, the ironmasters of North Staffordshire have increased the wages of all puddlers, shinglers, and forge rollers 7:1; per cent. The men, however, are dissatisfied with this, as they say iron has risen in price ever 50 per cent. during the last 12 months, and urge that the advance given them dces not meet their share of such increase.

At a meeting of the sh ireholders of the Greenacres Spin- ning Company, Oldham, held on Saturday night, great complaints were made in reference to adulteration of cotton. The Chairman said that of the cotton bought by the com- pany during the past quarter 19 to 20 per cent. was adul- terated. Several shareholders said that it was adulterated with sand to considerably above 20 per cent. The meeting was the stormiest that has been held in Oldham for some time past.

THE Inos TminE.—The under-hand puddlers employed at the Berry Hill Ironworks, Hanley, not having shared in the recent advance of 711 per cent. in the wages of other ironworkers of the district, struck work on Monday night. The over-hands refuse to give them any increase, on the ground that, when a reduction in wages was made during the recent depression, they did not reduce their under-hands, who now, therefore, have no claim to an advance. At a meeting; of the shareholders of the Darlington Iron Company, called by the liquidators, resolutions were adopted for the reconstruction of the company by raising £50,000 consolidated preference shares at 7 per cent., and appointiue• as directors the four gentlemen who have been suggested for that purpose. Mr. Barmingham, who origi- nally opened the concern, it was stated, would take £lo,o'oo of the preference capital. An application will be made to the Court to stop the liquidation proceedings. SILT INIINEs.—A statute of 1872 provides that gunpowder or otter explosive or inflammable substance shall only be used underground in a tnetalliferous mine under ceitain stringent regulations. Mr. Robertson, ALP., proposed, ill a bill that he has introduced into Parliament, to authorize a Secretary of State to exempt any slate mine from the neces- sity of observing these regulatitns. The rules in question are that the explosive shall not be stored in the mine or taken into it in cases containing more than 41b.; that a workman shall not have in use in any one place more that one such else ; that certain c.mditione be observed in charg- ingholes f,4r blasting; and that a charge that bas missed fire shall not be unrammed.

A large and important meeting of cotton manufacturers from North and North-east Lancashire was on Tuesday held in Manchester, for the purpose of considering the advisa- bility of adopting short time. The position to which the trade has been reduced by over-production was said to be serious, and the chairman of the meeting (Mr. Ashton, of Darwen,) intimated that it was necessary something should be done to avert impending ruin. Shortotime was unani- mously recommended as the only practicable remedy, and a resolution was passed declaring it to be "necessary in the interests of the trade to adopt shPrt time in the manufactur- ing department." A committee to consider how this resolu- tion could be carried out most advantageously was appointed, and the meeting was adjourned for a week. THE CORN TRADE.—The Mark-lane El-press says:—" A week of changeable weather has brought heavy storms of rain and snow in the north, but very Tittle rainfall in the . southern districts of England. The interruption to spring work has been very slight, and good progress continues to be made with sowing. All crops remain healthy, and as the rapid growth which characterised the start has not been ! continued they are now in an exceedingly good position for the time of the year. The trade kr English wheat has now no distinct feature, as compared with that for foreign, by which prices are completely ruled. Even the best qualities have sold slowly at rates which have continued to decline from Monday last, and inferior parcels for the present are practically unsaleable. Flour passes slowly into consump- tion at rates which show perhaps a smaller decline relatively than those for wheat. The trade for spring corn of all descriptions is now affected by the demand for seed parcels in the provincial exchanges, but rates for consumption may be considered to be unaltered from those of the previous week. Values for malt are scarcely so well maintained as they have been, but there is no quotable change nor any improvement in the demand. THE LANCASHIRE IRON TRADE.—Manchester, Wednesday. —There is still only a very limited amoant of buying going on in the iron market. Lancashire makers of pig iron are still kept well employedovith deliveries under contracts, but as these are being rapidly worked off without being replaced more anxiety is shown to secure new orders. No- minally the Nat quotations for Lancashire pig iron delivered equal to Manchester remain at 525. Gd. less 25 per cent., but both in local and district brands buyers with good offers could place them at under 50s per ton less 23,-. Finished iron makers in this district are also kept busy with work in hand, but the new inquiries coming in are less numerous, and the greater readiness with which specifications can now be completed is an indication that there is less pressure for deliveries. The advance of 2Jk per cent, in wages in Staf- fordshire stands in the way of any reduction in prices. Tho engineering branches of trade continue actively employed.

TEE LANCASIIIRE COAL TRADE —Manchester,Wednesday. —The coal trade of this district continues depressed. For household purposes the demand is extremely limited owing to the exceptional mildness of the serson. The limited de- mand for house-fire purposes has ales thrown supplies of the commoner classes of round coal upon the market. Best Lancashire c)als are only in exceptional cases realising more than about Os per ton at the pit, seconds average about is, and common round coal 5s to Gs per ton. Engine classes of fuel move off tolerably well, and, with the limited quan- tity of round coal now being screened, slack has rather a tendency ta harden ; supplies, however, are as a rule still quite sufficient to meet the requirements of the market. At the pit month bury averages about 4s Gd to ss; best slack 33 9d to 4s 3d; and inferior sorts 33 to 3,3 Od per ton. In the shipping trade there is rather more activity, but low prices continue to be quoted.

THE EXrRA.ORDINARY FRA.LTDS BY A WOMAN. Each succeeding thy adds to the marvellous story of the Liverpool adventuress, and asthe perusal of the hundreds of letters that were in her possession proceeds, the ramification, of her plot exfend. One of the latest discoveries is a full and extraordinary confessior, dated April 23, 1878, and addressed to Lord Coleridge. In it the writer alleges that her mother has had no hand in her extraordinary proceed- ings, but she then goes on to say that not more than the I two-hundredth part of her ill-gotten plunder was enjoyed by herself, the so-called Birmingham • dupes having black- mailed her to a terrible extent. Whether this confession is true, is,of course, a matter in which doubt may be reasonably entertained, but as she pointedly charges Gething with being the most devouring of her "friends," it is possible that between the two a-good deal of truth may come out. Mr, Poland, Solicitor to the Treasury, visited Birming- ham, on Tuesday, and after examining many of the docil- ments and letters rtating to the adventuress, returned to London. He expressed general opinion that the case was one of the most romantic within the -annals of the criminal law. It will in all probability be found, should the police touch on the romantic side of the case, that the adventuress did not on her own account assume the character cf "Lord Clinton," but that on the other hand the deception was suggested to her by different persons, who have since taken up the deceit for pecuniary profit, and 'who, it is not un- likely, will yet find themselves in the dock of the police court, together with the adventuress, on charges of con- spiracy. Apart from being an attendant at Prestwich Asylum, governeSs in Bnckinghamshire, and a barmaid at Wolverhampton, Miss Furneaux was for a short time an assistant to Mr. James Kent, a Birmingham boot manufac- turer.

Birmingham Police Court was on Thursday crowded by ladies and others, who considered themselves fortunate in finding a place into which they could squeeze themselves while the magisterial inquiry into the frauds of the woman Furneaux was in progress. Miss Furneaux, it appears, has changed considerably for the tfbrse in appearance since her arrest, and on Thursday presented a pinched and haggard appearanes, in strong contrast to her former self-satisfied and comfortable air. The case before the court was i tieat of the man Bevnon, the engineer. He described his ntro- duction to ihe woman by Gething, in 1874, the story then told him bin g that she was really Lord Arthur Clinton, lut le•ng under the Queen's displeasure she dressed as a woman, and called herself Furneaux. Gething re- marked, too, that it would be a very remunerative proceed- ing to supply his lordship witb money, and Beynon said he had a little, an .1 was wilting to speculate. He began with £5. and followed with other amounts, and in 1877, upon (riving up to Getbing all former receipts, received a pro- issory note for £6,000 signed ' Lanesborough." Miss Furneaux, it appears, frequently related the story of Boulton and Park, and explained that the Queen bad decided that she should be known as the Earl cf Lanesbotough. Beync,n then gave further information as to the sums of money he cil had advanced, the receipt of communications from Lord Coleridge, and his visit to Balmoral with Miss Furneaux, and said that Gething always acted as Furneaux's agent. The case was adjoutned until March 2.

div.p: , majority by which a debate may be closed should be a proportional one. But why if a simple majority carries a measure in the House, should there be a pro- portional majority to close a debate? As Mr. Gladstone stated on Monday—and his reminder is most apposite—a simple majority of five threw out the Melbourne Government in 1839, a similar majority overthrew Lord John Russell's Government in 1866, a smaller majority—three—threw out Mr. Gladstone's Government in 1873, a majority of two brought Government Education under the control of the Com- mittee of Council, a majority of one read the Reform Bill in 1831 while a like majority could have. thrown it out, and a majority of one enabled Pitt to go forward with the Act of 'Union. If, then, a small majority decides the fate of Ministries and is the means of carrying important measures, surely it is not unreasonable to ask that the same majority should rule in other and less important matters. The limita- tions within which the cloture can be applied, if the resolutions be carried, are sufficient to secure ample representation for the minority ; the bare majority is the only safe and sure principle on which to act, and as the country unanimously calls for a reform of Par- liamentary Procedure on that line,it is the duty of its representatives to carry out its wishes by adopting the resolutions which the Government in its collective wibdom and responsibile for the conduct of the busi- ness of the nation has thought fit to submit. The proposals are made ostensibly to facilitate the progress of legislation, but really to cope with the vexatious obstruction, of which Mr. James Lowther may be said to be the father. The Opposition when enjoying the sweets of office experienced so much of it that Sir Stafford Northcote himself proposed a standing order to the House, and which was generally accepted in the hope of being effectual, but which signally failed in the object it had in view. That being the case, the present Government are entitled to hearty co-operation and support from their opponents in an honest en- deavour to solve a difficulty which manifestly must be for the advantage of both parties alike.

div.head: LOCAL NOTES.
div.p: LOCAL NOTES.

The Rev. 'W. Preston, M.A., vicar of Holy Trinity Church, Runcorn, has been appointed honorary secretary to the Palestine Exploration Society, which is carrying on the interesting wotk of carefully exploring the Holy Land, where are—

" T,.ose holy fields Over whosb aci es walk'd those blessed feet, Which fouiteen hunched years ago were wird, For our advantage, on the bitter cross." The total nett receipts at the Farnworth Parish Church tea meeting, just held, amounted to £3O 3s. 4d.

Runcorn can now boast of a local musical composer in the person of Mr. EliNd Billingsley, the well-known organist of the very fine chapel which the Primitive Metho- dist denomination possess in Greenway-road. The work which Mr. Billingsley has produced is a Service of Song entitled " The Rasket of Flowers," which has been given during the week, at his own place of worship, and is spoken of in terms of high commendation.

Runcorn has been the scene of a very sad boat accident during the week, by which two young men lost their Mr. R. M. Brooke, J.P., happened to be near the spot where the accident occurred, at the time when the canoe was first observed to be in its perilous position, and the noble manner in 'which he exerted himself with the object of helping the unfortunate rung men, is the talk of the town. It is such deeds as these which tend to break down the harriers raised by etiquette between class and class. It is gratifying to know that the jury who held tire inquest in the case made a public acknowledgment of the humane comcluet of the son of Sir Richaid Brooke, Bart.

The members of the Young Men's Christian Association at Runcorn move to their new premises over the Runcorn Coffee and Cocoa Rooms on Monday next. Mr. George Rhodes has been elected to the vacant seat on the Runcorn Board of Commissioners, and I have no doubt he will prove quite worthy of all the good things said about him by his friend Mr. Meadowcroft, the worthy agent of the Bridgewater Navigation Co. Superintendent Barker is making matters very lively for the licensed victuallers of Widnes, and it is to be hoped that any of those who have been lax in the conduct of their houses of late will take the hint, and be more careful, unless they wish to see their names figure in the black list at the next Licensing Sessions. Quite a sensation was caused in the town on Tuesday, by the conviction of Mr. Sankey, the landlord of the Grosvenor Hotel, and surprise is expressed on every hand that a gentleman who has hitherto had the reputation of conducting one of the largest hotels in the town in a very creditable manner, should have been fined so heavy a sum as £lO and costs. Many of your readers will be a little astonished to hear that the death rate of Widnes for the year ending July last has only reached the low figure of 16.92 per 1,000. Con- sidering the state of the atmosphere in that town during many days of the week, I am inclined to think that this is only another proof of the statement that figures can be made to prove almost anything.

Like the Lord Mayor's fool, the officials at the Runcorn Workhouse evidently know what is good for them. For the purpose of having a good "tuck in" on Christmas Day, a quantity of ducks and fowls were procured and duly cooked, and subsequently they received the happy despatch. No doubt they were much enjoyed, but after the feast the " lawin " has to b:?. squared. In this instance it was intended that should be done by. the unhappy ratepayers, and it appear that they are to be the victims. The Master of the workhouse without any authority ordered the delica- cies, he charged the Guardians with the amount, and when his account came to be audited he was surcharged to the extent of 193., because the diet was not " necessary or justifiable," and also because the said sum had been "un- lawfully paid and charged japon the funds of ths Runcorn Union." The Local Government Board has remitted the surcharge and I very much regret it. Because a person feels his pocket being touched more acutely than anything else. However, the offeuce will surely not be repeated. Had ducks add fowls been held to be necessary and justifiable diet, next year the Runcorn officers would have wanted a case or two of champagne to wash them down. Poor Bradlaugh, what is to become of him? He is foiled on every hand. The House of Commons will not have him and the law courts nearly always decide against him. On Wednesday he was expelled St. Stephen's, whilst the follow- ing day the Lords Justices of Appeal refused him a new ' trial in the action successfully brought against him to recover penalties for having unlawfully taken his seat in the House of Commons. Though I detest the irreligious views which Mr. Bradlaugh holds, and abhor some of the moral doctrines to, which he has given publication, yet I sympa- thise with his political creed, and I would that there were more such earnest advocates of advanced Liberalism. From the hour that he was first elected member for Northampton up to Wednesday last he has occupied. a somewhat unique position. He ha S himself personally been partly within and partly without the House of Commons, and the constituency, noted for its cobbling, was somewhat humorously represented by Punch the other day as being in the position of a person with—
"One shoe off, and one shoe on, Hi diddle dumpton North-amp-ton."

Mr. Bradlaugb, in an excess of zeal on Tuesday and Wed- nesday, tried to put the other shoe on, and he was defeated. I am afraid that by his indiscretion he has alienated much of that sympathy which might otherwise have been ex- tended to-wards him in what may be termed the "battle of the oaths," but I sincerely hope now that another appeal is to be made to the ballot box he will not suffer there. It may be a misfortnne that so important a question as that now at stake should have to be fought over a person who is obnoxious; but when a ?matter of into oblivion. is involved, personality must sink oblivion. Why, the Tories have only, to use a homely phrase, been providing a stick with which to break their own back, for they can no more keep Charles Bradlaugh, as the representative of Northampton, out of the House, than I can. I think it was O'Connell who was elected for Limerick three times before the House of Com- mons became alive to a sense of its duty. Mr. Bradlaugh has been elected for Northampton twice, and I confidently predict that on Thursday next he will be elected a third time its representative. There may be again another struggle on the floor of the House, but it is as certain as that the sun shall rise to-morrow he will be admitted within the chosen circle. I have heard it said—and not, I believe, without some truth—that it is Mr. Bradlaugh's motion on the pen- sion list which is the great bugbear. If ever that celebrated resolution is moved, I pity Lord Randolph Churchill and others of his class. FLACCUS.

RUNCORN ELLESMERE STREET IMPROVEMENT CLASS.— At the weekly meeting on Monday evening, Mr. E. Jones presided, and an interesting essay on "Total abstinence," was read by Mr. John Holford. A discussion followed in which Messrs. C Undy, R. Moore, F. Clark, J. Stubbs, and Davies took part,

div.head: EXAMINER, SATIIIII)AY, FEBRUARY 25, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATIIIII)AY, FEBRUARY 25, 1882.
HALTON PARISH' CHURCH CHOIR FUND.—The Revs. L. D. Lyon Bennett, of Little Leigh, and E. Preston Ander- son, of Hulrne, preached at Halton Parish Church on Sunday on behalf of this fund. .

REVIVAL SERVICES AT WIDNES. —On Sunday, revival services were held at the Primitive Methodist chapel Hutchinson-street, and addresses delivered by the Rev. J. Morton, superintendent (of Warrington), Mr. J. Bray, and others.

RUNCORN CONGREGATIONALISM—HOME MISSION SER- vlcEs.—On Sunday, two sermons were preached by the Rev. J. D. Thomas, the pastor at Bethesda Congregationll chapel, Runcorn, on behalf of the Home Mission Fund. The collec- tions realiset4 £4 15s. 9d.,—a sum slightly in advance of those of last year.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.—The fort- nightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tues- day. There were present Messrs. John Ashton (in the chair), James Darbyshire, C. Rigby, J. Midwood, J. Chal- loner, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). Tha business was of a routine character.

HALTON MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY. —0 II Mc.n. day evening, the weekly meeting wu held, and the Rev. J. Bateman presided. Mr. R. Hughes read a paper on "The opening of national graveyards to Nonconformists!' The esslist considered that Nonconformist raisisters ought to receive the fees in the case of persons buried by them. A discussion followed in which Messrs T. Miller, S. Barrow, J. Looker, J. Hencock, and A. E. Davies were the principal speakers. RUNCORN AND THE SPRING TIDES. 024 Sunday and Monday, large crow& visited the pier head at Runcorn, in order to satisfy their curiosity as to the predicted height to which the spring tides would attain; and many of the visitors were from Widnes and the surrounding districts. Though the river was, of course, exceptionally high, it was not so boisterous as the inhabitants have seen it on many occasions, owing to the wind not being a favourable one for increasing the force of the waves.

HALTON PARISH CHURCH MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETL—The weekly meeting of this society was held in the Girls' Schoolroom on Tuesday evening, when Mr. Miller gave an essay entitled, "The mistakes of the late Govern- ment." Mr. B Haddock officiated as chairman, and there was a good attendance of members. The following gentle- men took part in the discussion :—The Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs. James Craig, John %V. haddock, Frederick J. Nor- man, and Benjamin Haddock. A vote of thanks to the essayist was proposed by the Vicar, and seconded by Mr. J. W. Haddock, and one to the chairman was proposed by Mr. Hancock.

Mn. MARK Dow AT RuNcom—On Monday night, Mr. Mark Dow's concert combination company gave their entertainment in the Public Hall, Runcorn. There was a poor attendance, and this was, probably, attributable to the fact that though the date upon the placards announcing the entertainment was correct, the word Tuesday was very pro- minent, so that many people were unaware that Mr. Dow was in Runcorn that evening. Owing to the small atten- dance, only part of the usual programme was gone through, but it is only fair to add that the performaa gave the greatest satisfaction. At the close a number of presents— some of considerable value—consisting of gold and silver plated goods were distributed amongst the audience. RUNCORN PRISONERS AT CHESHIRE INTERMEDIATE SESSIONS.—At the Cheshire Intermediate Sessions on Tuesday, Patrick Whelan (30), labourer, pleaded guilty to obtaining by false pretences the sum'of 31. from Mary Elli- son, at Runcorn, on the 31st December, and also 40 oysters from Sarah Ann Bolton, 'also at Runcorn' and he was sen- tenced to three calendar months' with hard labour.—On Wednesday, Thomas Jones (23), labourer ; Mary Casey, al LAS Riley (19), s,ervant ; and Mary. Jane Gallagher pleaded not guilty to stealing £1 es., a knife, illOileyB and property of Charles Dowdell, at Runcorn, an the 3rd of February.—Mr. Burke Wood prosecuted, and the evidence clearly showed that all the three prisoners were aezing in concert. They were found guilty and sentenced to three months' imprisonment. Thomas Green was indicted for stealing a pair of trousers, the property of George Hill, iron turner, Union-street, and was sentenced to two months' im- prisonment, with hard labour.

UNITED LODGE MEETING OF Tilt 1.0.G.T. AT WIDNES.— On Thursday evening-a meeting of the united lodges of the 1.0.G.T. in Widnes took place at Unsworth's Dining-rooms. The following appointments for the night were made: Bro. T. Reay R.W.C.T.., Bro. Bradshaw W.S., Bro. Rescorl W.C., Bro. T. Glover WM., T. Baron W.1.G., Sister J. Reay W.D.N. A Telegram was read from Bro. J. Williams, District Chief Templar, saying that he could not possibly attend, but wishing every success to the meetiug. The !cretary (Bro. Bradshaw) read the report of the week's temperance mission,'and it was unanimously adopted. Bro. Webb moved a vote of thanks to Bro. Bradshaw for the efficent manner in which be had conducted the week's temperance mission. It was decided that united lodge meet- ings should be held quarterly. The election of a visiting deputy concluded the proceeding.

THE DOCK BOARD FRAUDS BY A RUNCORN CONTRACTOR. —John Jones (51), clerk, and John Beckett (58), contractor, Leinster Gardens, Runcorn, who had been found guilty at the previous Liverpool szsgions of committing certain frauds on the Mersey Dock and Harbour Board, were brought up for sentehce. Mr. Carver, who conducted the prosecution, said he had nothing further to say in the case. The specific charge was that the prisoners, on the 17th December, ob- tained, by means of false pretences, from William Noble, the suns of £1 13,3. di, the money of the Dock Board ; and also, on the 9as of November and the 12th of December, the sums of .El 6 and £1 Ns. by similar means, with intent to defraud the Dock-Board.—The prisoners were sentenced to three months' imprisonment esch, to date from the commencement of the last sessions.

"GOOD THINQ3." —Messrs. Goodall, Backhouse, Co., of White Horse-street, Leeds, have juft issued the sixth edition of a useful book of over a hundred pages, with the title of "Good things made, said, and done for every house and household." It contains an admirable selection of recipes for the preparation of various "good things for the table, compiled with the view of enabling houoekeepers, however humble their station in life, to prepare plain, whole. some, every-day dishes in an appetising manner, and also designed to show how simple fare may be rendered more tempting by the addition of certain delicious preparations that are worth much, but, fortunately for hungry humanity, cost little. The border of each page of the interesting little volume sets forth "words of wisdom " in the form of pro- verbs and mottoes, and at the end are a number of prescrip- tions for the cure of common ailments, and bills of fare for fourteen tasty dinners. Enough has been said to give an idea of the contents, and, when it is stated that a copy can be obtained by forwarding to the firm a penny stamp for postage, no doubt a goodly number of our readers will recognise the desirability of providing themselves with this aid to the provision of good things." - - -

WIDNES SCIENCE AND ART CLASSES.—On Monday even- ing, Major Plunkett, of the Royal Engineers, made the annual inspection of the above classes. After examining the register and the apparatus, he express6t; his complete satisfaction with the general management of the classes, and addressing himself more particularly to the students he urged upon them the importance of taking full notes of every lecture. Many failed, not because they were not suf- ficiently well up in the subject, but on account of the diffi- culty of expressing clearly in writing the answers to ques- tivs. The practice of taking full notes and correcting them at home would, he considered, obviate the difficulty, and when the Government examinations came the competi- tors would find that many of the questions were very similar to those they had already written fully about in their note books. (Hear, hear.) lie was glad to see such a large number-37—present at the chemistry class. Chemis- try was •a subject more closely connected with Widnes than with any other town in the kingdom—(bear, hear,)—and from this circumstance lie should naturally expect to find a large number of passes. However, as many of them were young, and this was probably their first year, they would not be discouraged if they failed, but continue to persevere in their studies, and another year they should find the ex- amination comparatively easy. (Applause.) He regretted they had not a laboratory in which to do practical work, but the next time he visited Widnes he hoped to find that they had established one in connection with their classes. (Applause.) The proceedings shortly afterwards terminated.

RUNCORN CAMDEN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS. —A pleasant literary evening was spent at the Camden improvement class on the 17th instant., when Mr. G. S. Hazlehurst gave a lecture entitled :—" An hour with the poets." There was a large attendance, and Mr. H. Randle, the president of the class, was in the chair. Mr. Hazlehurst had selected a few poets from whose works he read pieces and extracts which brought out the distinguishing feature of each. His method of dealing with his subject was very successful. The fist selection was from the "Ingoldsby Legends"—"Misadved- tures'at Margate"—the quaint humour of which was keenly appreciated by the lecturer and greatly enjoyed by the audience. By way of contrast, a few stanzas were read in a spirited manner from Sir Walter Scott's" Lady of the Lake." Then followed Coleridge's " Rhyme of the Ancient Mariner," a most weird tale, told in a manner that held the listeners spellbound. The many pithy sayings with which the writ- ings of Pope abound were laid under contribution by the lecturer, and numerous couplets were read containing senti- ments of value and instruction. The gem of the evening, however, was the ." Songs of sevens" by Jean Ingelow, in which a girl's history is given in seven periods of seven years—thus "Seven times one—exultation." "Seven times two—romance." "Seven times three—love." "Seven times four—maternity." "Seven times five—widowhood." "Seven times six—giving in marriage." "Seven times seven---longing for home. " The beauty of the subject was greatly enhanced by the reading of the lecturer, who seized I the spirit of the gifted poetess. Two humorous punning I pieces of Tom Hood's brought the lecture to a close. On the motion of Mr. Shore, seconded by Mr. Hopkins, a hearty vote of th:aik.c li.aE Accorded tc the lecturer.
On Monday Sir R. A. Cross presented to the House of Commons, a petition from the Warrington Conservative Association against the adoption of the new rule of pro- cedure.
The member for Warrington, Mr. J. Gr. MeMinnies, was amongst the minority who on Wednesday voted against the expulsion of Mr. Bradlaugh from the House of Com- mons.

H.R.H. the Prince of Wales has invited Dr. Henry Hiles to attend the great meeting at St. James' Palace on Tuesday next, and to support the motion for the estab- lishment of a Royal College of Music. GENEROUS GIFT TO ST. PAUL'S, WARRINGTON.—Mr. and Mrs. Matthew Chorley, of Scotland-road, have just pre. sented to St. Paul's Church an exceedingly handsome gas lamp for the west entrance to the church. The gift is both useful and ornamental.

ENTERTAINMENT AT 'WIDNES. n Saturday evening, Mr. Mark Dow gave his entertainment in the Volunteer Hall, • Widnes. Professor W. Stevens, a ventriloquist of considerable ability, highly delighted the audience, and Mr. W. Lacy's negro songs were well received. Mr. I'. W. Hall, an imper- sonator of character, gave a very satirical representation of a Tueton on board ship. WESLEYAN METHODIST HOME MISSIONS : WIDNES ,BRANCH.—The annual sermons, on behalf of these missions, were preached on Sunday by the Rev. R. Crozier. The usual public meeting took place on Tuesday evening, in Victoria-road Chapel. Mr. R. Fogg presided, and was sup- ported by the Rev. 'l'. H. Cummings (superintendent), and Messrs. 'l'. Sadler, 'l'. Robinson, and Benjamin Brown. Tne Rev. J. H. Cummings read the report, which showed that the local contributions during the twelvemonths had been of a satisfactory character. The Chairman, in eis opening speech, first referred to the general work in counection with the home mission and contingent fund. He remarked that perhaps the latter might require some explanation. Those who were the heads of households and places of business knew very well what contingencies were, and that they often proved a serious item. The Methodist Chtuch was one of the most prosperous in the world, and he believed that their prosperity was, to a great extent, the outcome of home mis- sion labours. After describing the advantages of the con- tingent fund, he pointed out that 272 circuits were assisted by it. He went on to speak of the position of ,England amongst nations, and argued that teis was greatly owing to our people being, to a huge extent, religious. if we kal more religious feeling, we should hear of fewer strikes and conflicts between capital and labour. Even if they took into acconnt the Roman Catholics in Widnes, there were thousands in the town who never attendtd any place of worship. He was very pleased to see that the Sunday school officers were taking up this matter amongst the children, but there was much scope for work even amongst children of a larger growth. He concluded with an appeal to those present to do what they could in a financial sense to assist the funds of the society, which was worthy of their heartiest. support—The Rev. R. Wilberforce Starr, of Liverpoo/, said that, in the course of his remarks, the Chairmm had alluded to Widnes as the black spot on the Mersey. They often heard this expression applied to the neighbouring city of Liverpool. He, nevertheless, thought that both the places referred to had been painted blacker than they desired, and they all knew the old proverb that even the Prince of Darkness was painted blacker than he really was. In Liverpool, during the year 1874, there were 21,000 summonses issued on account of drunkenness against 14,000 in 1881. This, he thought, was a matter on which they might congratulate themselves; and it certainly showed that the coffee and cocoa houses in that city had done a good work. The speaker next alluded to the home mission work in towns; and said that very often when he pissed through the ditty streets and frowsy courts of Liverpool, he thought of that other city, the heavenly Jerusalem, whose walls are of flaming jewels, and whose gates are set with pearls. Then, in imagination, he went inside the city, and saw that the smallest house was a mansion, and the meanest man a king and a priest. The air in that city was pure, and there were no coPrO there ee in the other; aneenw and sill had fled away, and crime was unknown. Mr. Starr referred, at some length, to his own experience in the Shetland islands, and next to the work which the society was doing in the armv and navy, lie pointed out that soldiers and sailors were peculiarly exposed to temptations, as they lived, so to speak, in a crowd. The public-house tempted them on one side, and on the other there was the house of her whose "feet took hold on hell." Lately, at Chatham, by the Munificence of a gentle- man who had purchased an old mansion as a home for the soldiers and sailors, a place had been provided which would be the means of effecting a great reformation in their morals, and prove a mighty engine for good. Re- felring to London, he spoke of the noble work which had been done by Lord Shaftesbury. If they had more such men as his lordship, they would bear less talk about a bloated aristocracy. If the delicate hands of England's nobles were oftener stretched out to the masses, there would been less bitter feeling between class and class. Lord Shaftesbury now wore a coronet, but the time would come when he would wear a crown. _ (Loud applause.)—On the motion of Mr. T. Robinson, seconded by Mr. T. Sadler, a vote of thanks was passed to the Chairman amid deputation, and the proceedings terminated. LECTURE AT WARRINGTON.—Under the presidency of Sir Gilbert Greenall, a lecture was delivered in the Work- men's Club, on Monday evening, by the Rev. James Mackie, a clergyman of the National Church of Scotland. There was a good attendance, and the lecture entitled, "A trip from Liverpool to Niagara," was attentively listened to. The tide in the Mersey was unusually high on Monday,. and the low lying land near the river was flooded to a nen- siderable depth. At Ellesmere Port a 22ft. tide was chronicled. At Frodsharn the marshes were flooded, and the vast expanse of water presented a magnificent spectacle. A vessel broke from her moorings, and was carried Jay the tide up the Weaver, but was rescued by a tug. At Chester the tide in the Dee was higher than for many years past, and cattle were surrounded on the meadows, and were rescued by boatmen with great diffictilty. se.

THE PROPOSED NATIONAL SCHOOL or Music.—The Prince of Wales has forwarded autograph letters to the Mayors of the more important provincial cities and towns announcing that he has acceded to the request to call a meeting in London, on Tuesday, the 28th inst., for the pur- pose of establishing a National School of Music for the instruction of all classes of Her Majesty's subjects, and requesting the favour of the attendance of the respective Nlayors. His worship the Mayor of Warrington (J. R. Pickmere, Esq.) is amongst the list of Mayors who have received letters, and he has accepted the invitation. PRESENTATION TO MISS CLARK, OF STOCKTON HEATH. —For upwards of 25 years this lady has led successfully what is termed by the Methodist body a society class. On Wednesday evening, the members of her class and a few friends met in the large vestry at Bold-street Chapel, and, after partaking of tea, the Rey. John Eglinton, the superin- tendent minister, took the chair. The meeting was opened in the usual way, after which he called upon Miss Pendle- bury to perform a very agreeable' task, viz,, to present t 9 Miss Clark a pair of gold spectacles, in recognition of her long and valuable services in connection with the class. The presentation was made in an appropriate speech, and was suitably replied to. Addresses by the Chairman, Messrs. Ford, Collier, and others, with sono-s by Miss Sherlock and harp solos by Miss Hettie Toft, brought a very pleasant evening to ?close.

Ont L.R.V. SHOOTING CuTn.—A handicap competition of the members of this club took place at the Lytum range, on Saturday afternoon, under very unfavourable circum- stances, the wind blowing from the left front and occa- sionally veering to the front. The distances tired at were 200, 500, and GOO yards, under the new Wimbledon regula- tions for 1882. This being the first practice of the club in the new position, combined with the stormy weather, had a serious effect on the scores, a few of which are given below :
