ST. MARY'S SCHOOL, LA'TCHFORD.—On Monday evening last the annual tea party and ball in connection with St. Mary's schools, Latchford, was held in the Public Hall. Tea was on the tables at six o'clock, to which over 300 per- sons sat down. The arrangements appeared to have been very satisfactorily carried out, owing chiefly to the strenuous efforts of the Rev. F. Thompson, who is acting for the Rev. F. Dallow, the latter being away recruiting his health. The committee of management, to whom great praise is due for the efficient manner in which. they discharged their duties, was as follows :—Messrs. T. Mather, J. Boyle, and J. Cranigan. After tea had been partaken of, the Rev. F. Thompson thanked those who had so generously assisted him in his endeavours to promote the interests of a mission that was in so much need. The hall was then cleared, and dancing indulged in until a late hour to the strains of Mr. iNlaskell's quadrille band, after which the assembly broke up, everything having passed off without a single hitch, and all having enjoyed themselves thoroughly.

COCIIIIEDGE MISSION MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.— The above society held its sixteenth weekly meeting on Monday night last, in the Mission-room, the chair being occupied by the president, Mr. B. Farrar. There was a large attendance of members and friends. The Chairman. in opening the meeting, explained the objects of the society and pointed out the success which had attended it, bringing out some of its members so as to enable them to speak with freedom before others. Mr. Wm. Runcorn sang "She wore a wreath of roses;" Mr. Wm. Willett gave a Lancashire reading, and Miss Travis sang "Cottage home." Mr. Wm. Willett then read an essay entitled "Home," upon which an animated discussion took place, and the views of the essayist were approved by 18 to 7. Miss Travis sang "Isle of beauty fare thee well ; " and Mr. Runcorn gave an ex- cellent rendering of "Tom Bowling." At the conclusion of the programme Mr. Hankinson proposed a vote of thanks to all who had taken part in the entertainment, which was seconded by Mr. Johnson, and carried with acclamation. The meeting was closed by the singing of the .Doxology.

div.head: RUNCORN COFFEE & COCOA HOUSE CONVERSAZ lONE AT WARRINGTON. COMPANY.
div.p: RUNCORN COFFEE & COCOA HOUSE CONVERSAZ lONE AT WARRINGTON. COMPANY.

IMPORTANT MEETING. The annual meeting of the Runcorn Coffee and Cocoa House Company was held yesterday afternoon, at the rooms, High-street. Mr. J. 0. Jackson, the president, occupied the chair, and there were also present the Rev. Canon Barclay, Messrs. John Simpson, G. S. Hazlehurst, Elijah Billingsley, S. C. Beckett, James Higgins, and Kniveton (secretary).— The annual report, which was taken as read, stated that the directors regretted the • , result of the year's business was not more favourable. The receipts for the twelve months amounted to £B9l Ns. Id. The calls had been mostly paid, and the bank charges would be largely reduced in future. The directors had let the rooms on the first floor to the committee of the Young Men's Christian Association,and had reason to hope that this arrangement would considerably increase the returns. Whilst regretting that the financial results were not more satisfactory, the directors were pleased to know that the company continued to confer a very great boon on the working classes, and contrihuted largely to sobriety and good order in the town.—Mr. SIMPSON moved the adoption of the report, which motion was seconded by the Rev. CANON BARCLAY, and passed.-31r. HAZLEHURST said that in the past the company had certainly not been a commercial suc- cess, but he considered it quite possible to adopt some means by which their financial position might be retrieved. Mr. Charles Wigg had written him a note stating that the whole business of the company had suffered from extravagance ' and mismanagement.—Mr. Stmrsoer said that Mr. Wig,* had never favoured them with a visit since the concern corn- menced.—Mr. HAZLEILURST remarked that he did not defend the observations made by Mr. Wigg.—Mr. BILLINGSLEY ob- served that he had often heard it said in the town by share- holders that it would beta great advantage if the real respon- sibility as to the management of the concern could be placed in the hands of some particular person.—Mr. Tiros. NORMAN did not think they would find one man in a thousand who would take such extensive premises, as the directors could not let them for lfss than £l3O a year.—Mr. HAZLEHURST explained that be referred to the lower rooms only, where refreshments were sold.—Mr. NORMAN replied that to let the rooms referred to by Mr. Hazlehurst would be handing over to seine one what was the very cream of the whole concern. It such a proposal were carried out, how could they make the other parts of the building pay? Their difficulties arose from the simple fact that certain parts of their large premises could not be profitably utilized, and that they had to pay interest on the large sum of money which had to be expended in various ways. He had, from the very first, said that the place was too large.—Mr. IlezryernusT observed that the bottom rooms mieht be let for £3O or £4O a year, and thcise above had now been rented to the Young Men's Christian Associa- tion.—Mr. JOHN SterpsoN did not think it would be possible for any private individual to work the concern on a more economical basis than that pursued by the present manager. (Hearrhear.) A year or two ago •Mr. Hazlehurst was a member of the Board of Directors, and one 12 months about £ll was lost owing to carrying out an idea submitted by him. Last year Mr. Hazlehurst wished a pastry cook to be obtained, who would have wanted 30s. a week, and a kitchen and ovens would have had to be provided for her. Mr. Hazlehurst wished to make their own buns and pastry, on , which a profit was now made, but he (the speaker) was sure that this would not continue to be the case if they did not purchase them and then resell them. Another idea of the gentleman referred to was to alter one of the front windows, so that pastry could be exhibited in it, which would spoil it as far as its present purpose was concerned. The suggestion as to letting the premises was quite impracticable. He (the speaker) believed the company were doing a good work in the town. Rather than the company should go to the wall, he took up a second hundrlld shares, and he would be quite willing, if necssary, to take up another hundred. He had not the slightest doubt, if they had a little patience, that the concern would prove a commercial success, as they had taken:nearly £9OO during the past twelve months. If this BUtal was spent at the public-houses instead of at the rooms, the consequence would be most disastrous to the moral welfare of the town„—Mr, HAZLEUCEST said Mr. Simpson had made rather an imam tent omission in his re- marks, and that was that when he (the speaker) asked that a pastry cook might be engaged, he agreed to pay any loss which might be incurred, if the proposal proved a failure.— Mr. SIMPSON thought it would have been a pity to name this circumstance.—Mr. PHILIP SrEarcere,N higlify compli- mented Mr. Hazlehurst for the interest which he had always shown in the rooms, and said he trusted that in the course of a year or two, they would be able to pay a dividend.—Mr. StemsoN said the sole cause of the peculiar position in which the company was placed arose from the fact that they had anticipated they could have commanded it large first class Custom, which had not been the *cese.—Mr. S. C. BECKETT criticised the balance cheat, and spoke hopefully of the future.—Mr. MEADOWCROFT thought there was some ground for the charge made that the concern had been begun rather extravagantly. [The Vicar: Hear, hear.] Had it not been for this, the results would have been very encouraging. (Hear, hear.) He did not think the concern could be better manag:,d than it was.—Mr. HAZLEIMRST said many poor men, who could not afford it, had been con- strained to put money in the society,' and now they were not getting any diyidend.—lt was resolved that the suggestions made by Mr. Hazlehurst should be considered at a directors' meeting.—On the motion of Mr. BILLINGSLEY, seconded by Mr. BEcKErr, and supported hy Mr. HAZLETIUBST, a vote of thanks was passed to the chairman and directors, after which the proceedings terminated.

By the legislative enactments of recent years the position of elementary teachers in this country has been greatly ! altered. The whole system of imparting instruction has been changed, and there has been adopted a more approved method by which greater responsibility is thrown upon the teachers. Statements which have appeared in these columns, from time to time, have amply proved that the teachers in ' Warrington have discharged their increased responsibility with honour; and, in further illustration of this, we need only refer to the high position which Warrington holds in the matter of education. About 12 months ago the Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. Pickmere) showed the estimation in which they hold the elementary teachers of Warrington and the district by inviting them to a conver- sazione, which was highly successful, and they again manifested their desire for the welfare of the teachers, on Tuesday evening, when another gathering of a similar nature took place. On the previous occasion the conver- sazione was held in the Art Gallery, but this year the invita- tions, which numbered over 300, were extended to the managers of schools, members of the Town Council, cor- porate officials, and private friends, and the assemb!y took place in the Public Hall. An attractive appearance had been imparted to the hall by Messrs. S. E. and R. Johnson, ! Bridge-street, by whom the decorations had been ably carried out. The Prince of Wales' Feathers, surrounded with small flags, were placed over the entrance door. The gallery rails were enveloped in white calico, festooned with dark crimson and relieved with the shields and flags of different nations, a feur-cle-lis being placed along the top. The floor under the centre gallery was laid with carpets, and two of the pillars were draped in muslin. Under the gallery was placed a large mirror, and on either side there was a cabinet on which were a number of flowers. Couches, chairs, and tables were also placed at this end of the room, which had a most comfortable aspect. The platform was decorated with a number of ferns and plants, and on a table in front was arranged a collection of atlases, copy books and other school requisities. The ante-room was utilised as a refreshment room, and every arrangement had been made to promote the comfort of the guests, who began to arrive soon after seven o'clock. Immediately on pas- sing through the ante-room into the ball the guests were re- ceived by the Mayor, who wore his chain of office, and the Mayoress, who held a splendid bouquet. During the recep- tion there was a performance on the organ by Mr. W. H. Spence, of Montreal, and W. S. Woods, of Warrington. His WORSHIP afterwards ascended the platform and ex-", ' pressed the pleasure the Mayoress, and he, himself, had at seeing so many present. The Mayoress, and himself, he stated, had done their best to obtain the names of, and send invitations to, the managers and teachers of all the schools in and around Warrington, and if any had been accidentally omitted he hoped they would be forgiven. The conversa- zione had been got up in honour of the elementary teachers of Warrington, and he remarked that the question of education was now regarded in a different light to what it was years ago. The teachers had not only to give lessms but to elevate the minds of those under their care, and to do all they could to enable them to became good men and woman. It was thought that teachers should be placed in a higher status ; .and the Mayoress and himself, in their humble way, were endeavouring to bring the teachers to the front. He hoped that a very pleasant and enjoyable evening would be spent, and that the gentlemen would attend to the wants of the ladies and see that they were well supplied with refresh- ments. His Worship concluded by thanking them for assembling in such large numbers, and for the kind recep- tion which had been accorded to him.

The carnavale havinc, been well sung, by Miss Pleb:mere, Mr. Reddish, and Mr.'Thurnham, Miss Riley gave "Love bail'd a little maid," in a charming manner and she was deservedly applauded. Mrs. E. and Miss Pickmere ably acquitted themselves in the duet " May bells ;" which was followed by the song "I fear no foe," sung with much power by Mr. Wright. Alderman Davies then engaged the attention of the audience for a short time by a humourous reading which created great laughter. "The lost chord," afterwards received an adequate interpretration at the bands of Miss Pickmere, and the musical part of the programme was concluded with "The gallants of England," ably rendered by Mr. Wright. An agreeable change was afforded by Professor Trevior, whose clever and entertaining con- juring and ventriloquial performances were much appre- c'ated. At the conclusion of the musical portion of the entertainment, _

Mr. D. W. FINNEY ascended the platform and briefly addressed the audience. He observed that he recognised in the entertainment something more than a mere desire on the part of the Mayor and Mayoress of Warrington to give physical enjoyment to a large number of teachers. He re- cognized in it a desire on their part to raise the tone of edu- cation in the borough of Warrington as well as the status of the teacher. And nothing, he ventured to think, could be more appropriate to secure those ends. Such 'gatherings would strengthen the hands of teachers in their arduous work, and he was sure it would encourage managers in their self-imposed tasks, and stimulate all classes of people to send their children regularly to school. He believed there was no class of men engaged in a work of a more momentous character than the teachers of this great country. They had ' to deal with the rising generation in their threefold char- antes of body, mind, and soul; and would anyone say there was no skill required here ? They might cultivate the , intellect and develope the physical powers, but if they negle,cted the moral part of a child's natuFe they made him, to say the least, only a clever man of the world, and not a Christian. Teachers had the moral and intellectual pro- gress of the world in their hands, and he thanked the Mayor and Mrs. I' ickmere for recognizing this fact. In speaking about education there was always on sad aspect about it— , there was no provision made for teachers in their old age, and no system of education would be perfect until it pro- vidtd for old and decayed teachers when their work had been well and faithfully done. On bshalf of the teachers he thanked the Mayor and Mayoress for their great kindness and liberality. The company afterwards Ojourned to the anteroom, where refreshments, which it is almost needless to add were of ex- cellent quality, were served. Subsequently, dancing was commenced, and continued until about a quarter to twelve, when a most enjoyable evening's entertainment was brought to a close. Messrs. C. White, D. W. Finney, W. div.head: SERVICE OF SONG AT RUSCORN.
div.p: SERVICE OF SONG AT RUSCORN.

Mr. Elijah Billingsley, the well nown and ab!e organist of Greemay-road Primitive Methodist Chapel, Runcorn; has lately compiled a service of song entitled "The baskct of flowers," which is published by •Mr. F. Pitman, Pater- noster-row, London. The " readings in connectior with the service are taken from a little work which is a great favourite with all juveniles, and we doubt not has been read weth much pleasure by many " children of a larger growth," entitled "The basket of flowers,' published by a London firm whose name is a household word amongst the lovers of cheap literature,

- The composition was given for the'first time in Greenwav- road chapel, on Wednesday and Thursday evenings. The handsome edifice had been beautifully decorated with ever- greens and artificial flowers. A basket of choice flowers was also hung in the centre of the chapel, which was very well filled au both evenings. The music was rendered by a select choir, numbering 100, under the able conductorship of Mr. William Handley. Mr. George S. Litzlehenst gave the readings from;which the interesting story, on which the composition is founded, in a very pleasing. manner ; and Mr. Billingsley presided at the organ with his customary ability. The various solos were rendered very effectively by a numter of willing friends. ;The audience appeared to be highly pleased with the performance, the profits upon which Mr. Billingsley has generously agreed to give to the trust funds.

At the close of Wednesday evening's performance, the Superintendent Minister (Mr. Pickwell) proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Hazlehurst, which was seconded by the Rev. J. D. Thomas and agreed to. The Rev. J. NOWELL moved that a similar resolution be passed in the case of Mr. Handley, which was seconded by Mr. SHAW, and carried. Mr. PICKWELL, on behalf of the trustees of the chapel, proposed a hearty resolution of thanks to Mr. Billingsley for Permitting the performance on the organ. Mr. MC/MA'S SPENDER seconded the proposition, which was carried with acclamation. _ _

Mr. BILLINGSLEY, in the course of a brief reply, remarLed that during the last three years he had been to a great num- ber of what were popularly known as services of song, and at the close of each had felt a strong prompting to see if he could not put "The Basket of Flowers" to music. The result of meditation upon the subject was the service to which they had listened that evening. They would no doubt he pleased to hear that it was already down for per- formance at 18 places, and he felt convinced there was a successful ,carreer before it. If he had afforded them any pleasuro that evening he was highly gratified. A complimentary resolution was also passed to the friends who had decorated the chapel. This terminated the proceedings. We may add that at the close of the performance on Thursday evening, Mr. Pickwell highly complimented the choir and the conductorlupon the manner in which the music had been given ; and his remarks were received with loud applause.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

GOLBORNE,CONSERTATIVE WORKINGMEN'S CLEl3.—AbOut 100 persons were present at the annual dinner held in con- nection with the above club at the Legh Arms, Go'borne, on Saturday evening. Mr. Arnot occupied the chair. The usual loyal and patriotic toasts having been duly honoured, the vice-chairman, Mr. Fairhurst, proposed "The Golborne Conservative Workingmen's CM." The Chairman, in replying, severely criticised the foreign and home policy of the present Government. He strongly condemned Mr. Bradlaugh's attempt to enter the House of Commons, and also the chlture. The next toast, "The patron of the club, Mr. W. J. Legh," was proposed by the Chairman, and responded to, on Mr. Legh's behalf, by Mr. Laycock. The health of Mr. Brew's; president of the club, was proposed and responded to, and other toasts followed, a pleasant even- ing being spent.

THE SANITARY COAMITTE—EAND THE LONGFORD DEPOT: INTENDED RESIGNATIONS.—We hear that the offer of Messrs. Manlove, All iott, and Fryer, of Nottingham, to construct at Longford, at an expense of About £B,OOO, new works and machinery for dealing with the whole of the town's refuse, has been declined by the Sanitary Committee. A week or two ago 3 deputation of the committee was appointed to visit other towns and inspect the different systems in opera- tion there, an the report of the deputation is to the effect that what the have seen supersedes Messrs. Manlove, and Co.'s appliances, and will be less expensive. They consider they will be able to put down plant at Longford to deal with the whole cf the town's refuse at an expense of £2,000. In consequence of the action of the committee, Alderman Burgess (chairman), Councillor Crosfleld, and Councillor Milner intend, at the next meeting of the Council, to resign their seat as members of the Sanitary Committee.

div.head: NOTES FROM "THE LOBBY."
div.p: NOTES FROM "THE LOBBY."
BY TELEGRAPH FROST OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT.
LONDON, FRIDAY NIGUT.

Considerable excitement was visible in both lobbies, this evening, owing to the general anxiety as to whether the Lords would appoint their committee or shrink from such a Proceeding. lamin a position to state that the resolution of Mr. Gladstone is by no means a blank cartridge fired off for the purpose of idle protest, and your readers should not be taken by surprise if, before ten days have passed away, events of stirring importance ensue from the present state of revision between the two Houses. In a word, the form and language of the Premier's resolution was long and anxiously debated, considered, and selected at a Cabinet meeting, with the full resolution of following up by deter- mined action what the resolution would express. The Government are of opinion and declare that they cannot carry on or be responsible for the Government of Ireland if ' the Lords. persevere in arresting or dragging to pieces the machinery of the Land Courts, and by Parliamentary usage it will devolve upon those accountable for such conduct to take the responsibility of maintaining the peace of the realm. In fine, the Government will not allow the work of the Lords to commence to proceed whila they hold the rains of power, and if Lord Salisbury allows his fliends to per- severe in a course deprecated by the Queen's adviser, he must be ready to take the reins himself. The rumour is to- night that Her Majesty herself will exercise, as it is said she did in the threatened crisis of last August, a wise and moderating influence between both parties, and probably avert the collision which seems inevitab:e.

I may say in this connection that I have to-day seen a resolution which a private English member sitting below the Ministerial gangway will submit to the House of Com- mons against voting a single penny for the committee, and. that the House exercising the power which it undoubteTy possesses will not sanction the expenditure of a single shil- ling in that direction, should the action ol the House of Lords hereafter; render a vote necessary.: A letter in tie Standard of this morning signed " <lndex," and written in a high oracular vein, has given enormous satisfaction to the Conservative peers and Commoners by its contention that their lordships, in virtue of their judicial functions, may demand whatever money they think needful for their judicial purposes ; but as a member of the House of Com- mons said to me the other night, the present committee Is an extra judicial performance, and must, therefore, be dealt with in an exceptional form. But really the question of money to print the report is a secondary matter compared with the enormous and momentous interests which lie in the background.

The certificate of the return of Michael Davat as M.P. for Meath was, to-day, received by the Speaker and deposited in the office of the Clerk of the House of Cotpmons. Tte document is signed J. Ferguson Davitt.

THE LORD'S CO3IMITTITT ON THE LAND ACT.

Four lined whips were sent out last night by both the Liberals and Conservatives, asking their supporters to be in their places in the House of Commons on Monday afternoon, between four ad five o'clock. div.head: FRENCH TREATY.
div.p: THE FRENCH TREATY.

The Central News telegram dated Paris, Friday evening, says the Anglo French Treaty negotiationsare not yet out of danger of collapse. It seems there is a disposition to object to ratifying the most favoured nation clause on the part of a not inconsiderable number Of Peputies. The prevailing • opinion, however, inclines in favour of completing the treaty, at,d this will probably be done by Monday at the latest.

div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT,

HOUSE OF LORDS. Earl Delaware presented a bill on the subject of contintions Railway brakes, and it was read a first time. THE IRISII LAND ACT COMMIITEE.—EarI of Do:Tot:on- MORE moved the appointment of a Committee upon the Irish Land Act.—The Marquis of LANSDOWNE hoped the appointment of the Committee would not be persisted iniut all events at present.—The Earl of DONOUGHMORE declined to accede to the suggestion —The Earl of DERBY also urged the postponement of the appointment of a Committee.—The Marquis of SALISBURY could not accede to the suggestion. He advised the appointment of a Committee at once. —Earl GRANVILLE denied that a vote of censure on the House OE' Lords had been proposed in the other H mse, and insisted that great evils would likely follow the apoointm eut of a. Ccm.nittee. The motion for appoinnag a Committee was agreed to, and the House adjourned.

TIIE BERLIN TREAT.—Sir G. CAMPBELL gave notice- on early day to call attention to the failure of certain por- ous of the treaty of Berlin with regard to the improvement! in Turkey.

TILE EGYPTIAN QUESTION. Sir CILARLES DILSE said papers on the subject of the commission sent by the Sultre to Egypt last autumn would be presented early. THE FRENCH TREATY-Sir C. DIRER replying to a ques- tion as tothe Commercial Trea'y, said the new arrangemeir.S, must depend upon certain degotiations now going on between France and other countries. Papers on the subject would be presented in a few days. The statements in the newspapers were generally correct with this addition, that if the till at present under considelation in the French Chambers became law there would be a prolongation of present arrangements until the 15th of May. THE WIGAN ELECTION.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL said it was not intended to make further inquiry into the late Wigan election. LOCAL TAXATION—Mr. GL ADSTONE said Mr. Harcourt had a motion for to-night, stating that immediate relief should be given to ratepayers from the present incidence of rates appropriated for the maintenance of main roads. He ad- mitted the time had arrived for dealing with that subject, and in his financial statement tie would make a proposal for that purpose. lie could not then give details. Under these circumstances he hoped Mr. Harcourt would not proceed with his tdottion.—Mr. IfAucouar accepted the assurance of the right lion. gentleman, and agreed to withdraw the motion.

SCPPLY.—The HouselWent into Committee of Supply on the supplementary civil service estimates.— On the supplementary vote for the expenses for constabu- lary in Ireland oeing proposed, Mr. HEALY wished a return made of all firearms seizAl under the provision of the Coercion Act.—Mr. FORSTER declined to give the information re- quired. The arms surrendered did not amount to a large number.—Mr. SEx-rosr said the increase of the police force and the inereas,d cost for arms, ammunition, and r c2omr.- ments for the constabulary, showed that the present Govern- ment was detested by the people of Ireland. who had showed by their action that they would not in any way assist in providing either food or transport for police. He severely censured the conduct of the police at B ilmull. t, where they, saturated with whiskey, acted with such violence, that the death of Ellen Mcllonagh was the result.—The ATTORNEY- GENERAL for IRELAND said he would have full inquiry made, and if it Tree found the police had acted unlawfully he would see the offenders punished. He justified the action of the Government as regarded the Prisoner's Aid Society, as the supporteis of it were carrying I out their objects by illegal and criminal measures.—Earl PERCY and Mr. O'SHEA, having made a few observations, 'IIr:RICHMOND strongly condemned the conduct of the pollee, and said the Attorney General's statement as re- garded the Prisoner's Aid Society, was absolutely opposed to the facts.—Mr. Forts:En contended that the Prisoner'• Aid Society were not confining their operations to the relief of Prisoners in jail, but on the contrary, were acting in an illegal mann-cr. He thought the certain action of cerin persons in. Ireland left no alternative but severity and repression--Mr. HEALY said the Government were acting on information given by perjured informers. lle said the Land League would exist a; long as landlordism continued in Ireland, and all the attempts of Government to extinguish the former would be useless. Ile cmdemned the Irish policy of Government, and asked whether it was expected that :peace would ever prevail as long as buckshot warriors were allowed to murder unoffending men and women.

Four men, named Owen, Rowlands, Jones, and Davies, were killed on Tuesay evening, at Park New Pit, Croni- park, near Pontypridd. the property of the Orrell Steam Coal Company. div.head: Tatters to the o.`,!'ditor.
div.p: Tatters to the o.`,!'ditor.

THE ELECTION OF AUDITORS. Sir,-1 am very much annoyed at the manner in which the Conservative party have acted in this matter, and if sae: a policy as has been for some time past shown, is carried out much longer, the chances of recovering their old position in the borough is hopeless in the extreme. I want to know why Mr. Mainwaring, who has been the nominee of our party for some years, and has ,done his work creditably, and. I believe, conscientiously, should without any notice whatever be thrown over for Mr. Turstall. It is said that a certain meddlesome busybody has done this dirty job, and that although nominally the Conservative Council are re- spocsible, Mr. Mainwaring's:overthrow is the Lesult of a ! scheme prompted by private jealousy, and that dislike which sometimes arises on the part of an unsuccessful, against a successful business man. Be this as it may, this sort of work is plaving our oppon9nts' game thoroughly, and is only ona par with that same spirit which has uow for several years past kept Alderman Harrison out of the civic chair. Thee are only two instances, out of many which I could enumerate, that are helping to make me, along with numbers of others, A DISGUSTED CONSERVATIVE. February 24; 1882,

div.head: MAYOR'S AUDITOR.
div.p: MAYOR'S AUDITOR.

Sir,—Can you C;r--a-n-y—o-f your numerous readers dispel at,7 ignorance upon the following subject :—ln a certain borough which shall for the present be nameless there are three auditors of tt,e Corporation accounts, two of whom are elected by the burgesses and the third by the Mayor. The Mayor's auditor is also a member of the Town Council. Every year there is a sum of money voted by the Town Council to the auditors—presumably the two appointed by the ratepayers—as remuneration for their services. The position of Mayor's auditor is considered to be a purely honorary office, and the only remuneration the gentleman so appointed is supposed (?) to receive is a " vote of thanks," awarded in this case also by the Town Council. lam informed that no member of the Town Council can hold any office of profit in connection therewith and retain his seat. Would the action of the Mayor's auditor in re- ceiving (with or without the consent of the other to elective auditors) one-third of the sum voted as the auditors' fees disqualify the said Mayor's auditor from re- ' taining his position in the Town Council ; and further would the said Mayor's auditor be liable to a heavy "fins" for so acting, and if so would a portion of the " fine " so enforced be due to the person who took proceedings to recover the same? I shall be glad to have the opinions of any persons who may be better acquainted with the law upon this matter than myself, and pending further steps, I am, ycurs, lIECTOR. February 23, 1832.

THE ST. HELENS DEBATING- SOCIETY. Sir,—Would you kindly allow me space to corroborate the statements of "Peace with Honour" in your last issue. Mr. Prescott and his colleague know well the extreme contempt which they have earned from both parties by their conduct it the House. The manner in which Mr. Prescott boasts of his intereet in the society is truly characteristic of himself, as his only object in joining the society was to gain self- importance, an end which he accomplished in a most ignominons manner. None bat. a stupid -public could fail to detect the spirit in which Mr. Prescott's letter was written. Obstruction was a favourite hobby with that gentleman (a term which his conduct in the House has not warranted) and a report which appeared in your columns some time ago, of the proceedings of the House at the time proved such to be the case. In a letter to the Premier, when resigning the position of Home Secretary, he himself stated • that he could not conscientiously retain that position, not having proved himself to be an orderly Cabinet Minister. 11:e fact of this having been placed before the public, so Vaected Mr. Prescott, that he more than once moved the House into committee to consider the report which had been inserted, and demanded an apology from the person who had caused the insertion of the report, a concession which was not granted. Thus nearly a whole night was occupied in discussing the personal affair of the trouble- some, ficklesome member for Scarboro'. Oa the night of the adjournment for the Christmas recess, Mr. Westworth gave notice that be would move the House into committee . to consider the manner in which he was concerned in the same report! What a prospect for the second half of what might have been a prosperous session. Now, is it likely, Mr. Editor, that young men, who had joined the society for the purpose of discussing politics, would attend, and be forced to sit and listen to "the hair-brained chatter of such irresponsible frivolity" coming from persons who might truly be described, as was their leader, sophistical rhetori- cians, inebriated with the exuberance of their own verbosity. How Mr. Prescott can for shame come before the public in the manner he does is difficult to say, though there is one characteristic feature in human nature which is very pro- minent in him, which will doubtless account for it, and I hope the public will be satisfied that Jr. Prescott and his inseparable aesthetic colleague have done more to disband the society than those negligent Conservative members, who would not meet to discuss the personal affairs of Mr. R. M. Prescott. Thanking you, Mr. Editor, for your forbearance, I remain, yours, he, "CONSERVATIVE." St. Helens, Feb. 23rd, 1882.

OPENING OF THE FIFTH COCOA. HOUSE IN WARRINGTON. Within the short period of three months the Warrington British Workman Public House Company have added two 'cocoa houses W their establishments in the town, of which there are now five. The fifth, which is situate in Winwick- -street, was opened, on Tuesday evening, by Mr. John -Crosfield, J.P. The building is a three storeyed house, having four rooms on the ground floor. Each room is carpeted, and comfortably fitted up. A room is set apart for ladies. Upstairs on the second floor is a large well fur- nished room which will be very suitable for holding club and committee meetings, small entertainments, doo. Accomoda- tion is afforded for about 80 persons, and it is intended to provide sleeping accommodation for a considerable number ..en the 3rd floor. Financially the other establishments of the Company are a success, and judging from the large n am- leer of men, women, and children who crowded round the house when the opening ceremony took place, the fifth will be no exception. Arnoag,st those present at the opening were Alderman and Mrs. Holmes, Messrs. Thomas Morris (chairman of directors), E. Place, R. Siddall, J. Gardner, H. eßoberts, and W. Roberts. The Rev. J. Yonge, who was 'lway in London, had sent an apology for his absence. Mr. Charles Broadbent wrote :—" Very sorry indeed not to be with you on the happy occasion of the opening of the fifth cocoa house. You know what great interest I take in this movement, and I look forward to no small benefit to our geed old town through the :nfluence of these places of rest and ieireshment." In apologising for his absence the Rev. T. Rippon said he heartily sympathised with the movement, 'believing it to be a counter attraction, in mere tenses than. one, to the drink shop which wee Warrington's cttrse. There ought to be as many cocoa rooms in the town as public- Louses, and he hoped they would not be satisfied until that state of things was accomplished. • Mr. THOMAS Moan's said he thought it only right to say a few words about the success that had atteudedlhe coffee Louse movement, before he asked their friend Mr. Crosfield to formally open that—the fifth house. It seemed only yesterday since a few gentlemen mapped the localities of the town where they thought these institutions would be most useful and beneficial. But even the most sanguine ' amongst them never thought that in so short a time they would have been able to open the fifth house, and at the same time 9.07 that all their houses were successful; not enly pecuniarily, but in being able to find a cheap cup of coffee and food, clean rooms, and newspapers of all shades of politics for people such as he was addressing, who could not afford to buy luxuries. WI en they could go to a place like that, where at a cost of a few pence they could obtain cleanliness and comfort for a few hours, it was far better than being in the streets in the cold, which sometimes caused death. He then called upon Mr. Crosfield to open the house. Mr. CROSFIELD said it was a pleasure to him to be there that night to declare that coffee room open. He had had nothing to do with the formation of the other coffee rooms that had been established in the town, beyond that he took corns shares. He was anxious to do what he could to have these kind of rooms established in the town, because he knew they were of the greatest possible benefit to the work- ing people—(hear, hear)—and they were more important, perhaps, for the wives cf working men themselves—(hear, hear) ;—for if a working man kept sober and steady his wife and children would very soon find the benefit of it. (Hear, Lear.) He knew that the club which had been opened in Bewser-street for working men had been a great blessing to many 'families in the town. (Hear, hear.) Many a wife had blessed that place since it was opened. (Hear, hear.) And for this reason. Her husband came home at night sober and with his money in his pocket instead of having spent it in the gin palace and ale house. Gin palaces and public- houses were a great evil to workingmen; drink was the greatest curse to England—(hear, hear),—and almost all the crimes were committed through drink. (Hear, hear.) It was only that day that he read in the newspaper a letter from a man who was to be hung next day in Manchester. He wrote to the people of Burnley warning them to keep out of the public-house and gin palace, for drink had brought him to the gallows. (Hear, hear.) That man had murdered the roman with whom he lived through drink. At that end of the lowa in which that coffee house was situated "there had been a sad want of some clean, respectable place like that fcr the people he was addressing to go into, and be hoped they would support the place, and feel the benefit of it. He was sure they were much indebted to Mr. Morris and other gentlemen who had taken the trouble to open those kind of places, and they deserved to be encouraged by being sup- ported. (Hear, hear.) He hoped they were going to make a good start that niebt. At the coffee house at the corner of Bewsey- street they had an income of £25 per week—(hear, hear,)—and he should be glad if they could take £2O a week there. (Hear, hear.) The way in which the workingmen in this country squandered their money in drink was most lamentable. Ile had lately been abroad to a place called hientone, a beautiful spot cm the shores of the Mediter- ranean. He was there ten days, and he never saw a symp- tom of a drunken man the whole time. On the Continent they never saw any drunken men. He came back to Eng- land, and ha could not be here 24 hours without seeing evidences of this evil of drink. Mr. Crosfield then formally declared the premises open, and was supplied with a cup of coffee.

Alderman HOLMES was then called upon to speak. He said it afforded him much pleasure to take part in the pro- ceedings because the opening of that house right in the face of a couple of public-houses which were in the immediate neighbourhood, must be a very great boon to the people who lived there. Thera was an attraction afforded by the public- houses, and they had brought a counter attraction by open- lug a capital coffee-house, and he hoped they would come there whenever they wanted refreshments of any sort, and eat and drink. They would take no harm by it, but receive good. That was what he wished to see. (A Voice : "God love you.") They had a coffee room there, and if they could by any possible means convert one of those two public- houses on the other side of the way into coffee rooms as well they would have done a grand thing for Warrington. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Upwards of 200 cups of coffee were then distributed to the people who had congregated.

div.head: WARRINGTON POLICE COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON POLICE COURT.

MONDAY.—Before the Mayor, Councillors, Fairclough, . and J. Crosfield, and Major Cartwright. SPENDING HIS FERLOUGII.—John Marsh, a soldier, on furlough from Aldershot, was charged with being drunk and disorderly and refusing to quit the Corporation Inn. He was further charged with assaulting P.C. Clynes. The pri- soner created a disturbance in the Inn on Saturday night, and was with much trouble removed to the street. There he twice struck P.C. Clynes, and acted very violently.—The prisoner said he had been teetotal two years, and had a good conduct badge.--He was ordered to pay 2s. 6d. to the poor box and he was discharged. A RorGrt PEISONEU.—John Lofthouse, a rough looking fellow, was charged with being drunk and disorderly on Saturday.—P.S. Bowen said the prisoner became so dis- c,rderly in the police station that his clogs had to be re- moved. For four hours Mr. Hunt said the prisoner carried on shamefully, disturbing everybody.—Prisoner was fined 20s. and costs.,

NEGLECT OF FAMlLY.—Michael Melior was charged with allowing his wife and three children to become chargeable to the common fund of the Warrington Union.—He was ordered to pay ss. costs. CHARGE OF PERMITTING DRUNKENNESS.—Thos. Clare was charged with having, on the 14th February, permitted drunk:nness to take place upon his premises, the Old Packet Rouse. Three respectably dressed men named Phillip Har- court, Austin Hanlan, and Stephen Johnson were charged with being drunk on the premises.—Mr. Rehert Davies appeared for Clare, and pleaded not guilty, which was also pleaded on behalf of Harcourt and Hanlan by Mr. Percy Davies, and Johnson, who was unrepresented, pleaded not guilty.—lnspector Singleton said at a quarter past six on Tuesday evening, the 14th instant, he was or duty in Bridge-street. In consequence of a report made to him by P.C. Clynes, witness, P.S. Spinks and the constable went to the Old Packet House. On arriving at the front door they hoard a loud noise of talking, and they entered. In the kitchen they found five men sitting round the table each with a glass of beer before him. Harcourt said, "Here's the bobbies ; what do they want. I am a •—• thief; if lam rot one now. I have been." He then got up from his seat and asked the Inspector to drink from his glass of beer. Johnson and Hanlan were also sitting at the table ; the former of whom called P.C. Spinks "all the names that a man could lay his tongue to, especially bad ones." Mrs. Clare coming into the room, the Inspector called her atten- tion to the drunken state of the three defendants, and she replied that she had only supplied each man with a glass of beer. Mr. Clare then entered the room, denied the men were drunk, and took them down to the police station so that the Chief Constable could see them.—Mr. P. Davies having examined the Inspector, P.S. Spinks was called and confirmed his superior's statement, adding that Johnson called him a scamp, and that the defendants were disorderly at the police station. Hanlan was so drunk that he stag- gered against the inspector's window.—By Councillor Cros• field : I saw the men walk down Mersey-street, and they could not walk like sober men.—P.C. Clynes also gave cor- roborative evidence, and P.S. James stated that at half-past six on the day in question Clare, accompanied by Johnson and Harcourt, went to the station and asked him if the men were drunk. He replied that they were decidedly drunk. Johnson and Harcourt wished to see the Chief Constable. Witness replied that Mr. Hunt did not want to be bothered with drunken men, when they became noisy and boisterous. The Chief Constable blew the whistle of the speaking tube, and told the witness to lock the men up if they did not go away. Johnson sat down on a scat, and said "I will be -- if I will leave the office until I have seen the Chief Constable." Hanlan with the first three witnesses then entered the office. Hanlan was drunk.—The Chief Constable also gave evidence, and stated he saw from his office window Clare, Hanlan, and Harcourt approaching the station. The two latter were drunk without a doubt.—Mr. Robert Davies contended that the evidence for the prosecution had cleared his client from the charge, as neither of the defendants had drank of the beer when the officers entered the house. He commented favourably on the fair and im- partial manner in which the police had given their evidence, and said bethought the case would not have been brought before the Bench but for the violent conduct of Johnson.— Mr. Percy Davies, having addressed the Bench, called two witnesses, who stated emphatically that Harcourt and Han- lan were saber. Johnson also denied being drunk, but did not call any witnesses.—Johnson was fined 103. and costs, and flee cases against the other defendants were dis- missed.—The Mayor did not sit in this case. MISCELLANEOUS. Thomas Conway, a young man, was charged under a warrant, with having on the 16th inst. as- saulted his father.—The prosecutor said he did not wish to Dem the case, but it was elicited that the prisoner pro- voked him "all roads," upset the table and broke the lamp. —The prisoner was given a bad character, and he was bound over to keep the peace for six months, himself in £5, and two sureties in £lO each, or in default three months' imprisonment. —Richard Chadwick was charged with al- lowing two horses to stray in Marshhouse-lane, on the 14th inst., and he was fined 23. Gd. BREACHES OF THE EDUCATION ACT. Mr. Riley, the school attendance officer, summoned the following persons for neglecting to send their children regularly to school,aud a fine of ss. was imposed in each case :—Thos. Garritty, Friars-green; Joseph Lightfoot, Longford-street; Michael Birmingham, Friars-green; Thomas Dutton, Foundry- Street; Wm. Quarmby, Latchford; Samuel Winsper, Stam- ford-street; Thomas Harrison, Winwick-street ; John McCore, Friars-green; Joaeph Richardson, SO, Allen-street; Henry Haswell, Tilley-street ; Michael Braney, Buttermarket- ' street.

TITESDAY.—Before Councillor Monks and Major Cartwright. MILITARY DESERTION.—Martin Lawlor, a native of Galway, was charged with having deserted from Her Majesty's 103rd Regiment of Foot, stationed at Salford, on or about the 6th instant. The prisoner was discovered by P.C. Hitchmough attempting to pledge his military boots, and the officer took him into custody.—He was remanded to Walton Gaol to await a military escort, and the Bench re- commended the payment to the constable of the usual reward of 10s.

div.head: WEDNESDAY—Before Aid. Davies and Aid. Chandley.
div.p: WEDNESDAY—Before Aid. Davies and Aid. Chandley.

PUBLIC MEETING. The attendance at St. Peter's mission room on Monday evening, in response to the announcement of a public meet- ing to consider the question of erecting a new church in the parish of St. Peter's, Warrington, was only moderate. The Rev. M. Schonberg presided; and there were also present the Rev. S. Wilkinson, Councillor Jeans, Messrs. G. Pow!- son, J. Roberts, Brown, &c.

The rev. CHAIRMAN gave an address substantially the same as that delivered at the church tea party, and reported in The Examiner a fortnight ago. He explained how the miesion was established, and how he came to labour amongst them; he showed that he had no private ends to serve in advocating the erection of a church ; and, in conclusion, he remarked that they could not do anything without patronage. This patronage he craved at the hands of the people of Warrington, though he must say there were certain leading spirits in Warrington who had fallen wofully short in their duty in promoting the Church's interest. He was persuaded he would have the patronage of the middle classes and the poor, and when the wealthy saw they had tried to help themselves they would give their share. (Ap- plause.) The Rev. S. WILKINSON moved the first resolution, as follows: " That in the opinion of this meeting it is desirable a church should be built in the parish of St. Peter's, War- rington." He said when asked to move the resolution he could not refuse to do so because of his great affection and veneration for the vicar, and because he was to a certain extent associated with the parish of St. Peter's. When he first came to Warrington, nine years ago, it was not then cut off from St. Paul's, but when St. Peter's was made a distinct parish the patronage was given to the Rector of Warrington and the vicar of St. Paul's alternately. The Rector made the first presentation, and appointed Mr. Schonberg. The chairman lad spoken about 'his work.. It had not been simply a work in that parish, but in the town of Warrington. Mr. Schonberg had already accomplished much in the building line. Those class rooms were built partly by Mr. Schonberg's own hands and the ready help of many in the parish • and the chair- man had done much towards building a chfl; for the benefit of his fellow men. Therefore he thought he might prophesy that, if their lives were spa.rei, in a year or two hence thy would see the Church of St. Peter's rising there in all its beauty. (Applause.) He believed if they really tried to do a thin, they would in the long run succeed.' Having advert'ed to the building of St. Zarnabas' Church and the restoration of St. Paul's, the rev. gentleman said everybody would acknowledge that if that workmanted doing at .31. Paul's, the work at St. Peter's wanted doing much more. The church would doubtless cost £4,000 or £5,000 which to a lot of poor people looked a large sum to raise, but everything was larger in comparison. With one day's in- come from 40,000 persons the whole thing would be done. However, if all of them put their shoulders to the wheel and did their best the work could be accomplished, and if the people of Warrington would only once make up their minds that St. Peter's must be a church they could have the church consecrated on the let of January, 1883. (Ap- plause.) Mr. G. PowLsosr had great pleasure, as a parishioner of St. Peter's, in seconding the resolution, and gave a brief sketch of the church work since he had been resident in the town. He said 24 years ago they were told that the ancient Parish Church of Warrington needed restoration. Notwith- standing the expenditure of considerable sums of money upon it during the rectory of the Rev. Horace Powys, it was announced that the arches supporting the tower had for some years been gradually giving way, and had then assumed so dangerous a character as to require immediate attention. The interior of the church was also said to be in a very dilapidated condition ; scarcely a pew or seat being perfect ; and it was therefore proposed entirely to restore the church, chapels, and tower ; to make a new north aisle to correspondiwith the south aisle ; to restore the chancel and crypt ; to remove the entire flat plastered ceiling of the church, and substitute a raised open roof; to make a division of the church into a nave and two side aisles; to remove the western gallery, and replace the organ in the new extended western end, to re-arrange the whole body of the church with open seats; and to light the church with gas for evening service. •The estimated cost of this work was stated by the architects to be not more than £5,000. ; But probably, before the work was completed, this amount was trebled. About 12 years later a scheme was formed for . creating three or four new Ecclesiastical districts in the ! town and building as many churches ; but this effort, for various reasons, failed of success. In February, 1863, how- , I ever, a serious attempt was made to establish mission dis-
tricts in Warrington, two curves leiugallotcsi to the Parish Church, two to St. Paul's, mid one to St. James's, . . . .

each curate having a sort of courtesy district assigned for him to work in, with a population not exceeding 2,500. To carry out this plan effectively it was estimated that at least £BOO pea' annum would be required, and the sum of £550 a year with £2OO from the Society for Providing Additional Curates, was promised for five years. In March, 1865, a meeting was held in the adjoining parish of St. Ann's, in a schoolroom, to sanction an effort for building a new church in that district. The circumstances under which that meet- ing took place were somewhat similar to those which now existed in the parish of St. Peter's, except that there had been a special mission effort in St. Peter's, much longer than had then been the case in St. Ann's. A curate. in charge was nominated there in 1862, and in January of that year an old ' and disused Dissenting chapel was opened. When the meeting was held in March, 1865, there was no other place of worship in the district, and Town's End bore an evil reputation for disorderly conduct, far beyond what could be said of it now. It was announced that in all probability a site would be given for the church, and that about £4,000 would be required for its construction. Some three years ago St Barnabas' Church was erected at Bank Quay, at a cost of £4,000, exclusive of site, which was given. Nearly two years ago a considerable sum of money, probably £5OO, was expended in altering the character of the interior of St. James's Church; and St. Paul's has just been re-opened after internal alterations which had cost about £1,500. Coming to St. Peter's, he said, like St. Ann's, they had here a minister in the enjoyment of an endowment, not very large indeo,—and he had unfortunately lost a satisfactory in- crease, because they too long delayed their present effort— but still with such a stipend as made it necessary for them at this moment to contemplate itc augmentation. In this parish the Rev. M. Schonberg had laboured for the space of 11 years. .He was known throughout the town, as well as the district, as a faithful and diligent pastor; and to his honour, be it said, his care was more for the edification and salvation of his people, than for the ceremonial of his ser- vice. He had in his parish upwards of 900 dwelling-houses, and therefore, according to the ordinary rate of computa- tion, more' than 4 500 of a population. He had commodious, admirably appointed, and successful schools and Sunday congregations which crowded his means of accommodation; congregations too of a character which claimed and deserved the conveniepces of a church in which to engage in public worship. This church it was their present object to secure, and it would require united and strenuous efforts to ensure succese, for they would probably have to purchase a site, as well as to erect the fabric. They needed the pence of the poor, the pounds of the middle class, and the hundreds of the wealthy, with whatever other help could be rendered by that opperative section of society in which Mr. Schonberg bad such, perhaps not ill-deserved, confidence. When the ; reatoration of St. Elphins' was projected, the collectors were told (1) to—Ask for a penny or a shilling. (2) To receive whatever was offered. (3) To write don the name of every contributor and the amount of the donation. And (4) when "weary in Well-doing," to remember that "the hand of the diligent maketh rich." " By much slothfulness the building declyeth ; and through idleness of the hands the house droppeth through." These hints might be profitably , adopted by themselves. They indeed had no apprehensions ! of their "lleuse dropping through," unless their project was to be regarded as a mere "castle in the air;" but, while ask- ing who were they that they should be permitted to engage in the erection of a temple for the glory of God, and the good of men's souls, might yet, renembering what had ! already nehen done in Warrington, encourage each other, and i determine to "arise and build." 1 The resolution was unanimously carried. I Mr. JOHN ROBERTS Proposed that the following gentle- men, with power to add to their number, be apia,tated a I committee to carry out the previous resolution :—Messrs. P. Stub, W. D, Jeans, J. Murray, J. Ellison, J. Hatton, W. V. Pothecary, J. Sniethuret, J. C. Ridgway, T. Draper, T. cawley, G. Powlson, the Rev. S. Wilkinson, Rev. E. C. E. Carlaon, the vicar, chuichwardens, and sidesmen of St. Peter's; and that Mr. Murray be appointed treasurer, and Mr. G. Powlson and W. D. Jeans secretaries. He thought the object of the meeting had been very plainly put before them, and they could only hope that it would end successfully. For some time be had been watching the cone'Tegation of St. Peter's, and he was pleased to say it had very much in- creased of late ; and the time had come when really a church was required. They could not for a moment think that Mr. SchOnberg bad any private object in desiring the erection of a church, as they all knew he was advanced in years, and that if a church were built he could not live many years to enjoy it. He thought it was their duty to assist Mr. FcliOoberg and the cemmittee,who he had not the slight- est doubt would use much energy towards carrying out the object in view. (Anplatiee.) Mr. PETER EDGAR seconded the resolution, and remarked that it was plainly to be seen they were determined to have la church, and he 'felt persuaded the gentlemen named on the Icommittee would do their utmost to carry into effect their object. (Applause.) The resolution was then carried. Mr. JEAN'S moved the next resolution "that collecting books be prepared and every effort made for obtaining funds for the accomplishment of this object." He observed that he need scarcely say the carrying out of Mr. SchOnberg's Wish to erect a church in the parish would require great efforts on the part of those present, and on the part of others. It could not be expected that those in the room could do much, and they must necessarily look to gentlemen with larger purses. He had had some experience in connection with Mr. Wilkinson, in building St. Barnabas' Church, and the reetcration of St. Paul's, and he therefore knew the difficulty there was in obtaining money for church building purposes. If they began without anything it would be very up-hill work to raise -04,000 or £5,060. They must appeal to the manu- facturers and others, and he trustedsuch appeal would not be in vain. Mr. Peter Stubs and also Mr. Beamont, he be- lieved, at one time had some notion of erecting a church in that parish, and be had no doubt if approached they would assist now. Before they could commence the church they must see their way to getting the money. He thought it would have shown greater interest if more gentlemen had

DESERTERS. Matthew White, a native of Denby, in Kent, pleaded guilty to having deserted from Her Majesty's 107th Royal Sussex Regiment of foot stationed at Chiches- ter, on or about the 20th December, 1880.—He was com- mitted to Walton Gaol to await a military escort.—Ed- ward Williams, of Liverpool, was charged with being a deserter from the Bth Liverpool Regiment, on the 24th September, 1881.—He pleaded guilty and was handed over to the military authorities at Warrington Barracks. THURSDAY—Before Captain Litton.

DisonDErmy WOMEN. Jane Riley and Jane Flynn, young women of bad character, residing ha Old-road, Lalch- ford, were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Horsemarket-street, at 11-20 on the previous night. P.S. Spinks, who proved the case, said Flynn lay on the ground on her back, and the police had to carry her to the polica station. There she struck an officer with her clog.—The prisoners had been More the court repeatedly and com- mitted to gaol, and they were each sentenced to 14 days' hard labour.

Mr. CALVERT, in• seconding the resolution, expressed his cordial sympathy with Mr. Schonberg, whose labours, he was sure, deserved hearty recognition. He rejoiced to see the beginning of a movement which he trusted would lead to the result desired, and that Mr. Schonberg would live to see it completed. (Hear, hear.) Mr. BROWN supported the resolution, and stlted they had to drive away from the services the rising generation of the district in order to make room for the adult members of the congregation. The resolution having been carried, the meeting termi- nated.
NEWTON AND EARUSTO-WN.

CHURCH TEA MEETING AT NEWTON.—On Monday even- ing the annual tea meeting, in connection with St. Mary's and St. John's Catholic Church, was held. About 50 per- sons sat down to tea, and afterwards the evening was devoted to dancing. HUSSARS' BALL AT ASHTON. The annual ball of the "A " troop of the Lancashire Hussars took place at the Public Hall, Ashton, on Monday evening. About 150 per- sons were present. The arrangements were carried out by the following committee :—Sergeant-Major Healey', Quarter- master-Sergeant T. Livesley, Sergeants Shaw, Long., and Tilling; and Corporals Glover, Reeves, Ogden, Turner, Pendlebury, Hurst, and Gardner. Quartertnaster-Sergeant Livesley made an efficient and courteous secretary. Sergeant Shaw was M.C. The music furnished by Mr. R. Peel's string band and dancing was continued until a late hour. 1.0.G.T HOPE OF EA'RLESTOWN LODGE. On Tuesday evening last, the above lodge held their annual pancake supper, when upwards of 25 members attended, a very en- joyable evening being spent. PUBLIC LECTURE AT ASHTON-IN-MAKERFIELD.—A public lecture, under the auspices of the Ashton Excelsior Lodge of Good Templars, was delivered in the British Schools, Ashton, on Wednesday evening last, the subject being "Heroism in Humble Life." Mr. George Clark, of Earles- town, presided, and after a few remarks, introduced the lecturer, Mr. John Paton, of Scotland, one of the lecturers for the United Kingdom Alliance, and who dealt with his subject in a most clear and argumentative style. He gave out his facts and truths in a very telling, manner, and they were fully appreciated by the audience, which was moderate. Votes of thanks to the lecturer and chairman, moved by Mr. John' Tunstall, seconded by Mr. Crompton, closed the , meeting. VOLUNTEER BALL AT NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS.—On Friday the annual ball in connection with the Lancashire Hussars, 91h and 19th L.R.V. (Newton Detachment), was held in the Town Hall, under the immediate patronage of the com- manding officer and officers of the different companies, the following being present :—Major Reif, Lancashire Hussars ; Capt. Wood, 19th L.R.V. (Newton Detachment) ; Capt. Seton, Bth Lancashire Artillery; Lieut. Thompson, Oth. L.R.V.; Lieut. Widdowe, 9th L.R.V.; Surgeon Beaman, Lancashire Hussars. Dancing commenced at 9 p.m. and was kept up with great spirit until the small hours of the morning. The company present entirely enjoyed them- selves, and the ball was one of the best successes of late years. The masters of ceremonies deserve praise for the efficient manner in which they performed their dillies. Refreshments were supplied by Sergt. Nash (19th L.R.V.), Blue Bell Hotel, and were all that could be desired. The music, of which too much cannot be said in its praise, was provided by Mr. Appleton; Earlestown, and reflects great credit on its conductor. EARLESTOW.N MUSICAL SOCIETY. The Earlestown Musical Society gave a highly successful concert on Mon- day evening, in the Viaduct Institute, which was literally crammed. The first part of the programme consisted of Pattison's cantata, " The Ancient Marine," by Coleridge. The recitatives and airs were sustained by Miss McCarrol, Miss Minnie Hayes and Miss Smith, Mr. George Barton and Mr. lly. Parr, and the band was led by Herr Isouard Oreste Prreger, of Warrington, who also played solo violin, and by his masterly disply of executive art called forth prolonged and energetic applause, to which the artist replied by play- ing the Emperor's Hymn with his bow unstrung and placed across all the strings to f9rdi tq-d.riette. Wet the feature of the evening as far as instrumentalism was con- cerned. The overture and first chorus by same 50 perfo- mere and band was followed by a second chorus, and a reci- tative by Mr. Parr, who has a good sonorous voice; and this was followed by Ass McCarrol in the air, "The. bride bath paced in the ball " in a fine mellow mezzo soprano voice. The choruses were acknowledged to have been well per- formed, and reflected credit upon Mr. Hayes's training. Mr. Barton's first appearance was greeted with loud applause, and his appearance was the second feature of the concert. Miss Smith also drew continued attention when the audience began to realise the effect of her fine contralto voice, and Miss Hayes' penetrating voice was clearly distinguishable in the lead throughout the whole cantata. The quartette and chorus, "0 happy living things," brought the four soloists together in a fine combination. The chorus " The coming wind did roar," was quite in keeping with the character of the piece. The finest piece was the duet between Miss Hayes and Miss Smith, "Swiftly, swiftly flew the ship," which went gaily and secured for them a well-merited encore. The chorus," What loud uproar bursts from the door," proved the capacity of the members of the society to underrate the musical performances. The second part opened with a part song, "Tile peasant's wedding march," by the chorus, and was very nicely sung. ' Miss Smith sang "The sea lies deep between" in a deep contralto voice, with marked approval, and Herr Prreger played a tremolo with a continued power of rapid execution. Mr. Parr sang "The village blacksmith" well, and was loudly applauded. Miss Hayes sang "The Kerry dance." Mr. Barton sang "Farewell, farewell, nay mountain home" so as to secure a reoall, when be gave "The Arab steed" very finely, and Miss M. Carroll followed in "Love not," which she sang wilh great pathos. Herr Prmger gave one or two marvellous performances on the violin. The concert closed with the glee "From Oberon in Fairy Land," which went well and was applauded. Miss Greenall and Mr. J. H. Profit presided at the .piano and harmoniuin respectively, and did efficient service; and Mr. Hayes is deserving of the highest praise for having so soon brought his company up to the mark and before the public. The society has been well patronized, and without much solicitation by the fore- most of the local magistrates and gentry, and has done credit to itself in this performance.

the expenditure of capital on a much larger area than many of them imagined. Besides security of capital, they must ! have free land—land free to sell, free to buy, easily sold and therefore easily bought—and the tenant must be given the liblrty to produce what he liked. He believed if they could get free land in this sense, that agriculture would be carried on much more successfully than at the present moment. No doubt some of that freedom could only be obtained by legis- lation, but he was under the impression that a good deal of it could be brought about by the good sense of the landlords. lie could not understand at the present moment how any landlord could be so short-sighted as to say to his tenant, "You shall not sell what you produce; or you shall not grow what you think best." He trusted, therefore, that they would take advantage at the present juncture to press first upon the Legislature the evils which existed, and which could be remedied only by legislation; and secondly, to farm well. He had no doubt that farming, at all events in this part of England, would rise again. With reviving trade their interest would also revive; but they must remember this, that the tastes of the people were .fickle, and they must grow their produce to meet the public want. If, as his good friend Mr. Lee Townshend said, the people wanted bad cheese, farmers must make bad checso and try and get a good price for it; if they would have cabbages instead of tur nips, cabbages must be grown.
