div.head: MID-CHESIIIRE ITEMS.
div.p: MID-CHESIIIRE ITEMS.

At the Northwich Police Court a provision dear living at Bowdon has been committed for trial at the assizes charged with bigamy. The adjourded Quarter Sessions for the county of Che- shire were opened on Tuesday at Knutsford. Tnere were 49 cases for consideration, as against 30 for the corresponding quarter of last year. At the last meeting of the Northwich Guardians a resolu- tion was passed that unless the relief business be finished by half-past three o'clock, it should be then postponed until the general business had been gone through. MR. G. W. LATHAM ON CLASS PRIVILEGES.—Mr. J. A. Clarke, B A., of Cambridge, lectured in the Providence Chapel; Sandbach, on Saturday evening, on "Landlord Privilege and Popular Rights." Mr. G. W. Latham, of Bradwali Hall, presided, and said that the subject was one in which lie had taken a deep interest. The people of Eng- land were being educated to a knowledge of the old feudal traditions and customs which existed in this land, and they were beginning to see that their existence stoosl in the way of popular riglats. To such an extent was this the case that the monarchy itself was only endured beciuse of the character of the monarch on the throne. This subject of laniard privilege and popular rights was one that must sooner or later be dealt with. Teudal institutions had had their day, and the time must come when they would be swept away.—Mr. Clarke argued that the eNistence of the old feudal customs of this country pwvented the growth of national intelligence an independence and fettered the agricultural, commercial, and industrial works of the country.

LIBERALISM IN MID-CuEsarnE.—The annual meeting of the Mid-Cheshire Überal Association was held at Northwich on Saturday; Mr. G. W. Latham in the chair. There was a large attenciatiGe Of members. The election of officers took ri.ne. Mr. G. W. Latham, preslient ; Mr. J. T. Brown, treasurer; Mr. A. S. Paterson, legal agent ; Mr. E. E. Press; secretary. The following resolutions were proposed by Mr. Latham, J.P., seconded by Mr. A. Hogg, J:P., and supported by the Rev. J. Johnson and Mr. E. Boyer :.—" Thatthis meeting, desiring to see progress made in legislation, long that the Government vill be cordially supported by the entirety of the Liberal party in the carrying out of such changes in the procedure of the House of Commons as may hasten the passing of the County Franchise MP, the Cor- rupt Practices Bill, • the Bankruptcy Bill, and all other measures of utility to the nation which have been hampered and hindered by the obstructive section of the House of Commons ; " that this meeting desire to expsess their unabated confidence in Her Majesty's Government and trust that they will not relax their efforts to amend the procedure of the House of .Commons so as to promote Liberal legis- lation."

MR. G. W. LATHAM ON THE PROSPECTS OF AGRICULTURE. The annual meeting of the Cheshire, Shropshire, and North Wales Farmers' Association was held at Crewe, on Tuesday, under the presidency of Mr. G. W. Latham. In proposing "Better Success to Agriculture," the CHAIRMAN said that if it did turn out that agriculture in England could no longer be carried on with'protit, then those of them who were landlords, depending upon their rents for existence, would have to go somewhere else, unless they chose to try their luck and see what the exercise of their own abilities would bring them in. The only possibility of tenant farmers attaining success now-a-days was, as far as he could see, by farming well. With America anchored as it were alongside of them, there was such a competition going on against them that they would not be able to hold their own unless they farmed well. English farmers were heavily handicapped ; whilst the Americans had next to nothing to pay in the way of rates or taxes. English farmers, however, Lad to obtain many other things before agriculture could prosper again among them. Security of capital was the very life of agri- culture, and until the tenant farmer was assured of that security he would never put capital enough into his land to make it produce the crops that would pay him. In Cheshire, on their great estates, they had always had, if not legally at all events morally, sufficient security to enable farmers to lay out their money safely ; but what he wanted to prevent was, not only on large estates but on small estates also, those instances of hardship which occasionally occurred,and which ftightened away capital trom the land. One sad in- stance of hardship on the part of a landlord would prevent

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

CONCERT AT WINSFORD. - A concert has been given in the Winsford Town Hall, by the Rev. Mr. Reader and party, towards the new chapel on Winsford Hill. This effort of the rev. gentleman was pretty well supported by the society which has long needed a new chapel but has had to be satisfied with the old one, while other parts of the circuit have been considered. This is thought to be hardly fair to the Winsford Wesleyans, who contribute no mean part to the quarterly expenses of the circuit. LOCAL GOVERNMENT INQUIRY AT WINSFORD. - Last Thursday, Mr. S. J. Smith, CE., an inspector of the Local Government Board, held an enquiry at the office of the Wintford Local Board, as to the power of the Board to bor- row £1,500 for sewage works, and £4OO for water supply. Many of the members of the Board were present and other ratepayers. The inspector decided to hear the application respecting the water supply first. This was to extend the three-inch" mains from Wharton Bridge to Hough's Points, about 1,200 yards. He (the Surveyor) stated that the popu- lation of the district is about 10,014, and the water needed was 95,000 gallons for 9,500 people, taking it at 10 gallons per diem. In addition 17,000 gallons were required for trade • purposes. In April, 1830, he found the town was taking 12 ' gallons per head. Few new were not taking water from the Board's supply, and these had water which had been analyscd, and so allowed. But in order that all might have water, it was necessary to connect Butt's spring with the 10 inch main after leaving the reservoir. The water so entering he would strain, and so fit for circulation. Part of the money would be required for fencing round the springs and reservoir. The total cost would be £4lO. He said Butt's springs would yield 40,000 per day, and Stretch's 103,000.— The next point of enquiry was as to the sewerage of Over. Mr. Smith said he disliked the syphon to carry the water across the clough. A bank he would not sanction. Girders, piles, and stage were discussed, and Mr. Smith said he would go on with the enquiry subject to alteration in this matter. As aeorge-street, Lower Weaver-street, Lower High-street, Church-street, Queen-street, and New-road were to be left out of the general scheme, Mr. Smith enquired what was to be done with this part. It was difficult to decide.: the Surveyor aid ; Mr, Smith would sea when they wint to inspect it. Mr. Smith seemed hardly satisfied that the Board had carried out as expected by the Central Board, the plan first pro- posed as to the sewage. If only 4- went to the . land, and on the cinders which formed the filter bed in the river, it was a question whether it did not violate the Rivers' Pollution Act. If the Board could show him that it worked rightly he would not say a word, as it was only for him to see the act carried out properly. Woodford-lane scheme, Chester-lane, Way's-green came in for discussion, some deep cutting being required in parts. After objections were heard, the enquiry closed to enable the inspector to go over the diFltlict with the sprveser,

div.head: ‘VEETI or MISSION SETIVICES.
div.p: A ‘VEETI or MISSION SETIVICES.

The anntial ltiStionary services connected- with the Fret,: Methodist Churches were preached on Sunday, at high. street Chapel, Winsford, by the Rev. J. Townend, of Roth- dale, returned missionary from Australia, where he laboured abut 20 years. The services were characterized more by fervour than intellectual force : yet there was an old and well-known ring in the truths he uttered. The missionary meeting began with the usual devotions on Monday at the same place, was well attended, and the cause of missions warmly upheld by the chairman, Mr. J. Slater, of Woodford Hall, whose genial remarks bath profited and gave a tone to the speeches following.—The report was read by the Rev. W. J. Hopper, which detailed what Winsford had done in the work as an example to the circuit. A grand feature nicely encouraged is the juvenile branch work; they being able to do a good quarter of what is accomplished in ordinary years, but this year more than one-third throughout the whole dis- trict, i. e. £285 out of £605, and for this amount Winsford and Sandbach raised £75 17s. 6d., while the juveniles raised £23 2s. 11d., and Winsford contributed £23 17s. 4d., the youths bringing up £l2 14s. 10!;-d.—Rev. J. Turner (Primi- tive), in an address, said he was glad to be present and con- sidered the time gone when it was needful to defend missionary operations. People regarded them differently to what they did when Carey. in 1792, began his good work at Serampore. He showed there was much done to be glad of, and vet much to accomplish to humble one and stir to great exertion, illustrating the point by a story of Garrett's.— Mr. Townend was glad to bear his testimony to the good work being done, and would speak mostly of what he had passed through as a missionary on the other side of the world. He detailed his trials and perils in New South Wales and Queensland to the evident interest of the young people as well as their seniors.—The Rev. IV. Wright would not inflict a speech at the late hour of the meeting, but simply move a series of votes of thanks to speakers, choir, who had done good service (Miss Buckley accompanied), the young and older collectors, and the chairman.—Mr. Massey seconded, and Mr. J. Hulse supported.—lt being carried with acclamation, the doxology concluded the capital meeting.

On Tuesday the Middlewich meeting was held, the same speakers attending with the exception of Mr. Turner. The sermons by Mr. Bayley, of Crewe, gave great satisfaction. The collections and contributions there amounted to .E 8 3s. 9d.

On Wednesday the Clive meeting was held, at which Mr. Slater again presided, and the great speech of the evening was Mr. Hopper's, but that which delighted most the general audience was Mr. Townend's. The Rev. J. Wright preached on the Sunday previous, when the collections, &c., amounted to £2 Os. Md. On Thursday the first missionary meeting was held at the Mission Room, Over, when not much less than 200 were present, and good speaking and liberal giving was the result. Mr. Wright, of Norley, preached on Sunday, and great results are expected to flow from this mission station.

div.head: WIGAN.
div.p: WIGAN.
The Wigan Town Council resolve(l, at a F!pecial meeting on Monday afternoon, to oppose the live Electric Light Bills now before Parliament.

Local, FAILURE.—A petition for liquidation by arrange- ment or composition with creditors has been tiled at the office of the Registrar of the Wigan County Court, by Mr. J. Wilson, solicitor, King-street, on behalf of Rachael Moly- neux, of GO, George-street, Hindley, recently .carrying on business as a provision dealer, but now out of business. The first meeting of creditors has been summoned to be held at the office of Mr. Wilson, on the 9th prox. THE ABRAM COLLIERY EXPLOSION. The inquiry into abo-,e has been concluded. The jury, after two and a half hours' deliberation, were of opinion that there was a sudden outburst of gas, but how it ignited there was not sufficient evidence to show. There ought to be extra air crossings, for while a sufficient quantity of air paysed into the work- ings, it was impeded in several places. They recommended wick instead of dirt stoppings. There had been a laxity of discipline in re-lighting and re-locking lamps, and they recommended that the key be only accesSible- to the fore- man or other authorized nerse a. They thought Mr. Taylor, the manager, gave his evidence most unsatisfac- torily. At the Wigan Petty Sessions, on Monday, two butchers' assistants, named Thomas Reece and William Gasket!, were n-tFrioned for grosiy iPtreating a cow, Defendants were driving a cow from Haigh to Wigan on Thursday night, and when ncar the entrance to Haigh plantations a constable saw the cow lying on the ground in a very exhausted state, and later on he found defendants with the cow further down the road with its throat cut. Several witnesses spoke to seeing the cow being dragged behind a cart down the road; they heard it groan and saw it kick. The bench characterised the case as a most cruel and disgracefal one, and sentenced Reece to two calendar months' imprisonment with hard labour, and Gaskell to one month's imprisonment with hard labour.

WIGAN COAL AND 111.0 N COMPANY, LIMITED.—The re- port of the directors of this company, the capital of which is nearly £2,000,000, for the half-year ending 31st Decem- lber, 1881, has just been issued. In it the directors say "The output and sales are much greater than last half-year, owing to the work having seen uninterrupted by strikes. There was a brisk demand ,for fuel in the month of Septem- ber. hut since that time the trade has been very languid. The selling prices of fuel were advanced in November, but owing to the subsequent falling off in demand the advanced prices have not been maintained. An advance of 10 per cent. was given to the colliers by the coal proprietors of South-West Lancashire at the beginning of November, when the pros- pects of trade were thought by many to warrant such an important step. The net result in the company's operations in coal and iron is a profit of £35,772 193 3d. This sum, with £230 103 25 carried forward from the last half-year, makes £36,C03 Os 55 available for dividend. Your directors recommend a dividend after the rate of 31- per centum per annum, which will absorb £33,032 Os 10,4 leaving £2,071 2s 7d to he canied forward." In their report the auditors state that there has been deducted for depreciation the sum of £31,240 193 44, whilst the additions' to plant amount to £10,834 18524. The debenture debt has been feduced by the sum of £32,543 178 Gd falling due and paid off within the half-year. A dividend has been paid during the half- year absorbing £9,048 123 Gd, towards which a sum of £1,500 was withdrawn from the reserve fund. The uiffer- encededncted from the disposable balance of 30th June last left £230 lOs 21 to be carried forward. The sum of £l,OOB 103 85 has been written off for loss on bad debts, and after providing for interest on debentures amounting to £4,324 16s 3d, the net profit is £35,772 19s 3d.

div.head: FARNWORTH PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: FARNWORTH PARISH CHURCH.

On Monday evening, the annual congregational tea party in connection with this church was held in the girls' school- room. There was a large attendance at tea, and the follow- ladies presided at the tables :—Mrs. Cross, Miss Cross (for Miss Meacock), Mrs. Hunter, Mrs. Wareing, Miss Lea, Mrs. Longton (Cronton Hall), Miss W. Longton (Milton-road), Mrs. Valentine, Mrs. Kershaw, Mrs. Lewis, Miss Grace, Miss Radcliffe, Mrs Barlow, Mrs. Carey, Mrs. Baker, Miss Riding, Mrs. Bond, Mrs. Ingham, Miss Whalley, Mrs. Hibbert. At the entertainment afterwards held Mr. John Brock, J.P., pre- sided, and the room was well filled. Songs, glees, pianoforte solos, dr.c., were given by Miss Bend, Miss Ida Bond, Mrs. Purver, Mr. Henry Lea, Mr. Cropper, the Farnworth Glee Party, and others. The Farnworth Negro Troupe also gave a performance.

The CeraertmaN, in opening the proceedings, said this waS I an occasion when they might appropriately review the events of the past year and take counsel as to the work for the future. During the past 12 months there had been one or two events of great importance to the parish. There had been a change of pastors. Many of them could go back in memory some 12 or 14 years, when the Rev. William Jeff was vicar of Farnworth, and whose name could not be men- tioned at a meeting of Farnworth parishioners without calling up feelings of reverence and respect for his memory. (Applause.) Mr. Jeff laboured there for 40 years zealously and well, until increasing age and infirmities obliged him to resign the charge. He did not long survive his retirement. Soon his Master called him home to rest, and he was gathered in like a shock of. corn fully ripe. (Applause.) To him succeeded the pastor who bad recently left them. When Mr. Holloway came to the parish, from causes which could not be avoided, the agencies at work were by no means com- mensurate with the increase of population and the extent of the parish. He set himself zealously to increase and im- prove those agencies, and he worked hard and well in the parish. He established the present capital schools at Bold., and then very soon he had the church extension scheme en his hands, which he did all he could to promote. In many ways he had left behind him an enduring remembrance in solid work, and he was sure he was expressing the feelings of all present, when he said that they hoped, they prayed, that God would abundantly bless him in the new sphere of labour whither he had gone. (Hear' hear, and applause.) He should like for a moment to speak about another work . that had been accomplished in the parish, which was com- menced and almost completed in Mr. Holloway's time ;—he meant the new church at Halton View. It was the original intention to build that church much less than it was, but the good people at flatten View saw that it would be a great mistake to build the church half its present size. They would have had an ugly building, and .one which would have been by no means large enough for the wants of the parish. (Hear, hear.) The building committee had expended as much money as they legitimately could, but they offered to build the church the full size according to the original plans, if the Halton View people would guarantee £lOOO. Fhey gave that guarantee most nobly—(applause)—and they collected about £BOO, But £2OO was still wanted, and the question was how to obtain that sum. It was suggested that a baz tar would successfully accomplish the desired end. The suggestion was adopted and they set to work at the hazier which was .held in November last in the Volunteer Hall. He was happy to be able to tell them that the nett proceeds of the bazaer,after paying all expenses, was ;2480 (Applause.) That at once paid off the balance of the gua- rantee fund, and the interest accruing, and had left in hand -P250, which would be required to furnish a repair fund, which was necessary before the church could be cense- crated ; so that not only was the church entirely free from debt, but there was in hand a sum of money which would remove one great difficulty in the way of the consecration of the church. Following Mr. Holloway they had their active vicar, Mr. Bond. (Applause.) He was glad to hear that responsive clap, because it told him that they sympathised with Mr. Bond in his weak, and believed, as he did, that he l was thoroughly earnest in working the agencies of the parish. Me. Bend Lee', eaine front e gentry dietrint where : the work was not nearly so onerous as it was at Farnworth, and he would need ali their assistance—(hear, hear) ;—and he wished to ask them specially that light, to extend to ele, Bend the right hand of fellowship, and to aid him in every Inze.4l they ressibly could. The working of a parish ought newer to bd left entirely in the hands of the clerey. The laymen and laywomen had quite as much duty to per- form as the clergy, and they could assist the clergy very ' greatly. If they were not in earnest the parish would cer- tainly suffer. there were a number of interests in the parish which might very well taken out of the hands of the clergy. He did not know whether the clergy would agree with him in his views, but his opinion was that the clergy ought to have nothing to do with the finance of the parish. (Hear, hear.) He thought it ought to be in laymen's band, and that all the care ofe getting money for parish work should rest with the laymen of the parish. (Applause.) There had recently been formed a finance committee to en- deavour to raise funds to discharge the debt on the Curates' Fund, and to raise for that fund a regular income in the future. He was very glad to say that so far the parish had responded fairly to that fund, and he thought that presently they should not only be able to wipe off the debt, but be able to place the fund on a much more sound and proper footing than it had hitherto been. (Applause.) There were many agencies in the parish, perhaps many that he could not recollect and enumerate, but he would impress . upon them this fact—that the work of the parish was as much the work of its lay members, in many of its depart- ments, as of the clergy; and if they held aloof from in- teresting themselves in the work, they would go far to spoil and nullify the efforts of the clergy. Mr Bond's SUCCCSS and that,of his curates would be measured by the aid they gave them. He urged the young people to throw them- selves heart and soul into the work, and said he was sure they would be heartily welcomed by Mr. Bond and his curates. If there was anything they thought they could eo to forward the cause of Christ in the place, they met not wait to be asked, but volunteer. (Hear, hear.) Do • the thing from spontaneous and hearty good will. (Applause.) The VICAR (the Rev. G. Bond) who was warmly received said that was the fullest, and perhaps the most successful gathering there had been in the parish since he came. He was truly and sincerely thankful to Mr. Brock, for the kind manner in which he had spoken of him, and still more for the wayin which he had spoken of Mr Holloway. He could only tell them that he had found the work so great, that if ever they found any deficiency in his predecessor, they must lay it on the work and not on him. There were certain things he had done far better than he (Mr. Bond) should; and if by any means he could tread in his footsteps, or arrive at the pitch or standard which he attained, and leave the parish with no worse name than he had, he should be very thank- ful. They must not count a man happy till the end. It was all very well to begin ; new brooms swept clean, and the novelty had a certain attraction ; but they meat wait for results, and see how things worked. He had been received with the greatest kindness, and he felt the greatest encourage- ment for the future. Everything seemed improved in many Ways. His predecessor had come forward and aided him very much. He congratulated them on the success of the party—a large congregation of people from all parts of the parish, which was fivemiles wide, he believed, and contained less than 10,000 or 11,000 people. They must not expect them to see all the parishioners at once. They intended to see all that they could do, but they must not expect too much. Their heart was right, their intentions were good, but they could not fulfil them at once; they meant to do so by-and-bye. (Applause.) Tea parties were new to him, but he considered them a capital institution, as the gathering together of the members of the church for one object, could not fail to be productive of good results. They had all their own work to do, their own salvation to work out, and they must try to do R. He asked them to help the clergy bear with them, and if they thought themselves neglected,if here and there they did not speak so kindly as they should, re- member they were all fallible. If they were not appointed exactly to the offices they should like, let them wait their time. It was in God's hands, and the day would come when they would find some office more to their taste. If anyone would come forward and offer his services a place would be found for him. Why should not the Church of England utilise its members like Dissenting churches? One of their great points was to find an office for everybody. The Church of England had plenty of offices and work to do, and on the anniversary of that day he hoped they would have not only more workers but better results. (Applause.) He believed they should get £3O from that play, and he begged to thank the subscribers and the lailiea who Ind presided at the tables. Referring to the Curates' Fund, the Vicar said he was one of the first to move in that matter, and the committee of four which had been appointed had discharged their office most successfully. All the arrears were wiped out, and they should have a nice fund so as to keep their two most efficient curates at work for the future. (Applause.)- This was very satisfactory. The district visitors—a new institution—bad not yetecorn- menced work, in consequence of their time having been so fully occupied with other things. There were lots of people who did not attend the church, but he thought the work of the tract distributors would do a great deal to remedy this, and induce people to attend church regularly. There was no reason why the church should not be filled, and from what he had seen lately, he believed it would soon be so. The collection on the previous Sunday was £2 more than it had tonally been. (Applause.) He was not all satisfied with the number of communicants, and there were a great many earnestly minded people present who did not attend the Lord's Supper, which every Christian ought to do. He urged them strongly to do so. On the motion of Mr. EUSTACE CARRY, a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to the I Idles who had given their services that evening, and the meeting subsequently ter- minated.
MessrsjSutcliffe and Son's corn mill, Rochdale, was des- troyed by fire on Thursd.ty morning. The loss is estimated at £60,000.
