div.head: CONSERVATISM AT WIDNES.
div.p: CONSERVATISM AT WIDNES.

The Widnes Conservatives held their annual tweeting on Monday evening. Major Cross presided, and there were also present :—Mr. J. Croston, J.P., Manchester, who was an- nounced to lecture on the "Blunders of the Gladstone , Government," the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, Messrs. John , Matthews, R. Lewis, James White, J. B. Imison, J. Craw- ford, Dwerryhouse, Palm, J. A. Bullough (secretary), itc. Mr. BELLO-UGH read the report, which gave a history of the were; of the Association during the year. The following are the concluding remarks of the somewhat singular docu- raent :—" Meetings have been held in the township of Widnes to carry on the work of registration, and your com- mittee are satisfied, that as a result of the year's working, there is a steady growth of Conservatism'in the towns. Not- withstanding the great efforts of the local Liberals at the late Revision Court, they failed to shake the majority of Conservatives upon the voting lists. The result of the late revision shows a gain to the Conservatives of 19 voters' names upon the list, and a gain of 2 in the actual voting strength of the party. This statement is fully borne out by the new and revised lists which came out last month. The Conservative majority in the polling district of Widnes is now close upon 90 voters. Your committee hope that all Conservatives in the polling district will become subscribers to the funds of the association, so as to aid the committee in the propogation of Conservative principles, and counteract, at least in this district, the growth of Radicalism, combined with Republicanism and atheism." The report was unanimously adopted, on the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. PALIN. ELECTION OF PRESIDENT AND VICE-PRESIDENT. Mr. BRISCOE moved the re-election of Major Cross as president of the Association. In doing so he said he felt that they, as Conservatives, ought to be proud that they had such a gentleman as Major Cross to preside over their Association, and to assist them in upholding constitu- tional principles. Mr. Weaaties TREACY, sen., seconded the motion, which was carried with acclamation. The CHAIRMAN said Ile felt it a great honour indeed to be the President of the Widnes Conservative Association, be- cause he felt they evele doing a good work. The report just read showed that they had a majority of 90, and this was a " majority after giving the other side the benefit of all doubt- ful voters. (Hear, hear.) It was a clear majority on the Conservative aide as opposed to the whole of the Liberals, Radicals, and other nondescripts of whom they knew nothing. (Laughter.) He thought this was a very satisfac- tory state of affairs. They would recollect that at their last meeting he (the chairman) spoke a few words about free trade. The Liverpool Daily Post immediately afterwards wrote a leading article on what he then said, and he was not surprised to find that it began and ended with scurrilous abuse. They could not expect that when Mr. Bright and others called every one who differed from them lunatics, that such a paper as the Daily Post should not follow with the same thine. But it did seem strange that a paper, pub- licked in a commercial centre like Liverpool, could not dis- cuss such a question, which in his (the chairman's) opinion should be discussed temperately and moderately, without in- ' del-ging ie such language. He was not going to drag them all through that leaden-but he sr ould read to them an extract from it and state a fact, and then leave them to judge whether he had been misleading the workingmen of Widnes, or whether it was not the Daily Post who had taken that role upon itself. The following sentence in the leader was used :—" The facts stands thus. Half the quantity of alka- lies made goes to America. America, though its tariffs on many things are very high, lets in some alkalies without duty, and does not charge a high or unreasonable duty on any." Most of those present knew that one of the alkalies manufactured in Widnes was caustic soda. The day that article was written in the Daily Post caustic soda was selling in Liverpool at per ton. It was about the same price now. The duty on that caustic soda when it got to the United States was 1 cents per pound, or close upon £6 per ton, upon an article the original cost of which was LS. Per- haps that was what the editor of the Daily Post called a reasonable duty. (Laughter and applause.) He did not for Oge moment go back from what he had said, which was, that sooner or later the question of Free Trade must be taken up, and that they must protect their native industries. (Ap- plause.) They perhaps objected to the words he had just lased, "protect their native industries." Now he himself • was a great free trader. He believed in FreeeTrade, but he di not believe in onesided Free Trade—(hear, hear)---and he said if other countries would not give them Free Trade they must try to make them. For 34 years Mr. Bright and his associates had been trying to induce other countries to adopt Free Trade. What was the result? England stood alone as an advocate of Free Trade. Every other countly followed with protection. Now, why should they not try to bring pressure on other countries to see the benefits of Free Trade? Could anyone doubt for a moment that but for the agitation that was raised about Free Trade there would have been a French Treaty most adverse to the , interests of this country negotiated and settled long ago ? It was only by the persistent utterances of different parties as to fair trade against the Free Trade of Mr. Bright and his friends, that notice was taken of what was proposed to be done with France. The French newspapers, one and all, then and there said, "Let England bluster as much as she likes; she has adopted Free Trade and cannot hurt us." But what was the result to-day? The Government, backed up by what they knew to be public opinion, whatever they might say and bluster about it, had insisted upon modifica- tions, and one and all had said, "We would rather have no treaty at all with France than have a bad treaty." It was quite certain that any treaty that was signed now would be, - at the very least, very much better than it would have been 12 months ago. It was a fact that these were questions in which the working classes of Widnes had as much interest as in anv that could come before them. Why had trade been so bad in Widnes, and why had so many men been idle lately ? He said, a ithout much fear of contradiction, that one of the chief causes had been that the chemicals manufactured in Newcastle which used formerly to go to Germany and other parts of the Continent, had been shut out by very stringent taxes: that these chemicals had been sent to An-ierica. had glutted the American market, which was peculiarly the market of the chemical manufactures, and this had had a great deal to do in causing the bad trade from which they were suffering. He thought he had now said enough on the subject, and would leave the question in the hands of Mr. Croston, who he knew was fully prepared to deal with it. (Cheers.) Mr. Kidd was elected the vice-president of the associa- tion, on the motion of Mr. DWERRYHOUSE, seconded by Mr. TanacY, Mr. DWERRYITOESE havipg thanked the meeting for the ;honour they had done him, Mr. JAMES WHITE moved the following resolution : "That la the opinion of this meeting the policy of the present (4overnment both at home and abroad is opposed to • the best interests of the nation. For peace, retrenchment, and --reform they eive us peace with dishonour ; retrenchment, by -an increase of taxation ; and reform, by a solitary measure of plunder and confiscation, by trying to aragat heists into Par- liament, and by stifling discussion in the House of Com- mons. This meeting therefore pledges itself to use all con- etitutional insane at the next general eluction to return al Conservative Government to power who will give us peace with honour, retrenchment with efficiency, and whose re- forms will be opposed to atheism and democraoy." (Ap- plause.) Mr. White said that the applause of the audience • showed that they were perfectly in favour of the resolution. After eulogizing the abilities of Mr. Cimston as a sound I politician, the speaker briefly reviewed the policy of the Liberal Government during their two years' administration. With reg,aril to the Afghan war he remin led them that one of the policies of Lord Br tconsfield had been to keep Russia from Treat, and how well be had succeeded in that they all knew; but owing to the blundering of the Liberal Government Russia was now 400 or 500 miles nearer I India than ever she was before. The present Ameer of , Afnhanietan was canine- usioa England to assist him, • because he knew his country was not sere, and by this time he (Mr. White) sew the Government must have seen their folly in giving up Candahar. All that the Got ern- ' ment could do was to write friendly despatches to the Cz ir ; bat he took no notice of England, and valued the despatches no more than he did the paper they were written on. • (Cheers.) In the Teensy tat the name of England had been dishonoured and a country given back to a people who were not entitled to it. (A voice, He gave them their own.") Mr. Gladstone them said to the world that he had done it to prevent blood-guiltiness. The country must, hold fast to her colonies. Sims derived much of her strength from these dependencies, and his opinion was the same as that of other politicians, that the country that gave up her colonies was Inst. Mr. White blaomd the present comAition of Ireland on i the Government. The Conservative Government, after six years of peaceful rule, left the country calm and undis- turbed, arid now it ws,s almost in a state or civil w tr. The Government were directly responsihle for scores of murders that had taken place there. awl for out:wages on loyal sub- jects in that country. He charged the members of the •Cabinet with inconsistency. He remembered hearing Mr. Bright, in one of his memorable speeches, say that England ought to be governed for 70 inillions a year. This was not . PO at the present day, but it 'a-Ade a great difference when a man held a sinecure office with L 4,000 a year for doing nothing.. Ile felt convinced that a general election would soon turn out of office a Government of blunderers and put in true Conservatives. (Loud cheers.) Mr. B. LEwas seconded the resolution. He remarked that though the Conservatives held the position of only having a small minority in the House of Commons, they would have »oticed with some gratification that before the session of 1882 was twelve hours old the Government had sustained a •- crushing defeat in the Rouse of Commons. (Cheers.) That defeat was brought about by the solid vote of the Conserva- tive party backed by the Home Rulers, who could be very useful sometimes, and also backed up by a very small respect_ . able section of the Liberal party. (Applause.) He trusted that sooner or later the Government would be defeated by a :similar majority, and that when that time came, Mr. Glad- stone amide, as he ought to do, throw up the reins of 'Government. (Applause.) They now saw the Liberal -Government taking Mr. Bradlaugh by the hand and ithtro- aincing him to the House of Commons. Such proceedings -was,not creditable to the Government. If they were sorry when they gave him a qualified and a passive recognition, they were now infinitely worse than sorry when they sup- ported the eetrance into Parliament of an avowed atheist. The greatness of Eng Lend was the Bible and religious teach- ing. and it was the duty of the people to maintain true religious principles and to sustain the connection between Church and State. Mr. Lewis severely censured Mr. Brad- laugh's attempt to over-ride all the rules of the House of Commons 1-y forcing an entrance. (Cheers.) •Elle motion was unanimously carried. .

Mr. CnosToN said they would remember two years ago they were told the country was blessed as it had Sever been blessed before. They were told that they had a Government possessed of all the talents and all the virtues, and they did suppose all the members of that Cabinet—those paragons of political purity, political sagacity and forethought—would have been the men who would have dealt successfully with the affairs of the nation, with honour to the country and with advantage to the people. (Applause.) But he main- tained that in whatever direction they turned they found that it was nothing more than a history of blunder, incom- petence, incapacity, dishonour and disgrace."( Cheers.) They had a Government that could not govern, one that sur- rendered to the most warlike and the most hostile Power in Europe the great advantages that had been gained by the and bravery of British troops. They had sacrificed a part of her enormous dominions, and concluded an ignom- inious peace. They were told that the Conservative policy was a policy of war, but if they referred to the past history of the country they would find that in the last fifty years nearly all the great wars in which the country had been in- volved, bad been caused by the feebleness of the Liberal Ministers, and it was the Conservatives who had gone in and concluded peace. Mr. Croston replied to the remark of a person in the audience, who, during Mr. White's speech, said that the Government had only given to the Boers a part of the country, which was their own, by remarking that the Boers were only half-civilized settlers in the country, to whom the country never did belong. His lecture on the blunders of the Gladstone Government was a sweeping con- demnation of the policy ef the present Cabinet, both in domestic and foreign affairs, the various points meeting with warm•applause from the audience. The usual vote of thanks brought the meeting to a close.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS

Mr. John Ashton (vice-chairman), presided at the fort- nightly of this Board held on Tuesday. Present: The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. James Darbysbire, J Midwood, C. Rigby, J. Challoner, W. Handley, J. Weir, W. Whittaker, J. Highfield, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy cleric.)
'UNJUSTIFIABLE DIET."

A letter was read from the Local Government Board for- warding, for the informatiom of the Guardians, the copy of a communication which the Board had addressed to Mr. R. Jones, master of the Workhouse, on the subject of the dis- allowance made in his accounts for the half-year ended at Lady Day, 1881. The copy letter was as fellows:—"1 am directed by the Local Government Board to inform you that they have considered your appeal against the disallowance of the sum of 19s. Od. which was made by Mr. Dolby, dis- trict auditor, at his audit for the half-year ended at Lady Day, 1881, of the accounts kept by you as master of the workhouse of the Runcorn Union, together with his reasons for making such disallowanceond the correspondence which has taken place in reference to the appeal. The Board find that the auditor has stated his reasons for the disallowance in the following terms In the accounts of Robert Jones, master of the Runcorn Union Workhouse, I disallow 198., viz, 15s. for three couples of ducks, and 4s. for three couples of fowls said to have teen supplied to the officers of the work- house. Because the said ducks and fowls were not neces- sary or justifiable diet for the officers of the workhouse ' • and the Guardians did not by resolution, or otherwise, authorize the workhouse master to purchase the same. Because the said sum of 19s, was unlawfully paid and charged upon the funds of the Runcorn Union.' It appears that the sum in question was paid for ducks and fowls purchased for consumption by cer- tain officers of the Workhouse. As you appear to have no -sufficient authority from the Guardians to purchase the articles referred to, the Board are of opinion that in disallow- ing the sum in question the auditor arrived at a lawful , decision. They are prepared, however, in the present in- stance to remit the disallowance in the exercise of the equitable jurisdiction conferred upon them by the 11 and 12 Vict., cap. 91, sec. 4, and they enclose a certificate to that effect in pursuance of the 29th and 30th Vict., cap. 113, sec. 5. The voucher forwarded by you is returned here- with." The DEPUTY CLErtit: If 111 r. Jones wants ducks and fowls in future he must ask the Guardians for an order.
Mr. RIGBY : Who has to pay for these? The DEPUTY Cr.EnK : It has been paid by the Board. Mr. RIGBY: Then if he wants any fowls he is to bring it before us?

The DEPUTY CLERK : Yes, to put it on the books. Mr. RiGny : And very proper, too. (Laughter.) It is very nice, I know, and fowls are very " grasy " and feed remarkably well. But I think the master ought to consult the Guardians about these delicacies. It is a piece of ex- travagance on his part to order them. Mr. WEIR: Perhaps it was Christmas time. Mr. RIGBY : Well, there was plenty of roast beef and plum pudding; why did he not get "a feed " on that?

div.head: RUNCORN PAY STATION.
div.p: THE RUNCORN PAY STATION.

A letter was also iead from the Local Government }bard acknowledging the reee;p.t of a letter forwarding for approval the draft of a lease of a house No. 111, Church- street, Runcorn, proposed to be hired by the Guardians for seven years as a pay station. The writer pointed out that it would be necessary for the Board to issue an order authorising the hiring. They would accordingly send the requisite form of order and consent for the signatures of the Guardians. The Board directed the writer to add that no steps should be taken to complete the hiring until the Board had issued their order and approved of the draft lease.

STATE OF TIIE HOUSE. The MASTER (Mr. R. Jones) reported that there were 191 inmates as against 173 in the corresponding week of last year. Of 9 vagrants relieved during the week, 3 were men, 3 women, and 3 children. There were 30 boys and 27 girls in attendance at the Workhouse school; and 12 boys and 20 girls receiving industrial training. Out-door relief had been administered to 645 persons at a cost of £62 15s. 6d. (Runcorn £34 19s. 61, Frodsham £l5 is. 6d., Budworth £l2 14s. 6d ) as compared with 631 persons relieved in the corresponding week of last year at a cost of £63 13%. id.

div.head: PRESCOT SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: PRESCOT SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of the Prescot School Board was held on Monday evening at the board-room, Derby-street, Mr. W. L. Evans, J.P., presiding. There were alse present Messrs. J. Wycherley, J. J. Brown, and T. P. Hewitt; with Mr. H. Cross (clerk) and Mr. W. Lloyd (attendance officer. —The minutes of the previous meeting were read and confirmed.

div.head: MONTHLY RETURNS OF ATTENDANCE AND FEES.
div.p: MONTHLY RETURNS OF ATTENDANCE AND FEES.

From the report of the attendance and fees at the schools, a copy of which was placed before each member, it appeared that during the past month, in the boys' school, the average attendance had been 148 as compared with 168 in the corres- ponding period of last year; number on the roll, 27, last year, 230; fees, £ll 10s. 3d., last year, £9 121. sd. Girls' school—average attendance, 76, corresponding month last year, 75 ; number on the roll, 119, last year, 113; fees, £6 7s. 10.1 last year, £5 15s. 11d. Infants' school—average attendance, 58, corresponding month last year, 77; nnmber on the'roll, 98, last year, 144; fees, £3 4s. id., last year, £3 15 lid.—ln the course of some desultory conversation respecting the attendance at the infant school, Mr. BROWN olyierved that of late the attendance of scholars had been affected by whooping cough. , When he was sitting on the attendance committee, there were frequent explanations by parents to the effect that their children had been kept from school owing to fever, or whooping cough or something of that sort, being prevalent in their families.—Mr. WYCHERLEY remarked that the avetage attendance was quite as high as tha Board could expect, considering the number on the roll. —The CHAIRMAN said he was glad to see an increase in the amount of fees received in the boys' school, Athough the numlier of scholars on the roll and the average attendance were not so large as last year.—The ATTENDANCE OFFICER remarked that a great many scholars who attended Mr. Lightfoot's school, resided just outside the board's district, and he had no authority over. them —Mr. BROWN said that the attendance might improve now that an additional at- tendance officer had been appointed by the Guardians.—The CHAIRMAN remarked that there were 35 children in the neighbourhood of New Brighton who were irregular in their attendance at school.—lt was resolved that the Clerk write to the Attendance Committee of the Union calling their at- tention to the matter, and stating that the Board's attend- ance office would be willing to give their officer any information about the children. ATTENDANCE OFFICER'S REPORT.

Mr. Wm. LLOYD reported that since the last meeting of the Board he had visited the parents of 223 children, who had been abs-.nt from, or irregular in their attendance at school, and in CA3:I where no excuses were given he had warned them. He had served notices upon 45 of those parents. Of the six summonses he was ordered to take out at the committee meeting on December 21st, five were heard on the 7th inst., the usual fine of 'ss. being inflicted in each case. In the case of the remaining one he was informed on making subsequent inquiries that the mother and boy had been sent into the workhouse the day previous to the com- mittee meeting. He therefore took no further steps in that case.

div.head: APPLICATION FOR INCREASE OF SALARY.
div.p: APPLICATION FOR INCREASE OF SALARY.

A letter was read from Mr. J. Guy, of Thatte Heath, stating that his daughter had been in the Board's service for twelve months, on the 17th January last, and had re- ceived no advance in her salary this month. He begged to call the Board's attention to it. The agreement as he under- stood it was that his daughter should have an advance at the end of each year's service. He was sorry to state that she had found the walk from Thatto Heath to Prescot and back too much for her, which had necessitated his getting her a season ticket per rail. If the Board could possibly allow her a little towards travelling expenses he would be greatly obliged.—ln answer to a question, the CLERK said the agreement was that Miss Guy should have Ms. per month for the first year, and an increase of 4s. 2d. per month in each succeeding year.—After a short discussion, the sub. int was postponed till the next meeting for further con- sideration.—Accounts amounting to £54 ss. were certified for payment, and cheques were drawn to that amount.

There is nothing more nourishing and warming in cold weather than a cup of really good Cocoa, but the difficulty has been to obtain it pure. This may be secured at a cost of ono halfpenny for a large breakfast cup by using Cadbury's Cocoa Essence, which goes three times as far as the adulterated and qtarrhy compounds ordinarily sold, the smallest packet making fourteen breakfaat cups of strong Oocoa.—Advt.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 25, 1882. UNITED KINGDOM ALLIANCE.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 25, 1882. UNITED KINGDOM ALLIANCE.
MEETING AT RUNCORN.

On Monday evening, a successful meeting was held in Bethesda Congregational school-room, Runcorn, under the auspices of the United Kingdom Alliance. There was a good attendance. The Rev. George Hack (Wesleyan Methodist) presided, and there were also on the platform Messrs. J. R. Frith, George Bellamy, S. B. Chadwick, and John Paton (one of the agents of the Alliance), who was announced to lecture on " The Liquor Traffic—a Poacher on the Domain of Labour." The drum and fife band belonging to the MerseY Missions to Seamen were also present, and during the evening gave several selections in a very spirited style. The CHAIRMAN having opened the picceedings with prayer, said that though he was not accustomed to presiding over public gatherings of such a nature, he was right glad to be anything or to do anything in connection with the noble work of temperance. He felt pleased that the friends of that movement in Runcorn had taken him by the hand, as the charm of his life was to do good. The work which engaged their attention that evening was surely greater than ques- tions winch were associated with sanitation, and the preser- vation of life, for there was nothing in pestilence or famine comparable with the evils of intemperance. Many people were under the impression that the vast preparations which had been made for war on the continent of Europe, in the shape of great standing armies, was the greatest curse of the 19th century; but he felt bound to say that there were no evils in connection with war which could parallel the evils to be found associated with the drink traffic. Therefore they had a right to call the temperance enterprise a great one. There were one or two things in connection with their work to-day which were very encouraging. One of these was that it was rapidly becoming respectable, and was being lifted out of the position it formerly occupied, when the believers in it were sneered at. The temperance movement had now got into the church, and amongst the foremost advocates of it were such men as Canon Farrar and Canon Wilberforce. (Applause.) He was not one of those who saw no good in the Roman Catholics. He, therefore, hailed the fact that Cardinal Manning was the foremost in the work of trying to rescue men from the effects of drunkenness. They were proud that this movement had managed to get into the Conference, and when a thing got into that body, they might depend upon its rarely getting out until some practical result was arrived at in regard to it. Temperance had also been lifted into what they might call a practical political question. This was evident from the fact that the publicans were in such a state of alarm to-day, that they were actually talking of sending forth tracts (or something of a similar character), for the purpose of replying to the arguments put forward by the advocates of total abstinence. He should like to see the arguments which could be put for- ward to show that the drink traffic was good for the country. This question had now got into the House of Commons, and they might depend upon it that it would never be allowed to rest until its friends carried before them their victorious banner, having succeeded in putting into effect the principles of local option. (Applause.)•

Mr. J. R. FEmt remarked that he was not ashamed to stand forward as one of the advocates of local option, or what was formerly known as the Main Liquor Law. Some few months ago, he had the pleasure of introducing into their local House of Commons (the parliamentary debating society), a measure for the suppression of the liquor traffic, by putting into the hands of ratepayers in towns the power of sayino, whether they should have a licensing authority, or abolish the drink trade altogether. The speaker then gave several instances of evil connected with the liquor traffic, which he had personally witnessed in Runcorn. Their gaols and workhouses were filled through drunkenness, and who had to suffer? The ratepayers, for such places were closed in certain towns in the world where no drir,k was sold, because there was no one to occupy them. The present system of granting licenses in this country had proved a failure, and the powers exercised by the licensing justices ought to be put into the hands of the ratepayers. (Loud applause.) They knew it was a fact that if a memorial was got up on this question, and presented to the in4strates, au i they did was to smile at it and not take any notice of it in a practical shape. If the sale of intoxicating drink were abolished, it would no doubt be a great loss to some, but it would be a great blessing to thousands. He had pleasure in moving "That this meeting, being impressed with the evils of the liquor traffic, pledges itself to do its utmost to support a parliamentary local option measure, in- vesting the people with power to veto the renewal of licenses." (Loud applause.) Mr. GEORGE BELLAMY seconded the resolution. Mr. PATON, who was received with applause, then de- livered his lecture, and observed that lie should dwell upon the development of our national, character as illustrated in industrialism. Until our national character was developed, there was no industry in the sense in which industry was now undeistood. He wished them to think of that fact, and he did not know if there was a greater fact that a patriot or Christian could confront. Slavery was crushed in the past because it was in antagonism with free labour. They got their science from the Greeks, and their law from the Romans, and he should tike to submit this fact to them, that these nations did not exist for nothing, ani neither did England exist for nothing. (Cheers.) In the providence of God these nations existed that they might have an in- fluence. A friend of his once directed his attention to some pieces of stone lying on the shore, near Jarrow, on the river Tyne, and said these were ships in process of develop- ment. The Ptealnships that sailed the ocean were developed

iron-stone. Let them take Glasgow for an illustrati )11. Seventy years ago the Clyde was unnavigable, and now it was one of the greatest entreptlis of trade in the world, and this was because Glasgow was nearly related to iron and coal fields, and had a people which, in the providence of God, were endowed with that, practical degree of brain which enabled Adam Smith to write his " Wealth of Nations." The city of ielasgow had risen from a population of 100,000 to one of 700,000—(applause),—not a pauperised, ignorant, or dependent population, for the skilled labour of the Clyde, like the skilled labour of the Mersey and the Tyne, was as independent as a man who did not toil, but depended on the interest of money. Why was this? Because a ship had vast value in labour, in usefulness, and in relation to the general and individual good. When he said general good, he meant the good of humanity, because the good of the savage districts of the world was as much involved in shipbuilding as the good of those who lived on the Mersey or the Tyne. Let the Irish believe it or no, we were one people, and this result had been brought about by the intercommunication which had resulted from steamboats. If the marvellous communica- tion that had been established between the various parts of the world were not begetting brotherhood, it was breaking down the barriers which formerly made brotherhood impos- sible. (Applause,) In order that men should love each other, it was necessary they should know each other. The men whom they knew least, they hated the most; those they knew best they loved most. (Applause.) He would make a prediction to this effect, that because of the constant and easy access which there was between England and America there would never be a war between those nations, but, in all probability, they would become one grand English-speaking people, with one great source and one grand aim. This was the 'eTed which Came from indus- trialism. In proportion as Rome conquered and enslaved the nations of the world, she killed the goose which laid the golden eggs. But the industrialism of England was of this character—the more they practiced it the more it gave, on the principle that there was to be no end to the resources of labour. Our industrialism was intended to pay, but there was no idea of this when the pyramids were built. The speaker spoke in scathing satirical terms of the work of Smyth, the Scotch astronomer, on the pyramids and their relation to the future history of the race, as shown by singular measurements of their various passages. The history of nations clearly proved that, like individuals, they had had their besetting sins, and when they had neglected to grapple with them, they had comeourpursuednational toi oaannas iernd diul , at yar s?c wo uolrvusleed. b be v he ed htgaott w ta religion c ie tltehi tahta nwi Englandsp stultifyingh il osi of p philosophy, ye, and we had fallen heir to all the industries of tle past. The drink trade was the besetting sin of England just as slavery was the besetting sin of Greece and Rome. The vices which arose out of the drink trade of thie conntry were debasing our moral character. The largest distillery in Europe was in the beautiful city of Edinburgh. In this establishment there were 150 men employed, who were all 103. a week chaps. (laughter) whereas in one linen works in Dundee 5,000 men were engaged. It did not re- quire skilled labour to produce whiskey. " Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging, and he who is deceived thereby is not wise," and not to be wise was to be foolish. (Laughter.) That statesman who maintained the drink traffic as a means of taxation, was, practically, as big a sinner as the Roman emperors when they conquered the world and reduced it to slavery. If shipbuilding, cotton spinning, the woollen trade, and all our various industries, were to give as little employment for the outlay of £2,000,000 of money as the whiskey trade did, our po-pula- tion would be reduced to 2,500,000 in three years. A poli- tical partizan cried "Crotchet monger" to a mart like him. Let them just think of that big head of his with a crotchet in it !" (Laughter.) He was sure that some of the heads of these partizans were so small that they would not take in a crotchet ; but every man who had an idea in his head which had saved his nation from a damning evil, wane called a crotchet monger. (Applause.) The grain used in the distillery was not devel- oped like the ironstone on the side of the Tyne, but it was destroyed, in order to evolve a substance the only outcome of which was intoxication; and still we called ourselves a Christian people! He did not say they were unchristianised by this conduct, but they were very shaky Christians. The lecturer then sketched the rise of the middle chase, and the action of Walpole in respect to taxing liquor. Now we derived from this drink trade £122,000,000 a year out of our industrialism, and men called this statesmanship! He, and those who agreed with him' called it wickedness and boughttd m them three stupidity ! It must be so, for .I.oohstetimedßri. y Bright h ad that of every four loaves they n of them from the foreigner, though they used 80,000,000 bushels of grain each year in order to produce liquor. Our Heavenly Father had, if he might use the expression, co- worked with them in their industrialism. in such ways as producing coal in natere, and developing it up to the point in which it was fit for our faculties to turn it to our use, but He did not make the grain to be thus used. God made the grain perfect, and adapted to the human body in every respect: but men frustrated the Giver of all Good, by mak- ing the grain into a substance which deetroyed men, soul and body. (Applause.) Mr. Paton concluded by supporting the resolution, which was passed unanimously. On the pioposition of Mr. S. C. BECEERT, seconded by
Mr. BOYLE, it was resolved that copies of the resolution should be sent to the Prime Minister and the Home Secre- tary.
A vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Paton, on the motion of Mr. SHAW, seamen's missionary, after which the proceed- ings terminated.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. George Pilkington. BREACH OF THE PEACE. Michael Flood and John Starkey were charged, the former with having been drunk at Widnes, and the latter with committing a breach of the peace, on the previous Sunday. P.C. Anderson said he saw Flood drunk in the street, and Starkey was swearing and making a great noise.—Starkey remarked that Flood was charged with being drunk, but the police said he (Starkey) was not so, although he had had eight pints of beer.—The Inspector of Police said this was Starkey's 20th appearance at the court, and Flood was also an old offender.—Flood was fined ss. and costs, and Starkey ordered to enter into sureties, himself in £lO and two in .£5 each, to keep the peace three months, with the usual alternative.

-WEDIIESDAY.—Before Messrs. E. K. Muspratt (chairman), and George Pilkington. THE Scuoor, BOARD AT WORK. Several people were summoned by the Widnes School Board, who were repre- sented by Mr. G. H. Danby, their clerk, for not sending their children to school. The cases were proved by the school attendance officers Davies, Woods, and Joynson, and each defendant was ordered to pay 55., including costs. WILFUL DAMAGE.—John Martin was fined ss. and costs for committing damage to property belonging to Elizabeth Hall, on the 11th inst. THE LANDLORD OF THE GROSVENOR HOTEL FINED £lO AND COSTS.

Mr. Isaac Sankey, proprietor of the Grosvenor Hotel, Victoria-road, was summoned,firstly for permitting drunken- ness, and secondly, for having his house open during pro- hibited hours.—.3.lr. Bremner, of Liverpool, defended.— Sergeant McGregor said that on the night of the 31st ult , he was passing defendant's premises, at about twenty minutes to twelve, when he saw a conveyance standing in Market- street, near the back door of the house, which was open. Hearing a eumber of people talking inside the building, be, with Police-constable Ormeroci, entered the yard by the wicket door of the large gates, and found that the back door of the hotel was also open... They went into the kitchen, which was empty, and next walked into the bar parlour, in which were seven men, the landlord, and his son. There were three glasses of beer and a glass of spirits upon one table, and on the other a glass of spirits. One of the com- pany, whose name was John Travis, was "far gone in drink." He asked the landlord Low he accounted for the company being in the house at that time, rand he said they were traveller'. Mr. Sankey, in reply to other questions, said the men had entered the hotel a little before 11 o'clock: He (witness) took the names of those present, and defendant said "These are friends of mine, and they have come from Rain- hill." One of the defendant's family also remarked "They are friends of ours, come to stay all night," on which Mr. Sankey observed" That is so." He told defendant that he should report him. A conveyance then came up, and it was backed into the yard, and the gates !hut. Having left the house, he listened at the front, and heard some one go into the vault-, who made a noise as if drawing beer. This person went into the vaults, and, on his return' threw some money into the drawer. After being joined by Sergeant Robinson, he (witness) heard some one jump into the con- veyance ; the back door was opened, and he saw a four wheeled drag taken out of the premises, in which the com- pany who had been in the house drove away.—P.C. Ormerod and Sergeant Robinson gave evidence in corrobora- tion.—Mr. Bremner. for the defence, said that on the night in question a billiard match had been held at defendant's; and a man named Foster, who had been invited by Seenkey's son to attend the contest, had taken with him a few friends. Immediately before eleven o'clock alt the remaining com- pany, except Feeler, went out for the purpose of getting into the wagonette, fo drive home, when Mr. Sankey's son asked them to re-enter the hotel, and have something to eat and drink. They did not pay for what was afterwards sup- plied to them, and the question for their worships to con- sider WeilM be whether defendant waenet justified in giving his friends some enlettaintnent. Mr. Safikey had ilea in Widnes many years, and, with the exception of being fined 20s. and costs, some ten years since' he had never offended against the terms of his license. Not one word was said by Sergeant McGregor when he entered the house, as to Travis being drunk. In fact, all the drink that the men in ques- tion had had was some lemonade.—Defendant was called, and said that on the night in question there had been a billiard match at the houseeand a Mr. Peter Foster, of Bain- hill, who was a friend of his son's, was there. Immediately before eleven, Foster prepared to leave, and the wagonette was drawn up for that purpose. His son invited Foster and his friends to stop and have a little supper, and they agreed to do so. The house was closed, with the exception of a wicket belonging to he large gate at the back. The drink and food the friends were ;eeovided with was given at his '; (witness's) expense. During the time ~„ had occupied the houv, he had never had a single application to? anything after hours.—The Chairman : That must be a somewhat rare experience !—Mr. Ellis Sankey, SOD of defendant, who manages his father's business, gave corroborative evidence. He maintained that Travis was quite sober, and, he believed, lad not taken any drink for 12 years.—lsaac Sankey, jun., said that on the night mentioned, he saw Mr. Forster and his friends in the bar parlour, and they left about 2 o'clock in the morning. He opened the door to the officer when he came to the house the second time.—Peter Foster, licensed victualler, Rainhill, said he was a guest of Mr. Sankey's son on the 31st ult., and was accompanied by six friends, including the cabman. He was invited to the house for the purpose of witnessing a billiard match. At 11 o'clock, or short'y before that hour, the cab in which he and his friends had come, was waiting outside the house for them. His friends were, however, asked in by the defendant, and the cab was taken into the yard. He was satisfied that Travis was not drunk, for the only drink he had in the house was lemonade. Subsequently the horse was again put into the conveyance, and the trap started, but was stopped by the officers, who asked if the old man (meaning Travis) was in- side it.—James Hubbersty, licensed victualler and brewer, gave similar evidence to the previous witnesses as to the entrance of the police. He added that he was certain Travis was sober.—ln reply to Superintendent Barker, witness said ' they had the bread and cheese after the entrance of the officers.—Mr. John Hampson, manager at the Rainhill Gas Works, also gave evidence for the defence.—Wm. Critchley, file cutter, Rainhill, said he was in the billiard room of the defendant's house at II o'clock, on the night mentioned. He went out because defendant told him it was closing time. The wagonette was then, ready to go, but they returned to the house on the invitation of Mr. Sankey.—By Superin- tendent Barker They got home. about twenty minutes to three. Whilst in Widnes they went to Mr. Tilley's, of the. Norton Arms, but had no drink there.—Frederick Robinson said he drove the party on the day in question,from Rainhill.' to the defendant's hotel. He took out the wagonette at 11 o'clock, hut he was told to put it up again after the police came. Before they arrived he was ordered to take it round into the yard.—Evidence was also given by Thos. Penketh Critchley, which closed the case for the. defence.—The magistrates having consulted, the Chairman said they were of opinion that defendant had unlawfully kept open his lieensed premises for the sale of intoxicating liquors during the -time it ought to have been closed pursuant to the Licensing .Act, 1574. Defendant would be fined £lO and £1 31. costs. As to the second charge, they were of opinion that it had not been absolutely proved drunkenness had been permitted, and, therefore, defendant would be given the benefit of the doubt in respect to that. The magistrates hoped that the conviction would be a warnipg. to him. Mr. Sankey's license would not be etelorsed.—etr. Bremner re- marked that he should like a week to consider, on the part of his client, whether the opinion of a superior court should be taken upon the conviction. Perhaps the Bench would direct their clerk to receive any notice on their behalf.—The magistrates said they would do so.—John Travis, John Hatnpson, Thomas Critchley, Frederick Robinson, James Hubberty, William Critchley, and Peter 'Foster were next charged with being on the premises of Mr. Sankey during prohibited hours. Evidence of a similar nature to that riven in the last case was briefly tendered.—The chairman -'said that several of the defendants were publicans, and must have known the law. It was in the power of the Bench to inflict a penalty of 40s. in each case, but as no drunken- ness had been proved, they would only be fined 10s. and costs each.

ALLEGED SERIOUS ROBBERY FROM A DRAPETe-S, SHOP. —Mary Morley and Ann Dalton, two women, were charged with stealing about 40 yards of tartan cloth, the property of Mr. William Miller, draper, Waterloo-road, between the Ist and the 7th insts.—The prosecutor was called, and said that the cloth, which was worth about £2 55., was seen by him in the shop about the Ist instant.—Catheriee, the wife of James Smith, labourer, Viaduct-street, said she lived next door to the prisoner Dalton, who, on the 3rd instant, saw her and asked her to buy five yards of the cloth, .stating she had obtained it from the prisoner Morley. She enquired where Morley had got it, and was told from a travelling draper who had been at the Central Hotel. Dalton added that Morley wanted to raise money to take a particular article- out of pawn. She bought four yards of the cloth, for which she paid 3i., and on the Bth instant purchased a further amount.—Mr. Wm. Craddick, Church-street, Run- corn, said that on the 9th instant, the prisoner Dalton pawned 12 yards of the cloth at his shop, giving the address Jane Edwards, Duke's-field, the same town. —Sergeant Robinson stated that he apprehended Morley, and, in reply to the charge; she said she bought several yards of the cloth from a Scotehman.--P.C. Thompson stated that on the 15th instant he went to the house of the prisoner Dalton arid asked if Mrs. ?Morley had given her any of the tartan plaid. She replied that she had received four yards from her to pawn. He gave Dalton into the hands of Sergeant Robin- son, who took her to the police station. He (witness) then went to Catherine Smith's. and received from ber 9 yards of the stolen property.—Mr. Hu.ssband, for the defence, argued that the prosecutor did not even say that his client had been seen in the shop.—Each of the prisoners was committed to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions for trial, and bail allowed in the case of Dalton.— Mary Morley was also charge ll:with sealing a pair of boy's trousers, the property of Mr. Mellor, draper, Waterloo-road. between the 20 th and 27th November; and 70 yards of stairs carpet, between the 14ch and 15th insts, the property of Mr. Birchall, Waterloo-road. Mr. Birchall gave evidence as to missing the trousers, and the prisoner was committed to the Sessions upon this charge also.—Mrs.Routledge, wife of an engine fitter and grocer, 63 Church-street, ,said that Morley was a customer of hers, and between five and six o'clock on the evening of the 14th inst., she visited her house, and pro- duced the roll of stair carpeting now produced, with the

object of borrowing 3s. upon it. Prisoner begged of her not to refuse the request, a,7 her husband would murder her if he knew she had pawned his things. She lent her 35., and Morley asked her to keep the carpet in pledge, but she de- clined.-The hearingof this case wasadjourned until Thursday, in order that Mr. Birchall might attend and give evidence. On that day the prisoner was again brought up and commit- ted for trial on this charge also. _

ASSAULT ON A WATCHMAN BY A BURGLAR.--A young man named Peter Riley was brought up on remand charged with being found on the premises of Messrs. Goulding, Davies, and Co., on the 11th inst., for an unlawful purpose. Walter Ray, sterekeeper and watckman at the prosecutors', said that during the night he saw the prisoner trying to conceal him- self on the premises. He turned the light of his lamp upon him, and told him he had no business there. Prisoner then told him that if he did not go away, he would blow his brains out. He replied that if he did not move, he would fetch a policeman, on which Riley picked up a half-brick, and hit him upon the right leg with it, causing a wound. On the following morning, he ascertained that the cc mpany's office had been broken open, two coats stolen, and an attempt made upon the safe. An iron screw key and an iron bar were found in the building.—After Mr. J. W. Coxon, manager at the works, had given evidence, Superintendent Barker stated that the prisoner was an old offender. In 1873 he was com- mitted for trial on a charge of felony; in the same year be was sent to a reformatory for five years, and there were also several minor matter recorded against him. Prisoners was sent to gaol for six months, with hard labour. THEFT BY LADS. Andrew Knockton, John Dolan, Joseph Murphy, and Patrick Cole, all boys, were charged with stealing a pair of boots, the property of Mr. Cookson, of Woolton. The boots were missed by the prosecutor, on the 20th instant, and two days before they were offered in pawn by two of the prisoners to Edgar Valentine Morton, of Garston, who kept the goods and took the names and addresses of the boys, who were afterwards taken into custody by P.C. Peddar.—Murphy was ordered to receive nine and each of the other lads six strokes with the birch-rod. MORE COAL STEALING. Two women named Ellen Martin and Ellen Tallon were charged with stealing 361bs. of coal, the property of Messrs. James Musrratt and Sons, from a coal siding in Anne-street.—Prisoners pleaded guilty, and each of them was sent to gaol one month with hard labour.

div.head: RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Messrs. John Brundrit (chairman) and
div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Messrs. John Brundrit (chairman) and
Alfred Thomas.

THE ASTON FARMER AND HIS SERVANT.—Thomas Bate, farmer, Aston, summoned Win. Worrell, a youth, for wil- fully absenting himself from his service on the 13th inst. Complainant stated that at the beginning of the year, de- fendant entered into a contract of service with him for 12 months, at the rate of £l3 a year. On the 11th inst., defendant left the farm, and he was told to be back by milking time on Sunday morning, but he did not return. until Monday night. When be called Worrell on Tuesday morning, he would not get up, and later on, as he (com- plainant) was returning from his other farm, he met defendant on the road, and asked him when he had to appear at Runcorn. He told him on the following Monday. He had not seen him since, and had to engage a man, at 15s. per week, to take his place. Complainant and defendant now stated that they were mutually agreed to renew the contract, and the Bench ordered Worrell to pay 15s. as compensation and Os. 6d. costs.
YESTERDAY.—Before Messrs: Alfred Thomas and John
Brundrit.

ASSAULTING A POLICE OFFlCER.—Patrick McAuley was charged, under a warrant, with assaulting P.C. Samuel Finney, in the execution of his duty.—The officer stated thßt on Tunday he was taking the prisoner's wife into custody, on a chirge of being drunk in Church-street, when McAuley came up, seized him by the coat collar, and said he must let the woman go.—Ordered to pay 10s. and 14s. cos ts, or, in default, be committed to gaol 14 days.
Before Mr. Alfred Tliomas.

Richard Taylor, a boatman, who had been apprehended under a warrant, was remanded till Monday on a charge of having, on the 22nd inst., feloniously stolen £1 2s 9d, the money of his employer, Mr. Wm. Bate.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

Mr. T. Suttori-Thnmis I,:eaicled at the monthly mceting of the Board held .0n Thursday. The 9ther members present were the Rev. T. Finegan, Rev. S. Clarke, Messrs. Brock, Hartland, O'Keefie, Bradshaw, Shaw, Davies, and G. H. Danby (clerk).

DISTRICT EDUCATION COMMITTEE. This committee reported that during the month of December (four weeks) the cases dealt with by the committee were—applications for paymeht of feces 102, for contraven- tion of the Education Act 233, total 335. Fees were recom- mended to be paid in 89 cases, out of which 13 were refused. There had been 11 prosecutions before the magistrates, and a similar number of convictions were obtained, one child haying been sent to an industrial school. _

On the proposition of the Rev. J. CLARKE, the minutes were a(..:‘,2ted. SC!UOLiiial4iiiofgNT COMMITTEE. The Warrington-road managers recommended that Mrs. H. Harrison be appointed care-taker and cleaner of the Warrington-road schools at a salary of Ss per week, with residence, taxes, water, coal, and gas free; she to provide all materials and labour for the thorough cleaning of the schools. The West Bank managers recommended that Miss Isabella Foster be appointed certificated assistant mistress in the senior girls' department of the West Bank school, at a salary of £5O per annum. The Rev. T. FrNEGAN moved the adoption of the minutes. Mr Sitaw remarked that the cost of teaching in West Bank school was considerably in excess of the amount paid for teaching at Simm's Cross school. He thought the atten- tion of -the School Management Committee should be called to the desirability of putting the schools on the same foot- ing, seeing that the results were better at the school where the expenses were less.

The Rev. I'. FINEGAN said they had taken notice of the matter Mr. Shaw had referred to, but the committee felt their hand were tied. They had, as far as they possibly could, struck off all they thought could be dispensed with. Mr. SHAW said that at Simm's Cross school the cost of teaching was £1,1311 16,. 7d.' and the average attendance was 6'93. At West Bank school the sum paid for teachers' salaries was £1,308 4s. 11d, and the average attend- ance 714; so that for about 21 additional scholars they paid over £2OO more in salaries.—[The CHAIRMAN: £l7a.]—The earnings in the school where they paid the smaller salary amounted to 178. Old. per head against 16s. Hid. where they paid the higher salary. .It might be that the teaching staff required revision, and if that was the case, he thought the School Management Committee ought to have the pnwer to do it. He thought this wasa very favourable opportunity of raising the question whether the committee ought not to re- port onthe teaching staff. at these two schools, a ad endeavour to assimilate the staff at West Bank school to that at Simm's Cross. That seemed to him to be the only feasible way of getting out of the difficulty. The CHAIRMAN thought Mr. Shaw's remarks were very pertinent indeed, and a very good reason ought to be given. why one school with a better class of children should cost more per head than another.
Mr. HARTLAND thought the books might account for the increased cost at West Bank.

The Rev. T. FINEGAN ths.ught the only thing that could be said, if they could take any credit to themselves, was that the school directly under the management of the Board, cost less than the other school.

Mr. BuocK asked if it would be advisable for the com- mittee and the managers to have a conference. The CHAIRMAN said he was sure if the Board thought they could manage the school better, the manager would place their resignations in their hands. The minutes were agreed to. FINANCE.

The Finance Committee—ieended accounts for pay- ment amounting to £371 193. 7d; and intimated that since their last report, the sum of .£lOl 18s. 5:1. had been paid into the bank. The Committee recommended that the resigna- tion of Mr. W. Riley, junior clerk, be accepted; and that another be appointed at a salary not exceeding £3 15s. per Month.
The minutes were c:mtirrneci, on t!)e proposition of Mr. Slaw, and the meeting terminated.
LYMIL

EVANGELISTIC SERVICES AT LYMn. —A series of evange- listic services have been held in Lyrnm. Wesleyan Chapel during the week, and they have been well attended. BEGGING AT LICMM.—Zor this offence Ann Cooper and John Morgan, tramps, were brought up before Mr. I'. P. Norris, at the Lymm Police Court, on Tuesday, and were committed to gaol for 14 days. CONCERT AT 01:GHTRINGTON.—On Monday evening a concert was given in the Schoolroom by St. Peter's choir, assisted by Misses Hall and Pearson, and Messrs. Hawxby, Pearse, and Smith. There was a large attendance, and the vocalists ably acquitted themselves. The concert was given in aid of the funds of the Oughtrington Park Association Football and Cricket Clubs.

BRASS BAND.—A grand tea °arty and ball was given by the members or this band in the Assembly Rooms, on Mon- day evening. About 100 sat down to tea, which was thoroughly enjoyed. After tea the room was cleared for dancing, which was kept up until 11 o'clock. Both the tea party and ball were a grand success, and the proceeds were sufficient to clear off the debt remaining on the new instruments.

SUDDEN DEATH AT LYMM.--Yesterday (Friday) morning, Mr. Coroner Ridgway ,held an, inquest at the Dog Inn, Oughtrington, Lyrnm, on the body of William Downward. 57 years of age, residing at Sandy-lane, Lymm, who died on Thursday under the following circumstances :—For a con- siderable prriod the deceased, who was manager of a spirit vaults, had been subject to piles and pains in the head. On Wednesday morning he went to Liverpool, and when he re- turned about eight on the evening of the same day, be com- plained of his breathing and of a pain in his head. He had some tea and gruel, and at his request his wife purchased some cough mixture, of which he took a dose. rShortly after 8-30 he retired to bed. He was very restless, and be- tween half-past ten and five o'clock the following morning he had four fits. A doctor was summoned, but he did not lttend. At 5-45 on Thursday the man died. Mr. W. P. Brabazon, M.D., who had made a post inortent examination of the body, stated that the cause of death was apoplexy. The jury returned a verdict accordingly.
TWO YOUNG MEN DROWNED AT RUNCORN.

On Tuesday afternoon, a boating accident happened at Runcorn, by which two youb-j men, who were highly re- spected, lost their lives. At plc I::..me of the sad occurrence the river Mersey was in a rather boisietPus condition, owing to the exceptionally high tide, which haJ brought many spectators from the surrounding neighbouthood into the town. Notwithstanding this, Mr. Albert Edward Littler, aged nineteen, a shorthand writer, son of Mr. Charles Littler, master slater, of Greenway-road, and John Williams, 'aged 18, a joiner living in Albert-street, agreed to have a sail in a canoe, which was partly owned by Littler. They started from the ferry slip at about two o'clock. Littler was distinguished by a vein of quiet humour, which occa- sionally cropped out in his literary productions, and whilst passing a number of men employed in connection with the engineering work now being carried out by the Liverpool Corporation, facetiously enquired if they were in want of any herring from the Isle o; Man. This question caused a little laughter amongst the workmen, and one of taliern, not to be outdone in wit, told Littler to convey his love to his mother. From this it is quite evident that the young men were in capital spirits, and thoroughly determined to get as much enjoyment as possible out of their nautical adventure, which, however, ended so disastrously. They went on their journey all right until they reached Cuerdley Marsh, not far from Norton Priory, the residence of Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., at which part the river is very narrow, and the tide consequently runs furiously. Mr. R. M. Brooke, the son of the worthy baronet, was walking through the estate at the time, and he noticed that the canoe in which the young men were seated was going at a most furious and dangerous pace, which Littler was increasing by paddling. He made some observation to them to the effect that their rapid flight through the water was attended with much risk. He turned away for a moment, and immediately afterwards found that they had come to grief. The rough water had proved too much for the craft, which was of remarkably light construc- tion, and it appears probable that it was capsized whilst the deceased were turning in order to return to Runcorn. Mr. Brooke observed that Littler was astride of the canoe and continued to paddle' whilst the other young man was cling- ing to the bow of the boat. Mr. Brooke shouted to the men who were employed on the work for the Liverpool Corpora- tkm to do what they could with the object of rescuing the deceased, and himself tried to launch a boat which was near the scene, but he could not move it. He then went to the stables at Norton Priory, and drove in his trap to the Run- corn Town Hall. Having communicated with Superinten- dent Williamson, the two proceeded rapidly to the Old Quay, with the object of sending out a boat to intercept the canoe as it came down the river. Whilst they were doing this, the boat in which the young men had been seen was observed nearing the Old Quay, but there was no sign of a living creature about it. On Wednesday Littler's body was found in the river, and his companion's on the following day. The occurrence cast a curtain of gloom over the town. Littler was a young man of considerable promise' and much respected in Runcorn. He was connected with Brunswick Wesleyan Sunday school, a member of the Young Men's Christian Association, associated with the order of the Sons of Temperance, and brother to Mr. William Littler, who is at present fulfilling an engagement for the Liverpool Daily Post in the House of Commons. He was a genial, kind- hearted soul, and has for some time been studying in order to take a position in the journalistic world. He has been a very frequent contributor to The Examiner during the past eighteen months.

—On Thursday afternoon, an inquest on the bodies of the two deceased was held at the Runcorn Town Hall, before Mr. Ridgway, county coroner, and at the close of the enquiry a high compliment was paid to Mr. Brooke on the efforts he put forth to rescue the deceased from their perilous posi- tion.

Mr. Charles Littler, master slater, Greenway-roid, gave evidence as to the identity of his son's body. He last saw deceased alive about nine o'clock on Tuesday morning, when he was sitting at the pianoforte playing "Almost per- suaded." He (witness) then went to his work. His son seemed in good spirits. Deceased was joint owner of the catioe. When he returned home from Liverpool he asked where Albert was, and was told he had one upon the river in the vessel unrres§ed rtgret ?,t hi! 5g tha tides were so high. Before lea,Thg, the deceased told his mother and sisters of his intention to visit the river. De- ceased could swim moderately well. Mr. Thomas Williams, 31, Albert-street, deposed that he was a waterman' and the deceased John Williams was his son, who formerly lived with him, and was a joiner. De- ceased was 19 years of age in November last. He (witness) returned from Birkenhead on Wednesday morning, in con: scq:rence of being sent for. His son had b:en at home some short ,:me owing to suffering from inflammation in one of his eyes. Qn the day of the accident his relatives at home forbid him to go I.;poo the water, but he persisted in doing so. Deceased could noti swim, did not understand boat- ing, and he had always warned him not to go near the water.

George Wool, Porter-street, Halton-lane,'well sinker, said that about half-past three on the afternoon of Tuesday last, he was working in connection with the Liverpool water scheme on Nerton Marsh, when be saw the two young men pass down the river in a boat, as if they were going to Run- corn. One of them, whom he took to be Littler, was pad- dblng, and there was no sail up. Littler acted as though he were experienced in paddling, and looth he and his coin- said "Do you want any red herrings from the Isle7f Sian ry pile of his (witness's) companions ad i•Ves athl give my to your mother." The tide was on the ebb, icrife running stro p> •7about eight miles an hour. The deceased rt were about 40 :from the side of the river, and in the middle of the streatn; Shortly after Mr. R. M. Brooks, J.P., came to him and the 'r men who were At work, and told ttb, them that two young mew ~-ere in the river, and they were to render them any assittanrs t:.'eY Could. They went to the stream, and a short distanct &low where they were standing SRN a piece of timber, which, at first, the thought was the boat, but it was not.

Mr. William Hurley (foreman:: Was the rfrar rough? Witness: Not so much so as on Monday. , Mr. Littler: As an index to the Om, I may state' ihatrny son's watch stopped at a quarter-part three. Mr. Richard M. Brooke, J.P., said that between three and four o'clock on Tuesday afternoon he was looking at sore repairs which had been dime to the bank below where the pipes are about to be laid iy the Liverpool Waterworks Com- pany, when he saw a boat crossover from the Cuerdley side of the stream towards the shed in which the men are work- ing on the estate. He then observed the pitremely rapid rate at which the men were going—about eight miles an hour—and also that, in addition to the sped at which the stream was carrying the vessel, en t of the persons in it was paddling. Having had some experience in canoeing, be con- cluded that they were in great danger' as the water was breaking over the bows. It was the latter fact that first called his attention to the boat. When it had gone about 100 yards further,, he saw that the men who had been in it were in the water, and the canoe was sinking. He put down the gun which he had in, his hand, with the object of swim- ming to the assistance of the young men, but he found that the tide was running. so very fast that any swimmer would have been. entirely powerless in it. One of the deceased was on the top of the boat,. and continued to paddle, and the other was holding on at the bows. He (witness) shouted and made signs to the young man who was paddling to make an effort to reach a point of land, which there is at this part of the stream, but, though the paddling was continued, in- stead of the vessel getting nearer the side, it went more into the stream. He had previously made some remark to the persons in the boat about the rate at which they were going, but they merely made some jocular reply. As soon as he saw there was no chance of the deceased getting to the land, he ran towards the shed where one of the other witnesses and a number of men were working, informed them of the critical state of the boat, and told them to put a boat: out. They answered that they could not, as they knew nothing of the management of one. He then left them, telling them to do whatever they could to, help the poor fellows,but on no account to attempt to swim, lest they should be carried away by the tide. As the canoe oppeared to fleet very well, he was led to think there might be a chance of rescuing deceased if a boat were sere, out to meet them from the Old Quay at liuncorn. He also tried to move a boat which was lying near where the men were at work in. the shed, but he found it utterly impossible to do so. He next ran to Norton -Priory stables, and drove to Runcorn with a horse and trap. He saw Superintendent Williamson at the Town Hall, and , told him what had happened. He and the superintendent went down to the Old Quay, and they had' hardly got a boat out before they saw the canoe coining down the river, but there was no sign of life in connection, with it. He was of opinion that the "wash" had c 'used the canoe to swamp, and the deceased bad been unable to maintain their hold of the vessel owing to the cold. The canoe would have floated about two miles' when it arrived at the Old Quay. The witness added that just before he turned round to go to the shed he saw that the young man who''was paddling had given up so doing, and one of the young men was at one end of the boat and the other at the opposite end. Samuel Cox, Wilson's-row, labourer, deposed that on Wednesday he was out on Norton Marsh, looking for the bodies. He found the deceased Littler on a bank in the river. Deceased was fully dressed. William Henry Broady, Surrey-street, stated that he was a waterman, and the same morning he _went with Thomas Williams to look for the other young raan. They proceeded , in a boat as far as Cuerdley-marsh, and en the Lancashire side of the river he discovered the body of the young man Williams. The body was fully dressed, with the e sception of a hat.

- The Coroner, in summing up, observed that it clearly ap• peared from the evidence of Mr. Prooke, that the young men were in a most dangerous part of the river, an 4 cold and exhaustion caused the deceased to let go their hold, and so fall into•the water.

The Jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." The Coroner said the jury desired to add the following re • marks to their verdict :—" We desire to record our sense of the very humane efforts made by R. M. Brooke, Esq., J.P., to rescue the youths from their dangerous and ptrilous posi- tion, and to cause every possible assistance to be rendered to them under the circumstances." Mr. Littler said he was glad, on behalf of himself and Mr. Williams, to thank Mr. Erooke for his humane efforts on the occasion.
Mr. Brooke said he wished he could have done more, T 9 IP any swimmer would have been quite helpless in the water at the time.

The Coroner expressed his pleasure that the jury had put on record their feeling in respect to the highly meritorious conduct of Mr. Brooke, who, without doubt, did everything he possibly could to cave the lives of the deseased.
The enquiry then terminated.

ter' The faneral of the deceased Mr. Littler took place Yes„,.. day afternoon, and was of an imposing character. 1 procession left the house of the deceased, in GreenwaY'rea at 3 o'clock, and the coffin was borne by several of bis 13.te_ companions. Several members of the Life Boat Crew of ttle. Sons of Temperance, of which deceased was a member ~Pre ceded the coffin, and they were headed by Mr. John 5,312; son, superintendent of the Brunswick Wesleyan Sann, school, of which the deceased was a scholar, and the /W.' Nowell ; atTed;, address at the latter spot was delivered by Rev. GO' At the request of the relatives, those present afterwards saw the 720th hymn, in Sankey's collection. The burial self of the order of the Sons of Temperance was :read b.! Thomas Faulkner.

In 1881 the attendance officer did not make his appearance in their township in January and February; he attended once in March, omitted April, and came twice in May. He did not make another visit from that month till the 20th of August. After that his visits seemed to be about every fort- night. They understood that the officer came to a township certainly once a month to attend the meetings of the committee, and they understood that on that day he made his particular visits. In the township of Little Woolton he understood from the report of the schoolmaster that the officer visited that locality about every six weeks. The population of Much Woolton consisted of one-sixth of the entire population of the district under the ' jurisdiction of the Union Committee, and they felt that the visitation was inadequate to the requirements of the town- ship which contained something like 1,800 children. It seemed to them of very great importance that another school inspector should be appointed to attend to this work. The feeling of the people of Woolton was that it would be a great advantage if the district was divided and two inspec- tors appointed, and that the men should have for their ex- clusive occupation and business the work of school inspec- tion, and then they would know that somebody was responsible for the work being carried out.—The Rev. Father Prest and the Rev. Mr. Davies having addressed the Board, the deputation withdrew.—After some discussion the motion and amendment were put to the meeting, when the former was carried by a large majority, and the resolution that Mr. Seddon be appointed was confirmed. The examiners for the Boden Sanskrit Scholarship have announced that they have awarded it to Mr. Charles Wynter Payne, jun., student of Christ Church.
